title: I agree with your basic opinion (the pandemic impacted society much more than people acknowledge)…
content:
severlos

:

queeranarchism

:

wrenchinator-central

:

zolltraak

:

Those tags make no sense. ‘Modern society’ did not start in the early 2000s. If this graph showed the loss of community in modern society (it does not), we would see a continuous development since the 1950s at least and probably long before that.

We would also see 'work’ and 'through family’ being less effected because capitalism has maintained these two social spheres. We do see 'work’ rising as a place to meet a spouse in the 1950s to 1980s, coinciding with a growth in the percentage of women in the workplace. But it would be ridiculous to argue that the dominance of work in our life has declined since then, and yet meeting your spouse at work also took a nosedive in the 2000s.

Instead, the decline we’re seeing can be completely, easily explained by the fact that since the 2000s online dating became an easy way to meet people and allowed people to explore, reject and select far more potential partners than ever before. Which says absolutely nothing about the state of community.

It does open up interesting questions. If over 50% of couples meet outside their existing social circles, does that reduce societal segregation along lines like ethnicity and class? Are people more likely to meet a partner outside their own home town and travel to be with them? Does the lower reliance on meeting friends through existing social circles make it easier for isolated individuals to find partners? The data doesn’t show us this but it would be interesting to explore.

Finally, note that this data was presented in this manner by Marriage Pact, a creepy matchmaking organization committed to pushing US college students to get married. It is worth asking where an organization that sees marriage as one of the highest goals in life stand politically and what it seeks to gain by presenting this data?

It’s been said before, and i’ll say it again: I wonder what happened in 2020 to cause people to stop meeting in person. If only there were some globe spanning explanation.


I agree with your basic opinion (the pandemic impacted society much more than people acknowledge) but just like the reaction that I was responding to, your statement is a complete mismatch with the graph. 2020 is the

 last

datapoint in the graph and it doesn’t show a change from the 2000-2020 trend. The data does not show us whether the pandemic impacted dating behaviors. It probably did, but we would need a few more years of data to say anything about that.

author: Unknown
title: Walter Borgius - Die Schule
content:
Katalog Liste aller Texte AutorInnen Themen Letzte Einträge Zur Bibliothek hinzufügen

Mehr Kontakt Material Sticker, Plakate, etc.

Ursprünglich freies Aufwachsen der Kinder.

Der Staat als Wurzel des Gehorsams.

Die spätmittelalterlichen „Stadtschulen“.

Die Reformation und die Schule.

Streben zur Vereinheitlichung des Volkes.

Die Schulen des neueren Frankreichs.

Die Schule als Staatsmonopol. — Die Lehrer als Staatsbeamte.

Schule und Revolution von 1789.

Süverns Entwurf eines allgemeinen Schulgesetzes.

Die Schulfinanzen zwischen Zollmisere und Sozialistenangst.

Kampf Kaiser Wilhelms gegen die Sozialdemokratie.

Militärische Vorbereitung der Jugend.

Die Staatsschule, der Fluch der Kindheit.

Vereinigte Staaten von Nordamerika.

Kollektivunterricht und Individuum.

Die künftigen Formen des Aufwachsens der Kinder.

Das Spiel, die natürliche Funktion des Kindes.

Eingriffe der Schule ins Privatleben.

Die Finanzierung der Neuordnung.

Dr. Walther Borgius' Buch gliedert sich in zwei Hauptteile. Im ersten Teil beschreibt er die Geschichte der Schule und macht darin ihre Funktion als Herrschaftsmittel des Staates deutlich. Im zweiten Teil geht er auf "Grundsätzliches" der Schule ein. Dabei analysiert er verschiedene Schulfächer hinsichtlich ihres Nutzens für den Staat, beschreibt selbstbestimmtes Lernen, fordert die Beseitigung der Schule und zeigt neue Wege auf.

Borgius Thesen und Aussagen sind erschreckend aktuell, bedenkt man, daß das Buch erstmals 1930 veröffentlich wurde. Seine Argumente für selbstbestimmtes Lernen und gegen die Schulpflicht sind auf jeden Fall eine Bereicherung für jeden, der sich diesen Diskussionen stellt. Seine Schulkritik jedenfalls hat nichts an Aktualität eingebüßt.

Damit jene tief eingewurzelten falschen Vorurteile ein wenig gelockert werden, empfiehlt es sich, zuerst einmal der Geschichte des Schulwesens, die ja stets und immer von Schulfachmännern geschrieben wird und daher stets nur in harmloser Gestalt an das Publikum herangelangt, einen kritischen Blick zu schenken.

Wenn die Auffassung vom Paradies, vom Goldenen Zeitalter an der Wiege der Menschheit, dem dann erst unfreundlicher werdende Epochen gefolgt seien, irgendwo richtig ist, dann ist das der Fall für das Leben des Kindes.

Zwar hat man Jahrhunderte lang das Märchen kolportiert, die „Wilden“ seien — nun eben „Wilde“: rohe, grausame, barbarische Menschen, bei denen daher auch die Kinder in strenger Zucht gehalten würden, den Eltern blinden Gehorsam und rücksichtslose Dienstbarkeit schuldeten, ein trübes, eng geregeltes Leben führten, aus dem sie erst später wachsende Kultur zu liebevoller und verständiger Behandlung gerettet habe. Aber in Wirklichkeit ist gerade das Gegenteil richtig: Ein überreiches ethnologisches Material liefert uns heute den bündigen Nachweis, daß gerade bei den primitivsten Völkern die Kinder überall in glücklicher vollster Freiheit leben und von den Eltern, ja Erwachsenen überhaupt geradezu verzärtelt werden. Es scheint, daß man bei ihnen das Kind für etwas noch dem Göttlichen Näheres, dem Alltagsmenschen Ferneres, etwas Feineres und Edleres erachtet. So ehrt und schont man sie in jeder Hinsicht und hält ihnen den Ernst des Lebens nach Möglichkeit fern, bis sie durch Eintritt der Geschlechtsreife voll in das Menschentum eingehen und durch die „Jugendweihen“ — mindestens die Knaben — dann feierlich als Mitglieder des Stammes aufgenommen werden:

Th. W. Danzel („Kultur und Religion der primitiven Menschen“; Strecker & Schröder, Stuttgart, 1924, S. 67/68) sagt: „Die häusliche Erziehung ist außerordentlich milde. Es entspringt dieses Verhalten weder der Bequemlichkeit noch einer bewußten Absicht, sondern unmittelbar dem Gefühle . . . In gleichem Sinne berichten Knabenhans von den Australiern, Nansen von den Eskimos, Nordenskjöld von den Indianern, andere von den Weddas auf Ceylon . . . „Besondere Unterweisung gibt es auch für die praktischen Fertigkeiten nicht, sondern das Kind ahmt früh spielend die Tätigkeit der Erwachsenen nach, hilft dann wohl auch mit und lernt so das Nötige“.

Hellmuth von Bracken („Die Prügelstrafe“; Dresden 1924, Verlag am andern Ufer, Buchholz-Friedewald, S. 82) führt aus: Bei den primitiven Völkern werden die Kinder nicht geschlagen, überhaupt nicht gestraft, es sei denn durch ein unfreundliches Wort. Ein Kind schlagen, das würden sie ähnlich empfinden, wie unsereiner die Tierquälerei eines rohen Gesellen. Bracken stellt hierüber interessantes Material aus zuverlässigen …

author: By Jo Kimmy, Contributor
title: ‘We Want the Keys to All of Madrid,’ Spain’s General Strike Takes on the Housing Crisis
content:
Madrid, Spain – “Huelga, huelga, huelga general!” – “Strike, strike, general strike!” – echoed across Spain on November 11. Throughout the day, workers walked off jobs, joined picket lines and took to the streets in large demonstrations, united in their demands for decent housing, fair wages and public policies that would allow working people to build stable lives.


The first nationwide general strike since 2012 was called by Spain’s two largest trade unions, CCOO and UGT, and supported by smaller unions and tenants’ organizations. The action went beyond workplace demands, reflecting wider frustration with an economic system that protesters say is increasingly pushing ordinary people out of the cities they call home.


According to the

organizers

, around

four million

 people took part in the strike nationwide, while approximately 750,000 joined the main evening demonstration in Madrid.


In Madrid and Barcelona, confrontations between police and protesters broke out, with reports of excessive police violence against demonstrators.


General Strike in Barcelona: Mass Protests, Pickets and Street Clashes


The scale of the economic and housing crisis is reflected in figures cited by Madrid’s tenants’ union,

Sindicato de Inquilinas

. According to the organization, rents in the Spanish capital have risen by more than 50 percent over the past five years. For many tenants, housing costs consume more than 70 percent of their income. As the union puts it: “We work most days for the landlord.”


“On a normal salary, all you can afford is a room in a shared house with four or five other people. I’m 26 and earn a good salary, but I still can’t afford my own place,” explains Ana, one of the protesters.


An Eviction That Sparked a Movement


The mobilization followed weeks of growing tensions over Spain’s housing crisis, with the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal becoming a turning point for the movement.


On September 23, after four previous attempts to remove her, a court order was finally enforced against

Maricarmen

, who had lived in the same flat in Madrid for over seven decades. The property had been bought by real estate company Urbagestión in 2018. The new owner increased her monthly rent from approximately €500 to €1,650 ($650 – $1,820) which she was unable to pay with her monthly pension of €1,350 ($1,480).

Hundreds of neighbors and housing activists gathered outside the building in an unsuccessful attempt to stop the eviction. She died on October 7.

Shortly after Maricarmen’s eviction, on September 26, protesters in Madrid occupied Puerta del Sol, setting up an encampment in the city’s central square. The camp remained in place for 38 days until an eviction took place without warning at 3 a.m., shocking those who were still at the camp, one encampment participant going by Isi, told Unicorn Riot.


Participants later described the operation as brutal, recalling how police tore down and destroyed tents. Protesters, including homeless people who had joined the encampment, reportedly lost their belongings and important documents in the process.


Madrid Streets Fill as General Strike Begins at Midnight


At midnight on November 11, hundreds of people took to the streets of Lavapiés, a multicultural neighborhood in central Madrid, marking the start of the general strike. Marching through the streets, they chanted slogans calling on workers to join the action. Some protesters banged pots, pans and spoons to create a rhythm for the chants, while others covered nearby walls with posters and stickers.


The midnight mobilization aimed to convince the remaining open businesses to close for the strike and encourage their workers to join the action.

At the same time, picket lines began forming across the city.

One of the first actions took place outside Mercamadrid, Spain’s largest wholesale food market. Around 1,000 protesters attempted to block deliveries. Police responded with pepper spray. According to the trade union

CCOO

, one of its members was arrested and 13 people required medical attention.

Tensions were also high that night outside an EMT bus depot on Calle Mauricio Legendre, in northern Madrid. Picket participants tried to persuade public transportation workers to join the strike. The police forced protesters off the streets, making it impossible to establish a picket line.

author: Alec Connon
title: The organizing gap in corporate campaigns
content:
This article

The organizing gap in corporate campaigns 

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Alongside a host of other movement practitioners, I’ve spent the last seven years building Stop the Money Pipeline. A national network of more than 200 organizations, our mission is to push the financial industry to phase out support of fossil fuels, boost backing for clean energy and respect human rights and Indigenous sovereignty in the process.


Our theory of change could be described like this: By pressuring the financial sector to support the energy transition, we can rob the fossil fuel industry of the resources it needs to grow and boost financing for clean energy. And if we achieve that, we will also have fostered divisions within elite power structures that help create the political conditions for transformational climate action at the governmental level. (This theory of change is well-articulated by historian Kevin Young’s 2024 book “Abolishing Fossil Fuels: Lessons from Movements that Won.”)


In the face of the recent right-wing backlash against corporate social responsibility, however, some on the left have begun to question the wisdom not just of Stop the Money Pipeline’s strategy, but of corporate campaigning more broadly.


So when Michael Marx’s “

Reining in the Bulls: How to Stop Corporate Abuse in an Age of Unbridled Greed

” was released in August claiming to be the first-ever comprehensive resource for “professional corporate campaigners,” I was eager to dig in and see what we could learn from it.  


Hard-earned lessons


Drawing on Marx’s impressive resume — 30 years of experience designing corporate campaigns for major foundations like the Rockefeller Brothers Fund and ClimateWorks, and leadership roles at Corporate Ethics International and Rainforest Action Network — “

Reining in the Bulls

” and an

accompanying website

 do an excellent job of outlining much of the knowledge required to build an effective corporate campaign. 


In 18 chapters, Marx breaks down key concepts and tools any aspiring corporate campaigner should be familiar with. Chapter 3, for example, introduces the key audiences to be aware of when designing a campaign ― employees (executives and mid-level), customers (retail and institutional), shareholders and legislators ― and breaks down tactics to reach each audience.


In later chapters, he provides useful overviews of how to “power map” a company’s structure, key tips for negotiating effectively with corporations, and how to create divisions between different company departments. An in-depth chapter details the minutiae of filing shareholder resolutions; another covers narrative strategy and generating media attention for your campaign.


One chapter that especially stood out to me is called “Researching and Selecting the Target.” In this section, Marx argues that choosing the wrong company to target is “the biggest mistake a corporate campaign can make,” because for corporate campaigners the real goal is not to change a single company, but the transformation of an entire industry. To achieve that, ”the target needs to be a company considered to be a leader that other companies will follow,” Marx says.


Did we make a mistake?


Probably the biggest corporate campaign I’ve been involved in was a campaign to pressure the bank Citigroup. With the goal of getting one of the world’s largest funders of fossil fuels to align its financing with global climate goals, we helped build out a “surround sound” campaign on the bank between 2022 and 2024.


Tactics included moms and kids organizing lemonade stands at the bank’s headquarters, activists routinely

bird-dogging

 Citi executives, and close to 1,000 people showing up at the board chair’s office for a protest. We organized corporate engagement meetings, swamped the bank’s social media, and wrote

reports

 and held public hearings on the role Citi plays in environmental racism.


One of the most innovative strategies we tried was the

Summer of Heat on Wall Street

. Over a period of several months in 2024, the campaign blockaded the doors to the bank’s headquarters more than 30 times, despite the NYPD arresting more than 700 protestors.


Activists block the entrance of the Citigroup Inc. headquarters during a protest in New York, US, on Friday, June 28, 2024.


Another was the

Costco: Clean Up Your Credit Card

 campaign, a multiyear campaign (still ongoing) to get Costco to end its co-branded credit card …

author: Mag
title: „Die haben Özay Tarim einen Maulkorb verpasst“: ver.di-Landesbezirk NRW mahnt mit Gewerkschaftssekretär sein „schärfstes Schwert“ in der Luftsicherheitsbranche ab
content:
Dienst-Handynummer, e-mail – zu wenigen Gewerkschaftssekretären pflegte die Redaktion so direkten Draht wie zum Gewerkschaftssekretär Özay Tarim in NRW, was die besonders umfangreiche Berichterstattung in den LabourNet-Rubriken zu

Flughäfen

 und

Sicherheitsgewerbe

 belegt. Doch im September, als Fragen zur (nun abgeschlossenen) Tarifrunde in der Luftsicherheit anstanden, war er nicht mehr zu erreichen. Seit erstmals die WAZ am 12.11.2026 (hinter paywall) berichtete, verdichtet sich durch immer mehr Artikel über den Fall „ver.di gegen ver.di“ das Bild einer Abmahnung durch die neue Fachbereichsleiterin Frauke Bendokat, weil er einen erneut kritischen Artikel zum ‚Frankfurter Modell‘ der

Privatisierung der Sicherheit

 nun auch am Flughafen Köln/Bonn nicht sofort löschte. Die mittlerweile am Düsseldorfer Arbeitsgericht im Gütetermin verhandelte Selbstentmachtung der Gewerkschaft bleibt inhaltlich/politisch nicht nachvollziehbar. Wir können nur hoffen, dass innergewerkschaftlicher Druck und zunehmend laute Austrittsdrohungen der in NRW betreuten KollegInnen zur baldigen Rücknahme der Abmahnung und Wiederherstellung der bisherigen und außergewöhnlich erfolgreichen Arbeitsweise von Özay Tarim führen. Siehe bisherige Informationen:


Eindeutige Vorwürfe: Wurde Flughafen-Kritiker mundtot gemacht?


„

Nach scharfer Kritik am Flughafen Köln/Bonn soll die Gewerkschaft Verdi ihren bundesweit bekannten Luftsicherheitsexperten gezwungen haben, einen Beitrag aus dem Internet zu löschen. Er ist plötzlich auch nicht mehr für Öffentlichkeitsarbeit zuständig. Sicherheitskräfte an dem Flughafen drohen Verdi mit Austritt. Sie werfen der Gewerkschaft vor, einen Vorkämpfer für ihre Rechte mundtot zu machen. (…)


Vor Kameras und Mikrofonen kritisierte er den Abbau von Stellen bei den Kontrollkräften, verurteilte die steigende Arbeitsbelastung der Frauen und Männer an den Passagierkontrollen. In Fernsehen, Radio, Zeitungen und auf der Homepage für Luftsicherheit der Gewerkschaft Verdi erreichte Sekretär Tarim ein Millionenpublikum. Tarim nahm kein Blatt vor dem Mund. Furcht vor Bossen von Sicherheitsunternehmen oder vor Chefs der Flughäfen kannte er nicht. Offenbar ist ihm das jetzt zum Verhängnis geworden.


Name gelöscht – Verdi untersagt Veröffentlichung


Bis Ende September stand Tarim noch im Impressum der Verdi-Homepage zur Luftsicherheit in NRW. Doch plötzlich ist sein Name aus dem Impressum verschwunden. Özay Tarims letzter kritischer Beitrag über den Flughafen Köln/Bonn ist dort nicht mehr zu finden. Seit Wochen gibt es keine Interviews mehr mit Tarim, keine Berichte, keine Reden auf Versammlungen und keine Posts mehr auf Tiktok. „Verdi hat Özay Tarim aus dem Spiel genommen. Das schärfste Schwert der Gewerkschaft ist verschwunden“, sagt Bernd Solf, Luftsicherheitskontrolleur und langjähriges Verdi-Mitglied. „Özay ist für uns nicht mehr erreichbar. Das sorgt für viel Ärger unter Kolleginnen und Kollegen an allen Flughäfen in NRW“, berichtet Solf. Sein Kollege Markus Zgorzalewicz nickt und sagt: „Özay Tarim legt sich mit der Bundespolizei an, mit dem Bundesinnenministerium, mit den Sicherheitsfirmen. Wenn wir so jemanden nicht mehr haben, kriegen wir viele unserer Probleme nicht mehr geregelt. Und die Luftsicherheitsassistenten und Luftsicherheitskontrollkräfte sind auf sich allein gestellt.“ (…)


„Personalmangel und Zeitdruck gefährden die Sicherheit“, sagte Tarim dem WDR zuletzt am 15. September. An diesem Tag hatten sich mal wieder lange Warteschlangen vor der Sicherheitskontrolle am Flughafen Köln Bonn gebildet. „Dass es heute hier nicht funktioniert an der Kontrollstelle, dafür trägt allein der Flughafen die Verantwortung“, sagte Tarim damals. „Das ‚Frankfurter Modell‘ wird in Köln zu einem reinen Kostensenkungsprogramm, ohne Rücksicht auf die Beschäftigten“, sagt Gewerkschaftssekretär Özay Tarim. „Der Flughafen will nur noch mit einem Minimum an Personal arbeiten. Wenn es deshalb Engpässe und lange Schlangen gibt, beschimpfen die Passagiere aber nicht den Flughafen, sondern die Kontrollkräfte.“ (…)


Im September soll die Gewerkschaft dann Özay Tarim angewiesen haben, einen gerade erst erschienenen Beitrag über die Misere am Flughafen Köln/Bonn zu löschen.


Wie aus einem Verfahren vor dem Düsseldorfer Arbeitsgericht hervorgeht, soll Tarim den Beitrag aber nicht sofort gelöscht, sondern nach den Gründen für die Anweisung gefragt haben. Daraufhin soll die Gewerkschaft ihm eine Abmahnung erteilt haben. (…)


Auf Anfrage …

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: A Tribute to Blacklisted Lyricist Yip Harburg: The Man Who Put the Rainbow in The Wizard of Oz
content:
His name might not be familiar to many, but his songs are sung by millions around the world. Today, we take a journey through the life and work of Yip Harburg, the Broadway lyricist who wrote such hits as “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?” and who put the music into

The Wizard of Oz

, the movie that inspired the hit Broadway musical and now Hollywood blockbuster,

Wicked

. Born into poverty on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, Harburg always included a strong social and political component to his work, fighting racism and poverty. A lifelong socialist, Harburg was blacklisted and hounded throughout much of his life. We speak with Harburg’s son, Ernie Harburg, about the music and politics of his father. Then we take an in-depth look at

The Wizard of Oz

, and hear a medley of Harburg’s Broadway songs and the politics of the times in which they were created.

author: Radikal Perspektif
title: Anarşist Komünizm
content:
Yazan: Sam Dolgoff


Çeviren: Gorthim


Çevirilen Asıl Metin


PDF Linki


I


Dünya çapındaki ekonomik çöküşün de gösterdiği gibi, hızla yaklaşan kapitalizmin çöküşü, insanları yeni bir toplumsal düzen hakkında düşünmeye itiyor. Kapitalizmin son nefesini verdiğine dair görüş, muhafazakarlar tarafından bile genel olarak kabul ediliyor. Ne yapılması gerektiği konusunda ise büyük bir kafa karışıklığı hüküm sürüyor. Papa’nın önerdiği samimi dualardan, faşistlerin, komünistlerin ve sosyalistlerin ısrarla savunduğu elli yedi çeşit diktatörlüğe kadar uzanan pek çok sözde çözüm önerisi ortaya atılmaktadır.


Önerilen çözüm yolları birçok açıdan farklılık gösterse de, hepsinde ortak olan tek bir özellik vardır. Bunlar,

devletin

 tüm kötülükleri giderebileceğine dair sarsılmaz bir inanca dayanmaktadır. Bu çözümler, devletin işlevlerini genişletecektir. Devlet, tüm endüstrileri kontrol edip işletecek, malların dağıtımını düzenleyecek, çalışma koşullarını belirleyecek, bilgi ve aydınlanma kaynaklarını – okullar, gazeteler, radyo vb. – tekel altına alacaktır. Devlet, her bireyin hayatına müdahale edecektir. Hiç kimse onun otoritesini sorgulamaya cesaret edemez.


Gücün her şeye kadir bir devletin eline devredilmesi, işçi sınıfının karşı karşıya olduğu sorunları – sömürü, tekel, eşitsizlik ve bireyin bastırılması sorunlarını – çözemez. Devlet bürokrasisi başlı başına bir sınıf oluşturur. Üretici emekle uğraşmayan bu ayrıcalıklı sınıf, işçiler tarafından desteklenmek zorundadır. Günümüz hükümetinin muazzam israfı, verimsizliği ve yolsuzluğu herkesçe bilinmektedir. Devletin yetkileri bin katına çıkarılsaydı, bu yük ne kadar daha ağırlaşır, bu bürokrasi ne kadar daha köklü hale gelirdi?


Özel ayrıcalıklara sahip bir bürokratik sınıfın büyümesi, kaçınılmaz olarak eşitsizliğe yol açacaktır. Yönetenlerin çıkarları ile yönetilenlerin çıkarları birbiriyle bağdaşamaz. Her şeyi kapsayan devlet makinesinin elinde salt birer araca indirgenen halk, bürokrasinin giderek artan gücünü dizginlemek zorunda kalacaktır. Devlet sosyalizminin doğasında var olan çelişkiler, metafizik bir “devletin sönümlenmesi” yoluyla çözülmek bir yana, ayrıcalıklı bürokrasi ile ezilen kitleler arasında bir savaşa yol açacaktır. Bu da bir toplumsal devrime yol açacaktır. Devlet, toplumun ekonomik yaşamını herkesin çıkarları doğrultusunda yönetemez. Devlet, sınıfsal karakterini yitiremez. Devlet ve bürokrasisi varlığını sürdürdüğü sürece, kapitalizmin ortadan kaldırılması yeterli değildir. Yeni toplumsal düzen, tamamen farklı ilkelere dayanmalıdır. Bir tür diktatörlüğe doğru giderek artan eğilimler karşısında, devlet merkezileşmesinin tuzaklarından kaçınacak bir toplumsal felsefeye duyulan ihtiyaç giderek daha acil hale gelmektedir. Anarşizm, bu ihtiyacı karşılayabilecek tek toplumsal teoridir. Anarşizm, ekonomik faaliyetlerin gönüllü gruplar ve federasyonlar tarafından yürütüleceği bir toplum kurmayı amaçlar. Bu, insan yaşamının temel ilkesi olarak zorlamanın yerine karşılıklı mutabakatı yerleştirmek amacını taşır. Bireyin gelişimi, toplumsal yaşamın tek amacı olmalıdır. Bireyin gelişimini sağlamayan bir toplumsal sistem başarısızdır. Sömürü ve baskıya dayanan bir toplumsal sistem, bireyin tam anlamıyla gelişmesine imkân veremez. Bu nedenle, yalnızca Kapitalizmin değil, Devletin de ortadan kaldırılması gerektiğine inanıyoruz.


Toplum, binlerce bağla karmaşık bir şekilde birbirine bağlı ve birbirine kenetlenmiş organik bir bütündür. Bir organın işlevini yerine getirememesi, diğerlerini derhal etkiler. Toplumsal yaşamın muazzam karmaşıklığı ve karşılıklı bağımlılığı, komünizme yol açmaktadır. Komünizm, sanayinin tüm toplumun yararına işletildiği bir sistemdir. Toplum,

“Herkesten yeteneğine göre, herkese ihtiyacına göre”

 ilkesi temelinde yönetilmelidir. Hiç kimse, nesiller boyu insanların emek vererek ürettiği şeyleri tekelinde tutma hakkına sahip değildir. Yaşam araçlarını üretmek için herkesin ortak çabası gereklidir; dolayısıyla herkes, hep birlikte emek vererek ürettikleri şeyleri eşit olarak paylaşma hakkına sahiptir. Böyle bir toplumda ayrıcalığa, eşitsizliğe veya diktatörlüğe yer yoktur. Anarşist komünizm, özgürlük ile eşitliği birleştirir. Biri, diğeri için vazgeçilmezdir.


Toplumun ekonomik yaşamı, sanayiyle fiilen uğraşan kişiler tarafından, kooperatifler, sanayi birlikleri, federasyonlar ve her türden ve her amaca yönelik gönüllü birlikler aracılığıyla yürütülmelidir. İnsanlığın ihtiyaçları o kadar sonsuz çeşitlilik gösterir ki, belirli bir sanayi …

title: MLSA 2025-2026 dava izleme raporu: "15 dakikada adalet"
content:
Medya ve Hukuk Çalışmaları Derneği (MLSA), 2025-2026 Adli Yılı Dava İzleme Raporu’nu “15 Dakikada Adalet” başlığıyla açıkladı. Dernek, 1 Eylül 2025-31 Ağustos 2026 döneminde 17 ilde 123 mahkemede 201 dava ve 361 duruşmayı izledi. Mahkemeler bu davalarda toplam 1.313 kişiyi yargıladı.


MLSA, 2018’den bu yana yürüttüğü Gazetecilik ve İfade Özgürlüğü Davaları İzleme Programı kapsamında hazırladığı raporda gazetecilerin, aktivistlerin ve öğrencilerin yargı süreçlerini, mahkeme kararlarını, tutukluluk uygulamalarını ve duruşmalarda tespit ettiği adil yargılanma hakkı ihlallerini ele aldı.


MLSA, raporunu 27 Kasım’da İstanbul’un Beyoğlu ilçesindeki Postane’de gazetecilerin, hukukçuların, sivil toplum ve diplomatik misyon temsilcilerinin katıldığı bir etkinlikte kamuoyuyla paylaştı.


Duruşmaların yüzde 55’i 15 dakikadan kısa sürdü


Rapor, adını duruşma sürelerine ilişkin bulgulardan alıyor. MLSA’nın süresini kaydettiği duruşmaların yüzde 55’i 15 dakikadan kısa sürdü. Dörtte üçü ise yarım saati bulmadı.


MLSA, sanıkların aylarca beklediği duruşmaların dakikalar içinde sona erdiğine dikkat çekti. Mahkemelerin mütalaa, eksik evrak veya yakalama kararının infazını beklemek gerekçesiyle savunmaları dinlemeden duruşmaları ertelemesinin yargılamayı bir erteleme rutinine dönüştürdüğünü belirtti.


Sanıkların yüzde 83’ü aktivist, gazeteci veya öğrenci


Mahkemeler, MLSA’nın izlediği davalarda 549 aktivisti, 289 gazeteci ve basın çalışanını, 246 öğrenciyi, 66 siyasetçiyi, 62 avukatı ve 29 sanatçıyı yargıladı. Sanıkların yüzde 83’ünü aktivistler, gazeteciler ve öğrenciler oluşturdu.


Derneğin izlediği 201 davanın 127’sinde en az bir gazeteci sanık olarak yer aldı. Gazetecilerin sanık olduğu davalar, toplam davaların yüzde 63’ünü oluşturdu.


En yaygın suçlamalar: Örgüt üyeliği ve örgüte yardım


Rapora göre savcılıklar 52 davada örgüt üyeliği veya örgüte yardım, 30 davada örgüt propagandası, 29 davada ise 2911 sayılı Toplantı ve Gösteri Yürüyüşleri Kanunu’na muhalefet suçlamaları yöneltti.


Mahkemeler, 2911 sayılı Kanun kapsamında 770 kişiyi yargıladı. Bu kişiler toplam sanıkların yüzde 59’unu oluşturdu. Cumhurbaşkanına hakaret veya tehdit suçlamaları ise 21 davada yer aldı.


MLSA, kamuoyunda “Sansür Yasası” olarak bilinen Türk Ceza Kanunu’nun (TCK) 217/A maddesi (halkı yanıltıcı bilgiyi alenen yayma) kapsamında 16 dava izledi. Mahkemeler bu davaların 14’ünde gazetecileri yargıladı.


Dernek, terör mevzuatına dayanan davaların toplam dosyaların yaklaşık üçte birini oluşturduğunu belirtti. Gizli tanık beyanları, telefon kayıtları ve sanıkların çalıştığı kurumlara ilişkin bilgiler bu dosyalarda en sık kullanılan deliller arasında yer aldı.


Saraçhane protestolarına ilişkin davalarda 542 beraat


MLSA, İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediye (İBB) Başkanı Ekrem İmamoğlu’nun 19 Mart 2025’te gözaltına alınmasıyla başlayan protestolara ilişkin davaları da raporunda ele aldı.


Mahkemeler, protestolarla doğrudan bağlantılı 11 davada 269 kişiyi yargıladı. Sanıkların yarıdan fazlasını üniversite öğrencileri oluşturdu.


Saraçhane protestolarına ilişkin 35, 49 ve 66 sanıklı dosyalar, haber takibi yapan sekiz gazeteci ile dört avukatın davaları ve Orta Doğu Teknik Üniversitesi’ndeki (ODTÜ) protestolara ilişkin davalar büyük ölçüde beraatle sonuçlandı.


Mahkemeler Saraçhane dosyalarında toplam 542 kişi hakkında beraat kararı verdi. Ancak MLSA, beraatle sonuçlanan davalarda dahi sanıkların aylarca yurt dışına çıkış yasağı ve imza yükümlülüğü altında kaldığına, 13 kişinin ise tutuklu yargılandığına dikkat çekti.


Beraat oranı düştü, mahkûmiyet oranı arttı


Önceki adli yıla kıyasla beraat oranı yüzde 57’den yüzde 46’ya gerilerken mahkûmiyet oranı yüzde 20’den yüzde 37’ye yükseldi.


MLSA’nın izlediği davalarda mahkemeler toplam 291 yıl hapis cezası verdi. Bu cezaların 196 yılı, aralarında tutuklu yakınları derneği yöneticileri ve 12 avukatın da bulunduğu 50 sanıklı Tutuklu Aileleriyle Dayanışma Derneği ve Özgürlük için Hukukçular Derneği davasındaki mahkûmiyetlerden oluştu.


Mahkeme, tek bir karar duruşmasında 28 kişiye toplam 196 yıl hapis cezası verdi. Böylece bu dosya, MLSA’nın adli yıl boyunca kaydettiği toplam hapis cezalarının yaklaşık üçte ikisini oluşturdu.


Mahkemeler toplam 36 davada 94 kişiye ceza verdi. Ayrıca 600 bin lirayı aşan tutarda tazminata hükmetti.


63 kişi tutuklu yargılandı, 11’i gazeteciydi


Adli yıl boyunca mahkemeler 33 davada 63 kişiyi tutuklu yargıladı. Bu kişilerin 11’i gazeteciydi.

title: JUSTICE CLIMATIQUE DANS LES QUARTIERS POPULAIRES - Projection-rencontre avec Banlieues Climat
content:
JUSTICE


CLIMATIQUE


DANS


LES


QUARTIERS


POPULAIRES


Projection-rencontre avec Banlieues Climat


Jeudi 10 décembre 2026, à 18h


Cinéma Le Zola – 117 cours Émile-Zola, Villeurbanne


Métro République – Entrée gratuite, ouverte à tous


La Maison de quartier des Brosses, l'Université Gustave Eiffel et le cinéma Le Zola vous invitent à une soirée consacrée aux inégalités environnementales, à la justice climatique et à l'engagement citoyen dans les quartiers populaires.


Projection du documentaire L'Air des autres de David Montfort


synopsis : Chaque année en France, la pollution de l'air tue des dizaines de milliers de personnes. À travers l'enquête de Sanaa, Feris et Abdelaali, cofondateurs de Banlieues Climat, ce documentaire met en lumière les inégalités environnementales qui touchent particulièrement les quartiers populaires.


Entre mémoire ouvrière, témoignages, archives familiales et paroles d'experts, L'Air des autres raconte le combat de celles et ceux qui se battent pour que respirer un air sain ne soit pas un privilège.


Échanges avec le public et table ronde


La projection sera suivie de témoignages d'habitants de la région parisienne engagés aux côtés de Banlieues Climat, puis d'une table ronde réunissant :


Sanaa Saitouli, cofondatrice de Banlieues Climat et autrice d'Enracinée.


Aliénor Wagner Coubès, historienne à l'Université Gustave Eiffel, spécialiste de l'histoire Villeurbannaise. Elle s'intéresse à la fabrique de la ville, notamment à l'histoire du logement et aux politiques publiques environnementales.


Les jeunes formateurs villeurbannais de Banlieues Climat.


Yamine Belhachemi, coordinateur de projets à la Maison de quartier des Brosses.


Les échanges permettront de faire le lien avec les initiatives menées à Villeurbanne en matière de justice climatique, d'engagement des jeunes et de participation citoyenne.


Modération — Naelya Belamri, étudiante et jeune engagée à la Maison de quartier des Brosses.


La soirée se prolongera autour du livre Enracinée de Sanaa Saitouli.

author: Acratosaurio rex
title: Votos negativos y positivos. Y dilemas éticos electorales
content:
De todas las reflexiones que he hecho sobre el próximo domingo electoral, esta es la que os va a parecer más ridícula. Voy a ello. Muchos de ustedes decís que hay que votar para evitar que el fascismo llegue a gobernar. Es decir, votar para que ese bestia no gobierne.

Pero es que resulta que no existe el voto negativo. No puedes votar en contra de. No puedes quitarle un voto a la derecha. El voto es siempre positivo, a favor de. ¿Qué es lo que se está pidiendo? Que la derecha no gobierne para evitar perder derechos. O sea, que lo que prometen para el mejor de los casos, lo que estás esperando del Gobierno, es el virgencita que me quede como estoy.

Y como resulta que en este momento histórico (o histérico) de circunstancias actuales, el fascismo está boyante, quedándonos como estamos, seguirán en pie todas las causas que han hecho que la ultraderecha crezca.

No digo que no votes. No hago campaña alguna, solo le doy vueltas a las cosas, y digo que es absurdo votar pensando que tu voto le va a quitar algo a alguien. Si los fachas llegan a gobernar, será porque les votan. ¿A que he dicho una estupidez que no habíais percibido?

El problema (ético) que nos plantean las elecciones es el siguiente: Si gana X, será menos malo que si gana Z. Habrá menos muertes en el Estrecho, menos mujeres maltratadas, muertes más dignas, que si gana B, que lo pondrá peor todo. Y tú votando puedes evitarlo.

En fin, es el dilema del tranvía. Se plantea en la Serie "El Buen Lugar". Temporada 2 capítulo 5. Un demonio plantea un problema ético a un profesor de ética. Lo pone a conducir un tranvía sin frenos, y llegan inmediatamente a un cambio de vías, A y B. En la A hay quinteto de trabajadores despistados, y en la B un solo obrero. El tranvía va a arrollar a A o a B. Y te dan una palanca para que elijas la vía. ¿Una vida a cambio de cinco? ¿A o B? ¿Sí, no? Hay que decir, además, que no es un experimento mental, si no real. El demonio pone al profesor en una situación real.

Primero el profe no sabe qué hacer, y matanza, sangre y tripas. Repite el diablo la jugada y esta vez el profe de ética decide salvar a los cinco. Pero resulta que en la otra vía está su mejor amigo. Más sangre y tripas y horribles sensaciones. Y así el demonio va torturando al profesor, haciéndole elegir entre Santa Teresa y un viejo pesado, o entre cinco científicos y tu profesor de literatura... O enfermos terminales que necesitaban varios trasplantes, que podían hacerse con los órganos del atado solitario… El resultado final es siempre el mismo: sangre y tripas.

¿Y yo qué haría a la hora de elegir vía? Mi respuesta es "nada". La vida no funciona de ese modo. No conocemos todas las variables, no puedo predecir las consecuencias que tendrá mi acción o mi pasividad, no puedo medir el valor de una vida ni de cinco. Ese es un dilema sin respuesta ética, propia de profesores especulativos. Y, sobre todo, yo no he puesto el tren en la vía, no he amarrado a esos prendas, y un demonio no puede obligarme a elegir entre dos males, haciéndome creer que tengo poder de decisión.

Sabed que quienes os plantean el tema del Mal Menor a la hora de votar, que la respuesta buena y ética al dilema, no existe –en mi opinión–.

title: Ephéméride des luttes : 28 novembre
content:
Le 28 novembre de l'éphéméride des luttes, il faut bien le dire, en prend plein la face : police, milices, nucléaire nous mènent la vie dure...


1972 :

 A Barcelone, le MIL-GAC (Mouvement Ibérique de Libération – Groupes Autonomes de Combat) cambriole la Banco Central de l'allée de Valldaura. 1 million de pesetas de butin.


 Deux membres de l'IRA meurent dans l'explosion accidentelle d'une bombe qu'ils confectionnaient dans le Bogside à Derry.

 A Fermanagh, toujours en Irlande du Nord, l'IRA réalise une attaque au lance-roquettes, tuant un officier du Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC).


1980 :

 A Bari, dans les Pouilles, le groupe armé Prima Linea abat un agent de police.


2011 :

 A Dannenberg en Allemagne, des milliers de personnes continuent de bloquer l'avancée du train de déchets nucléaires, lui faisant aujourd'hui perdre 18 heures sur son trajet du fait de plusieurs actions : enchaînage aux rails, affrontements avec la police, manifestations, sabotages divers...


2013 :

 En Argentine, dans la petite localité de Malvinas Argentinas, près de Cordoba, un campement de lutte contre Monsanto est attaqué par une trentaine d'hommes armés qui mettent le feu aux installations et menacent les militant-e-s pour la défense de l'environnement.


2017 :

 A Arenillas en Equateur, la jeune Nicol Escobar, 16 ans, est abattue par la police, provoquant de grands moments de colère parmi la population, dont plusieurs nuits d'émeutes.


 A Panama, capitale du pays du même nom, des affrontements ont lieu lors de manifestations contre la hausse du prix de l'électricité. Un jeune handicapé de 18 ans y trouve la mort suite à l'inhalation des nombreux gaz lacrymogènes tirés par la police.

title: Comprendere lo Yemen e la rivoluzione in Asia Occidentale
content:
di Nicola Casale da Carmilla


Comprendere lo Yemen

, a cura di Tim Anderson (Mario Pascale Editore) è un libro quanto mai opportuno e utile. Contiene diciotto saggi di autori diversi, in gran parte yemeniti, che offrono un nutrito insieme di pillole condensate di conoscenza su una realtà politica che si è imposta all’attenzione mondiale soprattutto da quando lo Yemen, pur devastato dall’aggressione decennale di Arabia Saudita (AS) ed Emirati Arabi Uniti (EAU), non ha esitato a sfidare le potenze militari di Israele e Usa e la nutrita schiera di semi-potenze loro alleate, per dare un significativo supporto alla resistenza dei palestinesi contro il genocidio di Gaza.


Pillole condensate per spiegare un paese con millenni di storia, ma che restituiscono una panoramica completa per comprendere le motivazioni di quel supporto da parte non dei

ribelli Houthi

, come il

mainstream

 spregiativamente li denomina, né della sola Ansar Allah, ma di un intero popolo.

Nella parte di paese controllata da Ansar Allah vive, infatti, oltre il 75% degli oltre 40 milioni di yemeniti, è praticamente l’unica area non desertica dello Yemen e corrisponde all’

Arabia Felix

 che i romani dovettero rinunciare a sottomettere per la resistenza dei popoli che vi vivevano.


Se si dovesse scegliere una sola parola per sintetizzare ciò che sta avvenendo in Yemen questa dovrebbe essere senza ombra di dubbio: rivoluzione. Una parola da maneggiare con la massima cautela, dato l’uso (e l’abuso) fatto in Occidente soprattutto in certi ambienti di sinistra che concepiscono la rivoluzione con schemini semplicistici e confortanti, mai sottoposti a rigoroso bilancio storico dal punto di vista materialista, e che hanno il solo scopo di dimostrare l’inevitabilità… che ne siano alla testa loro stessi.

La yemenita è vera rivoluzione con una lunga storia e profondamente radicata nell’intero popolo che, con la sua resistenza, ha ricostruito a ogni tornante le proprie forze sul piano materiale e ideologico-politico.

L’obiettivo è la costituzione dello stato indipendente. Aspirazione semplice, ma dannatamente complicata per gli ostacoli che deve affrontare. Gli ostacoli si racchiudono in un unico concetto: imperialismo.

Alla dissoluzione dell’Impero Ottomano, dai caratteri ancora feudali, il controllo dell’Asia Occidentale passò all’imperialismo moderno, a carattere capitalista. Dapprima sotto la guida di Francia e Inghilterra, in seguito, quando le guerre mondiali risolsero il conflitto tra paesi imperialisti più o meno alla pari a favore di un consorzio tra loro sotto la supremazia del più potente, dal paese che ne assunse la guida, gli Usa.


Il disegno post-ottomano seguiva le esigenze dell’imperialismo. La prima era di impedire che la nazione araba costituisse un’unica entità statale, in quanto sarebbe potuta divenire una formidabile concorrente capitalista. La seconda era di assumere il pieno controllo su una zona di connettività, commerciale e di logistica militare e politica, fondamentale tra tre continenti. La terza era di appropriarsi a basso costo delle sue risorse minerarie, tra cui iniziava a emergere l’abbondanza di petrolio e gas, inizialmente risorse importanti per la produzione energetica, e successivamente divenute, con i vari derivati, materie prime basilari per lo sviluppo di tutti i settori industriali. Con confini disegnati a tavolino furono creati nuovi stati con monarchie compiacenti e perennemente tributarie per il sostegno militare e politico delle potenze imperialiste e a presidio, militare, politico ed economico di questa costruzione artificiale veniva insediata in Palestina, l’area determinante come via di accesso e quella che si era più modernizzata sul piano economico e sociale, una colonia europea sotto forma di

focolare ebraico

.


Scongiurare la nascita di un’unica entità araba impediva la formazione di uno stato sufficientemente forte ed esteso in grado di sviluppare proprie forze produttive e divenire una potenza capitalistica autonoma, ma anche agli stati partoriti dagli ingegneri imperialisti era impedito uno sviluppo produttivo autonomo, in modo da integrarli nella struttura di sfruttamento imperialista come produttori di materie prime a basso costo e mercati di consumo di merci e servizi prodotti dal capitale monopolista nei paesi imperialisti o altrove.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Liberia’s Feminist Foreign Policy: A Feminist Assertion of African Agency amid Global Backlash
content:
Liberia’s launch on 17 November 2026 of its

Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy: A Feminist Foreign Policy

 is a continental milestone. The policy is rooted in Liberia’s anti-colonial legacy as Africa’s oldest republic and a founding voice in Pan-Africanism and multilateralism, an independent state that stood with the continent’s struggle for independence. That leadership, the policy recognises, has been carried forward in no small part by Liberian women. They are the long-standing custodians of this legacy, not new beneficiaries. The real test is whether the policy advances African agency on African terms amid a global backlash against gender equality, militarisation and democratic decline. The policy rests on five pillars, namely women’s rights; women, peace and security; women’s political representation and leadership; climate justice and natural resource governance; and women’s economic empowerment and inclusive trade.


The first pillar, women’s rights, builds on Liberia’s commitments under CEDAW, the Beijing Platform and the

Maputo Protocol

. As anti-gender actors push a narrow “African values” framing of rights, credibility depends on Liberia practising at home what it champions abroad, including guaranteeing SRHR and protection from gender-based violence.


The second pillar, women, peace and security, takes on new weight as Liberia assumes the UN Security Council presidency in December 2026. Conflicts in Sudan, the Greater Horn, the Sahel, the DRC and Western Sahara have caused mass

displacement and food insecurity

, while

democratic space is eroding

. Liberia’s own history, from the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace to the Peace Huts, proves

women’s leadership

 in peace is a strategy, not a sideline. Liberia should use its presidency to lead for feminist peace.


On the third pillar, women’s political representation and leadership, Liberia can draw on the legacy of former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and the grassroots women’s peace movement. As

autocratisation

 advances, some leaders engage in

gender-bashing

, invoking tradition to attack gender equality and target LGBTQ communities. Others engage in genderwashing, claiming credit for equality to appear progressive. Both use gender to hold on to power. Liberia must measure its commitments by the power they shift to women and work with its feminist movement as a strategic partner.


The fourth pillar, climate justice and natural resource governance, must reckon with Africa’s long history of extraction. Liberia’s own experience is a stark example: in 1926, it leased vast tracts of land to the American Firestone company for rubber. That pattern continues in today’s mineral trade, which offers Africa only an “

illusion of industrialization

.” COP31 ended

without a fossil fuel transition plan

, and the loss and damage fund has met only USD 342 million of USD 2.8 billion requested. Liberia must therefore make reparatory justice non-negotiable and ensure Africa’s wealth benefits its own communities, especially women.


The fifth pillar, women’s economic empowerment and inclusive trade, must contend with trade rules that reproduce colonial patterns and leave African women behind. Women carry out much of the continent’s informal cross-border trade, yet these rules and policies largely ignore them. Their unpaid care work goes uncounted, and as

debt service

 outstrips health and education spending, that burden grows. Liberia should rewrite the economic rules with women at the centre by backing the

UN tax convention

, domesticating the AfCFTA Protocol on Women and Youth in Trade, and embedding ILO labour standards in trade agreements.


The policy also leaves gaps. Reparatory justice should run through every pillar, building on the March 2026

UN General Assembly resolution

 on the transatlantic slave trade and the AU

Decade of Reparations

 (2026–2036). Migration is listed among the threats but not developed. Liberia should champion rights-based approaches grounded in ECOWAS and AU free movement protocols, and resist the instrumentalisation of migration, border externalisation and

forced returns

. Resourcing for feminist policy has long been under-prioritised, and

Global North aid cuts

, with little domestic funding to fill the gap, have undermined feminist organising. Liberia must put money behind the promise, fully cost the policy, and publish clear indicators.


Liberia’s feminist foreign policy, authored from Africa and on …

author: Richard Munang
title: Africa Is Not Waiting for Climate Finance. It Has Been Financing the World
content:
After two weeks of climate talks in Antalya, the debate is still about who will pay Africa. A better question is how much of Africa’s own wealth leaves before anyone counts it.


Every climate summit ends with the same image: Africa waiting at the door for money others have promised. That image is wrong, and it is costing the continent its strongest argument.


The number at the door


The money that does arrive is real, and it is growing. Climate finance flowing to Africa more than doubled, reaching about USD 74 billion a year in 2023 and 2024, according to the

Climate Policy Initiative’s 2026 report

. But the same report estimates Africa’s annual mitigation needs alone at USD 300 to 572 billion. In Antalya, a revised draft decision on 21 November

dropped a proposed target

 to raise adaptation finance to USD 120 billion a year by 2035.


So the door remains half closed. And Africa keeps knocking.


The number going out the back


Now consider the other side of the ledger.

UNCTAD estimates

 that about USD 88.6 billion leaves Africa every year through illicit capital flight, about 3.7% of the continent’s GDP and

close to the total aid and foreign investment

 Africa received in a year. That estimate is now six years old. Nobody has a better one, which is itself part of the story.


Put the two numbers side by side. The climate finance coming in is less than the money estimated to be leaving through the back door. Africa is not waiting for the world to finance it. In a very real sense, Africa has been financing the world.


Where the money leaks


Illicit flows are only the most visible leak. Most of what Africa loses leaves legally, through what it sells raw and buys back as finished goods.


Oil is the clearest example. One West African producer

earned USD 31.5 billion from crude in 2025

 and

spent USD 10 billion buying fuel abroad

: 32 cents of every crude dollar went back out on fuel. The same country flared between

204

 and

323 billion cubic feet of gas

 in 2025, depending on which regulator’s count you use. On the higher count, that amounted to about USD 1.1 billion burnt and 17.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide released. That is a climate loss and a cash loss in the same flame.


The pattern repeats on the smallest scale. In one Kenyan county, our research found that less than a third of the money budgeted for flood drains went toward drains that worked. The county saw the evidence first, cleared the blockage, and the water ran again on 14 November 2026.


Count what stays, not only what arrives


The climate debate counts pledges and disbursements. It rarely counts what stays. Yet what determines whether a community survives the next flood is not how much was promised in Antalya. It is how many cents of each dollar, whether a climate dollar or a resource dollar, reach the drain, the field or the clinic, and remain there.


That is what we measure at UNU-INRA. We call it the keep rate: the cents of each natural resource dollar that stay at home. Alongside it, we count the jobs each kept million creates, with pay compared with the minimum wage.

The method is public

.


What this changes


Counting what stays shifts Africa’s position at climate talks from asking to showing. A minister who can say “of every dollar our oil earned, we kept this many cents, and here is what we lose in flared gas” is not asking for charity. She is showing where the next investment pays twice: once in money kept, and once in emissions avoided.


It also changes what Africa can do without waiting. Gas that is not flared becomes cooking gas. Fuel refined at home keeps foreign exchange at home. A share of each oil dollar kept can pay for solar on farms and clinics, soils rebuilt with compost, and forests left standing. Let today’s barrel pay for tomorrow’s economy. Each of these creates work for young people, funded with value that was leaving anyway.


None of this replaces the obligation of rich countries to pay what they promised. It strengthens Africa’s hand in asking for it, because a continent that counts what it keeps can show exactly where each outside dollar will be multiplied.


The real door


Africa will keep going to climate summits, and it should. But the bigger door is at home: the customs desk, the central bank ledger, the gas flare, the county drain. That is where the counting starts, and where the jobs come from.


My grandmother never judged the year by what the neighbours had gifted. She judged it by …

author: Reem Abbas
title: Africa’s manosphere
content:
“He killed her because of a birthday cake.”

This is how researcher Dabney Evans began her presentation on femicide at the Sexual Violence Research Initiative Forum in Bangkok last month. The weapon involved in femicide is usually a familiar object: a rifle that a partner uses for hunting, a knife you have used many times to chop vegetables, or the hands you once held close to your heart. 

The United Nations

estimates

 that every day, about 137 women and girls lose their lives “at the hands of their partner or a close relative.” Africa

has the highest number of femicide cases worldwide

. 

For years, feminist activists have warned about the manosphere.

UN Women

 describes the manosphere as “an umbrella term for communities that promote harmful definitions of masculinity,” including podcasts, gamer communities, social media, and dating apps — the digital movements that are enabling femicide, supporting it, and teaching men how to be more strategic in their abuse. A recent

Lancet


paper

 by Sarah J. Hawkes and Kent Buse argues that the manosphere “is best understood and addressed as a public health problem.”

When people think of the manosphere, Andrew Tate comes to mind as perhaps the most recognized name, but in recent years we have seen the rise of Tate-style figures worldwide. In a

Guardian


article

 published earlier this year, African feminist scholar Awino Okech noted the rise of the manosphere in Africa and a growing conversation on the “red pill” theory, which is the belief “that men and boys were being left behind as a result of all of the investments that had been made around girls’ and women’s rights.” 

The manosphere draws in young men by offering self-improvement advice, simple companionship in the face of rising male loneliness fueled by economic hardship, reassurance in the face of their anxiety about independent women, and a sense of masculinity in repressive states where citizenship is contested through state violence and economic opportunities are scarce.

But these offerings come with a catch. The

Guardian

 article notes that the manosphere first teaches men to think of themselves as victims: of feminism, the state, the economy, or changing social norms. It tells them there is a way to take back their power through “domination and intimidation.”

This pattern is replicated in the African manosphere. Content creators and influencers market themselves as self-development coaches, advising men on everything from health and wellness to work opportunities, building wealth, relationships, and putting women in their place. In Kenya, Eric Amunga, known as

Amerix

, stands out. Calling himself a medical specialist and masculinity coach, he is prominent for his #MasculinitySaturday

posts on X

. In one recent post, he tells his followers that “a man’s salary pays artisans, plumbers, masons, technicians and mechanics. A woman’s salary buys an iPhone, earphones, bundles, airtime and subscriptions to online gossip. We are not equal.” His posts get thousands of comments and likes. He has 2.3 million followers on X, and he sells courses through his website. 

In Nigeria, Àgbà John Doe leads a community called “The Agbafians Community,” which he claims can’t be killed by woke culture. On X, he runs a main account, a backup account, and a premium account, where followers pay to access his content. 

The subscription model on X allows content creators to make money on the platform directly from their audiences, reflecting what

Hawkes and Buse

, in their research, refer to as the “commercial ecosystem” of the manosphere, where insecurities and perceived problems are monetized through different packages. In other words, the manosphere is an ideological ecosystem, but it also has a lucrative business model.

In Egypt,

the rise of the manosphere

 has coincided with the normalization of misogynistic terms such as

Nashez

, which means “disobedient woman,” as several cases of femicide against university students have gained mainstream media attention. One widely covered case was the 2022 killing of 21-year-old Nayera Ashraf, a student at Mansoura University who was stabbed to death outside its gates by a classmate whose proposal she had rejected. Her killer was executed less than a year later, but femicide cases across homes and university campuses have only risen since then. 

Recent research

 has exposed the links between the manosphere and violence. In Kenya, for example, femicide is

rising …

author: A. K. Kaiza
title: Healing the Elephant: Life and History on the Mental Edge of Uganda
content:
Colonial governors live in the half shadows of history, and in Uganda the ghost of Sir John Hathorn Hall, in power from 1944 to 1952, repeatedly returns to mind – to think of the psychological wreck of the man under whose tenure Britain lost Uganda.


What did Hall think on that afternoon of 17 January 1952 when his plane flew him out for the last time? Would it have been far from what was going through President Milton Obote’s mind that dusky 27 July 1985 when he crossed the Kenyan border, or President Idi Amin’s during his helicopter escape from Kampala on 11 April 1979? Much graver would have been the minds of Kabaka Mwanga and Omukama Kabalega when the two monarchs were sent into exile in 1899. We can only imagine with horror the state of Kabaka Muteesa’s mind during that most fraught and dramatic exit in the country’s post-colonial history in May 1966.


The one constant of Ugandan politics is the brutality with which it dispatches its rulers.


The question rarely asked is what goes through the minds of the masses these men ruled over. For the crowd that thronged the capital on 10 May 1899 as Mwanga and Kabalega were marched into Fort Lugard on Kampala Hill, the disturbance dug deep. The Acting Commissioner, Lieutenant Colonel Trevor Ternant, may have expected a triumphant entry; after all, he was marching into the capital two men he had labelled as rebels. The scenes of despair and wailing forced him to quickly send the two away to Entebbe and organize a rapid evacuation to Seychelles. Here was tumult their world had not prepared them for, the caving in of the cosmos their heritage knew nothing else of life without, now facing a future no prior narrative had prepared them for. 


When it was over, and this future came, and they had lost their lands and freedom, the closure that came, first for Buganda in 1910 when at last Mwanga was buried, provided some solace; he had been dead seven years. For Bunyoro-Kitara, there was only heartbreak. The kingdom was buoyed first by the announcement that the old lion was on his way back. At the very banks of the River Nile, a place Kabalega named Mpumudde, I have rested; he died. Barely a kilometre from crossing the river. The final caving in of their universe was not helped by the salty funeral speech sitting governor Sir Geoffrey Archer gave at the Rukurato on his burial that April 1923. Bunyoro-Kitara’s world ended. The age would not extend to them the hand of kindness for generations to come. For the next twenty years, more than a quarter million died of sleeping sickness; the plague took thousands; forced labour, punitive taxation, and decades of enduring racial abuse followed.


What we now know as “psychology” came to our consciousness four decades after the burial of Omukama Kabalega. When psychiatrist Dr Benjamin Kagwa made a study in 1963-64, some revelation of what the common folk were going through showed. 


Glimpses of this disturbance we can catch when TikTok, Facebook, X, and Instagram revelations leave us stumped. They return in quotidian form what in bygone eras Ugandans framed in mythological terms. I recall with my child’s mind the air around 1979, at the fall of Idi Amin, rumours of a wooden-legged monster stalking the land; it was whispered that homes without a cross dug into the front yard would be visited by this creature. In Kampala, news spread by “Radio Katwe” – literally “head radio”. I do not recall anyone in Aboke digging crosses into their front yards. As it was with these whispered fears, what the calamity would be was never concretely stated. This was code-speak foretelling the fall of big men. 


Just before the fall of the Tito Okello regime, cassava and sorghum slurry brewing in vats, one for liquor, the other for beer, bubbled prophecies of end times. The man driving the Okellos to their fall, Mr Museveni, was called a changeling, able to turn himself into any creature or object when his pursuers came too close.


Such stirrings are beginning to disturb Uganda once again. Under trauma’s blind impress, the concrete and the quotidian recede into the realm of fantasy while myth congeals into fact.


Towards the end of 2025, the word “

gumite

” – loosely translatable as “toughen” – began to puncture speech. “Chwezi dynasty”, the second oldest of Ugandan myth tales, sprung a second-coming, and in the byways of town edges, where mechanics and fabricators, hawkers and layabouts hold court, the words “basement” and “fridge” are tossed about …

author: WoMin
title: Practising solidarity economy: Women’s collective action and community finance in Memirlosho
content:
Conversations about economic development often portray rural women as people who need support, training, or assistance. Far less attention is paid to how women organise themselves to solve problems, manage resources, and build livelihoods together. During a recent visit to the

Memirlosho Women Cultural Village

 in Isiolo County, northern Kenya, we saw how Samburu women offer a powerful example of a community and solidarity economy in practice. The cultural village brings together four women’s groups (Narasha, Muruguti, Narupa, and Rapunye) that work as a collective to create opportunities, strengthen resilience, and improve livelihoods. Their lived experience demonstrates that solidarity economies are not solely theoretical concepts or future possibilities. They are already being built every day through cooperation, mutual support, and shared responsibility.


Collective organising as a condition for economic agency


The first foundation of Memirlosho’s economic model is collective organising. The women registered a Community Based Organisation (CBO) through which they transformed dispersed individual survival strategies into a legally recognised collective entity. This shift carries important economic and political implications as they gained greater visibility, legitimacy, and bargaining power. The umbrella structure allows the four groups to support one another while maintaining their own identities. Together, they can access external support, coordinate activities, and speak with a stronger collective voice.


More importantly, the organisation creates a sense of shared purpose. Members are no longer facing challenges alone, they have built a community that pools resources, shares risks, and works toward common goals.


Productive activities: turning livelihoods into collective assets


Memirlosho’s economic activities are rooted in skills and resources that already exist within the community. Hence, two productive activities form the backbone of the village. The first is beadwork. Women use their cultural knowledge and craftsmanship to produce traditional beadwork that can be sold for income. Working collectively allows them to purchase materials more efficiently, share information, and explore markets together.


Another important activity is goat rearing and trading. Through support from the

Samburu Women Trust

, the groups received forty goats, with ten goats allocated to each group. Rather than viewing these animals as a one-time gift, the women transformed them into a revolving community asset.


The goats are raised and later sold, with the proceeds used to purchase new livestock. In this way, the original investment continues to generate benefits over time. Instead of being consumed, the asset grows and supports future opportunities. This approach reflects one of the central principles of solidarity economies: resources are managed not only for individual gain but for the long-term benefit of the collective.


Financial solidarity: A savings system built around people’s needs


While productive activities constitute the foundation of

Memirlosho’s

 solidarity economy, the Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) serves as its circulatory system. The VSLA operates as a community-owned financial institution managed according to principles of mutual support rather than external profit extraction. The system has three main characteristics:


a

) Socially oriented lending:

  Women can access loans for socially important needs especially school fees, respond to emergencies, or meet household needs. Interest collected on loans is not extracted by an outside institution. Instead, it returns to the group’s common fund, benefiting all members. This way, capital serves the community’s wellbeing and social reproduction rather than simply financial accumulation.


b) Inclusive flexibility:

 The savings model is also flexible. Members contribute according to their means and circumstances, recognising that income can fluctuate throughout the year, as a pastoral community. This allows participation even during difficult periods and helps ensure that nobody is excluded because they cannot meet rigid contribution requirements. It’s a system that prioritises participation and inclusion.


c) Community control over finance:

 The VSLA enables members to maintain ownership and control over their financial resources. By keeping financial decision-making within the community, the group reduces dependence on …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Two men sentenced for Khayelitsha church sexual assault
content:
On Easter Sunday in 2023, two young men stormed the Showers of Blessings Christian Church in Zion, in Site C carrying a gun and a knife and robbed the women congregants before sexually assaulting and raping them. Yamkela Jobo and Okuhle Beya were found guilty on all 21 charges and were sentenced to 25 years in prison by the regional court in Khayelitsha today.


Thembinkosi Fati, the secretary of South African Zionist Churches, said they welcome the sentencing of the two. “The guilty verdict was a victory on its own, given how cases like this one just disappear into thin air. It might not be exactly what we wanted, but it shows that the investigating officers and the state did a good job,” he said.


According to Fati, Jobo and Beya took advantage of loadshedding, and the fact that the women and children were alone in the church hall where they were sleeping.


Nolukholo Jezile, one of the church leaders, said that they would sleep at the church during Easter. “It’s clear that they planned the attacks on us, because they waited until all the men were gone and they stormed the church,” she said.


She commended the courage of the women of the church for overcoming their trauma. “It was not easy at all; we could have easily given up,” but they are still not able to go to church alone.


Community-based organisations supported the church during the trial, including

Amadoda Aqotho

 and Sidima Sam Gentlemen’s Organisation.


Amadoda Aqotho supported the church members during the trial.


The prosecutors told the court that the pair ordered the congregants to strip naked, robbed 19 women of their cellphones, and sexually assaulted two of them before fleeing.


One of the mitigating circumstances offered by the defence lawyer was that the two young men were abandoned by their parents.


“Not having a parent does not give an excuse to be a thief and a rapist. Instead, it should teach you to be independent. I was not aware that they were this young. The women that the accused assaulted are old enough to be their mothers and grandparents,” said Sabelo Zekevu, the chairperson of Amadoda Aqotho. He called on men to stop abuse and report cases of gender-based violence when they witness them.
