author: Abahlali_3
title: South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity
content:
South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity

Address at a public meeting hosted by Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa at the Ellen Melville Centre in Auckland on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Comrades, thank you for inviting me to return to Aotearoa. I bring you greetings of solidarity from Abahlali baseMjondolo, the shack dwellers’ movement of South Africa, which was formed in Durban in 2005 and now has more than 200 000 members across South Africa.

It is fifteen years since I was last here, in 2011, when we commemorated the thirtieth anniversary of the great protests against the Springbok rugby tour of 1981. I want to begin by remembering that history, and by thanking all the people of this country who stood with us against apartheid. People marched, confronted the police, and sometimes faced arrest and violence. You refused to allow the apartheid state to present itself as a normal member of the international community.

This was an outstanding example of international solidarity, and an example that we should seek to emulate in our solidarity with the people of Palestine.

In our movement we speak of living solidarity. This means solidarity that exists in action, not just in words. It means solidarity between people who recognise one another as equals.

Settler colonialism in South Africa and Israel

South Africa and Palestine are both countries that have been oppressed by settler colonialism. This is part of the reason for the long solidarity with Palestine among South Africans.

But there are important differences between these two forms of settler colonialism. In South Africa, the colonial system was organised around the dispossession of Africans from their land, the theft of their cattle and the exploitation of their labour. The economy depended on African workers in the mines, on the farms, in the factories and in the homes of white people. The settlers wanted the land, but they also wanted the labour of the people they had dispossessed.

Huge numbers of people were forced from their homes and land as African people were pushed into ‘reserves’, based on the system used to oppress Native Americans, and later into the ‘Bantustans’, the so-called ‘homelands’. The Bantustans were not just used to confine the African people on tiny bits of land. They were also central to the migrant labour system that ensured cheap labour for white capital and for white families in their homes.

African workers were forced by economic necessity to leave their families and communities to find work in the mines and cities. Many were compelled to live in single-sex hostels, separated from their families. Africans were wanted as workers but rejected as citizens with equal rights. They were systematically dehumanised. This system was maintained through the police, the army, prisons, torture and killing. Those who resisted were treated as criminals and terrorists.

When we look at Palestine today, we recognise many of these methods of oppression. We see a fundamentally racist settler colonial system in which there is ongoing dispossession of people from their land by the Israeli state and settlers. We see homes being demolished. We see communities separated from one another by walls, checkpoints and military restrictions. We see people who stand up against oppression being called ‘terrorists’ and subject to mass imprisonment, torture and murder.

The struggles against racism and for land are central to the struggle for freedom, both in South Africa and in Palestine. But there are also differences between apartheid in South Africa and oppression in Palestine.

While Palestinians have been exploited as workers, the fundamental drive of settler colonialism in Israel is to remove or destroy the Palestinian people rather than to exploit them for their labour.

In South Africa, the apartheid system required the continued presence of a large and hyper-exploited African workforce, while seeking to control, segregate and impoverish it. In Palestine, the settler-colonial project has involved the destruction of Palestinian communities, the removal of Palestinians from their land and the attempt to establish and maintain territorial and political control through their displacement.

The Nakba of 1948 forced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes. Many became refugees in other countries, and they and their descendants remain unable to return. The occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem since 1967 has brought …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: A Tribute to Veronica Lucy Gordon: South Sudan’s Courageous Voice for Women’s Rights and Press Freedom
content:
On 12 November 2026, Veronica Lucy Gordon, one of South Sudan’s pioneering journalists and most steadfast women’s rights activists, was shot dead in Western Equatoria province. She was on her way with friends to Mundri Town, taking part in the political life of a country on the brink. She was

returning from party primaries

 and congress activities in Lui Payam in Mundri East County with eight  SPLM delegates when gunmen attacked their convoy at Miri Loko, killing Lucy and Justin Akim, a fellow party member and a delegate and leaving four delegates still missing. 


For more than forty years, Lucy was a formidable force through every phase of South Sudan’s struggle for self-determination. She worked alongside women, supporting their political ambitions—and was killed as she entered political leadership herself.


We met Lucy back in 2010, before South Sudan was born in 2011 and before the hopes of independence were dampened by the militarism and civil crisis that have taken so many lives. For several years, while we worked with the Women’s International Peace Centre, Lucy was our guiding light, making the work possible in an environment so difficult for women, both politically and culturally. Together, we travelled to different states across South Sudan, documenting women’s realities and taking their voices and demands into national, African, and international policy and action. On long, uncertain paths, bumpy, barely existent roads and in crowded community meeting halls, she was a calm spirit, cooperative, never demanding, and carrying a quiet authority. She asked nothing for herself. To the women we worked with, interviewed and communed with, she gave her patience and her listening ear. It was the highest form of feminist leadership we can aspire to, the kind African women have long practised: leadership rooted in care, solidarity, and the everyday work of holding space for others.


That is what we have been denied, and what South Sudanese women are being denied. This is a grief we carry personally. The conflicts and political stakes in South Sudan have taken so many lives since 2013, and now Lucy, too, has been stolen from us. 


Veronica Lucy Gordon at Radio Miray. Photo by Radio Miraya


Her life and leadership


Her journey began at Lui Girls Secondary School, where she edited the wall bulletin, in the very area where she would lose her life. By 1983, she was writing about girls’ education in the Nile Mirror. Through the long years of war, she kept broadcasting, sheltering her children in trenches before going on air at Radio Juba. She rose to become Director of the English News Department at SSBC Radio, part of the national broadcaster, the South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation.


A stellar veteran journalist, she refused to succeed alone in a profession shaped by patriarchy. With the late Apollonia Mathia and others, she co-founded the Association of Media Women in South Sudan (AMWISS). She became the first woman on the board of the Association for Media Development in South Sudan (AMDISS), later its first woman Deputy Chairperson, and helped found the Union of Journalists of South Sudan (UJOSS). In 2024, she was named one of Africa’s 100 Most Influential Women. Many of the women who lead South Sudan’s media today stand on ground she cleared. 


Her final step was into electoral politics through the SPLM, and shortly before her death she was reportedly nominated for a women’s seat in the National Legislative Assembly. She spent her life opening doors for women, and she was walking through one more when she was killed.


As we mark the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence under the theme “Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity,” the violence has claimed another life. Lucy’s death reminds us that this violence is political. African feminists have long named what Lucy’s killing now lays bare: patriarchy guards the doors of power, and violence is one of its tools. 


South Sudan heads to its first general elections since independence, on 11 February 2027, but in September the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan warned that the conditions for peaceful, credible and inclusive elections are not in place. Women who travel to campaign face ambush on the road and unspeakable violence. The killing of Lucy and Justine adds to the rising civilian death toll along South Sudan highways. Women who stand for office face backlash, online abuse and doctored images. The 35% quota for women’s …

author: Habib Badawi
title: When Europe’s Wars Reach Africa’s Shores: Benghazi and the Limits of Libyan Sovereignty
content:
From the Salvador Pass to the Mediterranean, Libya’s divided authority leaves it vulnerable to conflicts it did not choose.


An expanding European war, an African security dilemma


On 22 November 2026,

reports of attacks on Russian vessels in and off Benghazi

 brought the Russia–Ukraine war into Libya’s security environment. The following day, President Volodymyr Zelensky

acknowledged the operation

, claiming that Ukraine had sunk a Russian naval vessel and struck a cargo ship allegedly carrying military equipment. The full extent of the damage and the cargo ship’s reported military function still require independent verification.


For Libya, the significance of Benghazi extends beyond the losses Kyiv claims. The incident raises the question of who determines the security risks that foreign military partnerships create on Libyan territory. A European conflict need not become a sustained African front to affect African societies. Where national authority is divided, foreign military relationships can expose a country to conflicts that its institutions have not collectively chosen to enter.


Aerial image of Benghazi. Wikicommons.


When local partnerships become national liabilities


Libya’s vulnerability cannot be explained by military technology alone; its institutional fragmentation has deeper political roots. The

October 2020 ceasefire agreement

, negotiated by the UN-facilitated 5+5 Joint Military Commission, set a framework for ending nationwide hostilities but did not restore unified national authority. The Tripoli-based

Government of National Unity

, established in 2021 through an UN-facilitated political process, operates alongside competing eastern institutions, while Khalifa Haftar and his military establishment exercise considerable influence over eastern and southern Libya. Libya retains international legal sovereignty, but its capacity to exercise that sovereignty remains uneven.


Russia’s relationship with Haftar shows what this division implies. After the Benghazi incident,

eastern Libyan authorities acknowledged the presence of a Russian naval vessel and said it had stopped for supplies

 under a cooperation arrangement, the terms of which remain independently unverified. Such partnerships can bring local authorities military assistance, economic opportunities and political support, but their costs can extend well beyond those who negotiated them. A faction’s capacity to secure foreign assistance may grow while the state’s ability to manage its consequences declines.


Libyan actors should not be reduced to instruments of foreign powers: they pursue their own interests and exercise real agency in negotiating international partnerships. The institutional difficulty arises when separate arrangements reinforce competing centres of authority rather than contributing to a coherent national security policy.


Self-defence and the sovereignty of third states


On 24 November, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha

reportedly defended the operation by invoking Article 51

 of the United Nations Charter.

Tripoli, meanwhile, rejected Libya’s involvement in the conflict

 and objected to foreign military activity within its sovereign territory.


The dispute raises two distinct legal questions: whether the vessels qualified as military objectives, and whether force could lawfully be used within another state’s territory.

Article 51

 recognises the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence in response to an armed attack, but it must be read alongside

Article 2(4)

, which establishes the general prohibition on the use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of states. International humanitarian law adds a separate test. Under

Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I

 to the Geneva Conventions, the classification of an object as a military objective depends on its contribution to military action and the definite military advantage anticipated from attacking it. Establishing an object’s military character does not, by itself, settle the legality of using force within a third country.


Ukraine’s right to defend itself against Russian aggression must therefore be distinguished from the legal assessment of operations abroad, and Russia’s foreign military partnerships must likewise be examined in light of their consequences for host states. For African governments, the underlying concern is whether external security arrangements expose national …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Whale Cove’s Issatik Co-op reopens two years after fire
content:
Whale Cove residents have a grocery store once again, more than two years after a

fire destroyed

 their former Issatik Co-op.


The rebuilt store opened to the public Friday at 2 p.m.


The new building, constructed on the site of the old store, is more than twice the size of its predecessor, said Duane Wilson, vice-president of stakeholder relations at Arctic Co-operatives Ltd, in an interview Tuesday.


The roughly 10,000-square-foot facility will offer residents a wider selection of groceries, frozen foods, fresh produce and other household goods after shoppers had to make due with a

smaller temporary space

 for two years.


The purpose-built store includes more display space for fresh food, along with backroom coolers and freezers to help keep products stocked, Wilson said. 


Unlike the temporary setup in the community hall, the new store also has permanent refrigeration fixtures rather than relying on plug-in coolers, he added. 


The building also incorporates several fire-safety measures designed to reduce the risk of another catastrophic loss.


Those include a concrete floor, an exterior fire-detection system beneath the floor, upgraded fire-detection technology built into the alarm system and improved skirting to reduce the risk of unwanted access underneath the building, Wilson said. 


The former Issatik Co-op was destroyed by fire on Aug. 30, 2024. The cause is still unknown.  


 


After the fire, the community hall was converted into a temporary grocery store, which offered less variety and became congested when residents were shopping, said Brian Fleming, the hamlet’s senior administrative officer, in an interview.  


Fleming also said community events were moved to the Inuglak School gym. 


“This has had a little bit of an impact because we’ve lost a recreation facility during this period of rebuild,” he said. 


The hall will not immediately return to community use after Friday’s opening, Fleming said. Additional work and a final inspection are needed before it can reopen, although he said the building appeared to be in relatively good condition.


Wilson said dismantling the temporary store’s fixtures and cleaning the hall would likely take place in the days and weeks following the move.


The new co-op also includes office and commercial lease space, some of which Wilson said already has committed tenants.


“I think that, out of the tragedy that was losing their only store, I can appreciate that there’s probably been a lot of stress, a lot of difficulties and a lot of struggles in Whale Cove,” Wilson said.


“I hope that this reduces a lot of that stress and provides a good service to the members for many, many years to come,” he added. 


Friday’s opening program included a ribbon-cutting ceremony and a meet-and-greet with Nunavut Premier John Main. 


There was also coffee and cookies on hand for residents and prize draws scheduled throughout the afternoon.

author: Amy Goodman
title: A Tribute to the Blacklisted Lyricist Who Put the Music Into “The Wizard of Oz”
content:
A lifelong socialist, Yip Harburg always included a strong social and political component to his work.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

His name might not be familiar to many, but his songs are sung by millions around the world. Today, we take a journey through the life and work of Yip Harburg, the Broadway lyricist who wrote such hits as “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?” and who put the music into The Wizard of Oz, the movie that inspired the hit Broadway musical and now Hollywood blockbuster, Wicked. Born into poverty on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, Harburg always included a strong social and political component to his work, fighting racism and poverty. A lifelong socialist, Harburg was blacklisted and hounded throughout much of his life. We speak with Harburg’s son, Ernie Harburg, about the music and politics of his father. Then we take an in-depth look at The Wizard of Oz, and hear a medley of Harburg’s Broadway songs and the politics of the times in which they were created.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Today, we pay tribute to Yip Harburg. His name may not be familiar to many, but his songs are sung by millions around the world, like jazz singer Abbey Lincoln.

ABBEY LINCOLN: Bing Crosby sang it, Ike Quebec played it, and Yip Harburg wrote it.

[singing] Once I built a railroad, made it run Made it race against time Once I built a rairoad, now it’s done Brother, can you spare a dime?

TOM WAITS: [singing] Once I built a tower way up to the sun With bricks and mortar and lime.

AMY GOODMAN: Judy Collins, and Dr. John from New Orleans, Peter Yarrow.

AL JOLSON: [singing] Say, don’t you remember, Don’t you remember they called me Al It was Al, Al all the time.

AMY GOODMAN: That’s Al Jolson. And our beloved Odetta.

ODETTA: [singing] Don’t you remember, I’m your pal Say, brother, can you spare a dime? Buddy, can you spare a dime?

AMY GOODMAN: “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?” may well be a new anthem for many Americans. The lyrics to that classic American song were written by Yip Harburg. He was blacklisted during the McCarthy era. During his career as a lyricist, Yip Harburg used his words to express antiracist, pro-worker messages. He’s best known for writing the lyrics to The Wizard of Oz, but he also had two hits on Broadway: Bloomer Girls, about the women’s suffrage movement, and Finian’s Rainbow, a kind of immigrants’ anthem about race and class and so much else.

Today, in this Democracy Now! special, we pay tribute to Yip Harburg’s life. Ernie Harburg is Yip’s son and biographer. He co-wrote the book Who Put the Rainbow in The Wizard of Oz?: Yip Harburg, Lyricist. I met up with Ernie Harburg at the New York Public Library for Performing Arts at Lincoln Center years ago when they are exhibiting Yip Harburg’s work. Ernie Harburg took me on a tour.

ERNIE HARBURG: The first place is business about words, and one of them is that the songs, when they were written back in those days, anyhow, always had a lyricist and a composer, and neither one of them wrote the song. They both wrote the song. However, in the English language, you know, you have “This is Gershwin’s song,” or “This is” — they usually say the composer’s song. I’ve rarely ever heard somebody say, “This is Yip Harburg’s song” or “Ira Gershwin’s song.” Both of them would be wrong. The fact is, two people write a song.

So I’m going to talk about Yip’s lyrics and then lyrics in the song. Now the first thing we’re looking at here is an expression really of Yip’s philosophy and background, which he brings to writing lyrics for the songs. And what it says here is that songs have always been man’s anodyne against tyranny and terror. The artist is on the side of humanity from the time that he was born a hundred years ago in the dire depths of poverty that only the Lower East Side in Manhattan could have when the Russian Jews, about 2 million of them, got up out of the Russian shtetls and ghettos, and the courageous ones came over here and settled in that area, what we now know as the East Village. And Yip knew poverty deeply, and he quoted Bernard Shaw as saying that the chill of poverty never leaves your bones. And it was the basis of Yip’s understanding of life as struggle.

AMY GOODMAN: Let’s go back to how Yip got his start.

ERNIE HARBURG: Yip was, at a very early age, interested in poetry, and he used to go to the …

author: Victoria Law
title: Across the US, Incarcerated People Report Unsafe Meals — and It’s Getting Worse
content:
Stella longs for vegetables, sauce, and meat. She dreams of waffles with fresh strawberries, beef bacon and sausage links, and any type of Italian food.


But none of these are ever on the menu. Stella has been incarcerated in a Pennsylvania prison since the 1990s. “I always went to the dining room because the food was good, freshly made, and filling,” she recalled of that first decade in prison. “The menus were created by the supervisors and the inmates who worked there could cook food the way we wanted to.” (Stella, like nearly all of the incarcerated people interviewed for this report, asked that her full legal name not be published to avoid reprisals.)


In 2018, Aramark won the

contract for food procurement in Pennsylvania’s prisons

. While the contract allowed the prisons to continue controlling staffing, meal service, and menus, Stella traces the decline in meals to that change.


Now, she told

Truthout

, the meals are “disgusting, soy-based filler food. I live off of commissary and my health suffers because of it.”


Catherine entered prison the year that Aramark took over. “The food was more edible when I arrived,” she said. “There was more variety, especially with vegetables.”


When the pandemic hit, she noticed a marked decline in both meal quality and quantity. “I once found a two-inch metal nail in my mixed veggies,” she recalled. Now, she rarely goes to meals, partially because women must wait for staff to escort entire housing units to and from the cafeteria, an outing that typically takes 45 minutes, and in large part because of the unappealing offerings.


“I’d rather eat out of a package,” she told

Truthout

.


Relying on commissary has a steep price. Catherine spends $175 each month on food alone, a cost she can afford only because of family financial support.


In 2024,

The Appeal

 published a

scathing investigation into prison commissaries

, including a

database of commissary lists

 from 46 states. The investigation found an exploitative, inconsistent system requiring incarcerated people to purchase many necessities at high markups. It also found that incarcerated people frequently turn to commissary items to supplement, if not substitute, inadequate prison meals.


Sixteen state prison systems

 contract with Aramark to provide meals. People in more than a dozen state prison systems have shared similar stories with

Truthout.

 This includes people incarcerated in states that do not contract with an outside vendor for meals. Some, like California and Texas, operate their own commissaries yet still mark up prices, gouging people who choose to supplement, or replace, their meals.


Then there are the long-term health effects of both meals and commissary snacks. In 2025, the Correctional Association of New York, a prison watchdog non-profit, released an

analysis of the state’s prison meals and commissary offerings

. Meals were high in sodium and low on fresh produce while the commissary lacked a sufficient number of healthy options. The few on sale were frequently out of stock.


A Tomato Is Like Gold


It’s not that incarcerated people don’t want to eat better. They long for fresh produce. They want eggs that are hard boiled or served sunny side-up. One woman rattled off a list of Chinese foods that she misses — scallion pancakes, ribs in black bean paste, stir-fried green beans with ground beef, Japanese eggplant with water chestnuts, pork belly in sweet and salty sauce, stinky fried tofu, oyster pancakes, chicken noodles with peanut sauce and cucumber, carrot, and bean sprouts. Above all, each of the omnivores wants meat that isn’t ultra-processed or soy-based filler. Every single person wished for fresh vegetables and fruit instead of mushy or syrupy canned versions.


“The burgers would be beef. The chicken would be identifiable chicken meat,” said Jocelyn Heffner in Arizona, adding, “Actually, nothing they serve is identifiable.”


Eighteen states’ departments of corrections (more than a third of states) contract with private corporations for some or all food service management, according to a

June report by the Center for Science in the Public Interest

. But even in the 32 states that do not, people still report unappealing and unhealthy meals.


Jessi Silverman, deputy director of

Center for Science in the Public Interest

 and a registered dietician, has analyzed menus in jails and prisons across the country. Nearly all fall short of authoritative nutrition …

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Grieving her daughter, a Manitoba mother’s fight for answers from police continues: ‘I want transparency’
content:
Crystal Delvenne takes to Winnipeg’s streets to draw attention to her daughter Cassie’s arrest and death nine days later, after she was left with unanswered questions by police and investigators. She has kept a sacred fire burning by the provincial legislature for nearly 90 days.

Photo by Crystal Greene


This story was updated on Friday, November 27 to add details from a press conference with the family.


Content warning: This story details violence towards an Indigenous woman. Please read with care and look after your spirit.


Manitoba’s attorney general is asking the province’s chief medical examiner to call an inquest into the death of a young Indigenous woman who passed away nine days after being arrested by the Brandon Police Service.


Matt Wiebe, who is also justice minister, wrote a letter to John Younes asking him to initiate a probe into the circumstances of Cassity (Cassie) Marie Delvenne under the Fatality Inquiries Act. The letter was provided to Delvenne’s family and obtained by IndigiNews.


At a press conference on Friday, Cassie’s mother Crystal Delvenne closed a sacred fire she had been tending outside the Manitoba legislature for 87 days — saying although the fire is no longer burning, she won’t stop fighting for answers.


“I will continue speaking her name and seeking truth and accountability, justice for Cassie,” Delvenne said.


“I’m just glad that we finally got something, some progress.”


As Cassie’s family took questions from reporters, an eagle flew overhead — and it was mentioned that Cassie was of the eagle clan.  Cassie was a member of Shoal Lake 40 First Nation, with ties to Wuskwi Sipihk First Nation and “Barrows,” Manitoba.


Delvenne said the family “came to an agreement” to let the sacred fire go out after they met with premier Wab Kinew on Nov. 6 where he assured them that an inquest would be requested. A poplar tree sapling will eventually be planted in the same spot as Cassie’s fire, according to her family.


(Left to right) Donna Delvenne, Patrick Neilan, Barb Guimond, and Crystal Delvenne, were among 20 people who gathered for a closing ceremony of Cassie Delvenne’s sacred fire on Friday, November 27. Photo by Crystal Greene


Crystal tended to the fire for nearly three months. As the seasons shifted from summer to autumn, and the year’s first snowfall blanketed the grounds, supporters brought firewood, warm meals, and condolences.


The 24-year-old died on June 21 — nine days after her violent arrest by the Brandon Police Service, which her mother alleges left Cassie with severe injuries. She said an autopsy and toxicology results found a “long list” of 16 or 17 injuries. 


After Brandon Police Service (BPS) received the medical examiner’s report and toxicology results, the force issued a

Nov. 6 press release

 that her death was “non-suspicious in nature with no evidence of foul play.” 


But they did not publicly disclose its details, citing “respect for the family” and privacy provisions of the province’s Personal Health Information Act. 


The BPS said its “investigation into this matter is now concluded.”


But Cassie’s mother has not stopped pushing for answers about the chain of events leading to her daughter’s death.


“They’re not investigating properly, they’re covering it up,” Delvenne alleged. In an interview with IndigiNews, she spoke of what she perceives as a lack of willingness for the province’s police watchdog and the BPS to investigate further.


In Wiebe’s letter asking for an inquest, he acknowledged “family members still have unanswered questions about what happened in the days, hours minutes leading up to [Cassie’s] death” and said the probe would “hopefully provide clarity for her family” as well as provide recommendations.


‘She was full of life and full of love’


A Facebook profile photo of Cassity (Cassie) Marie Delvenne, 24, was posted only a few weeks before her June 21 death. She was a member of Shoal Lake 40 First Nation, with ties to Wuskwi Sipihk First Nation.

Photo courtesy Cassie Delvenne/Facebook


Cassie, who was nicknamed Sunshine, was set to enter her final year of studying psychiatric nursing at Brandon University. She was a mother of a young girl, Zoelille.


“She was an amazing mom,” Delvenne said. “She loved her little girl, and she just cared about everybody around her. She was full of life and full of love.”


Delvenne said Zoelille “misses her lots,” and “knows her mom’s in heaven.”

author: William Gillis
title: Il Vuoto della “Sinistra”
content:
Di

William Gillis

. Originale pubblicato il 21 febbraio 2017 con il titolo

The Emptiness of “The Left”

. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Non credo che la “sinistra” rappresenti qualcosa di coerente; mi sembra piuttosto una coalizione storicamente contingente di posizioni ideologiche diverse. Nell’assemblea nazionale francese, Bastiat e altri liberomercatisti sedevano a sinistra; se da un lato si trattava di una coerente tradizione di libero mercato di sinistra, dobbiamo anche ammettere però che questo non significava molto in quei particolari frangenti rivoluzionari, e ancora meno in frangenti rivoluzionari in generale. Ci sono sempre rivoluzionari che ambiscono a sistemi molto peggiori del nostro, e molti rivoluzionari riconosciuti come “di sinistra” avevano propositi che erano un veleno per la libertà.


Sinistra e destra oggi sono generalmente considerate egalitarie e gerarchiche. Si tratta non solo di una lettura imposta di una realtà storica e sociologica molto più complessa, ma anche filosoficamente priva di contenuto. Nessuno sa dire chiaramente cos’è l’egalitarismo, o anche il potere gerarchico, molte teorie non solo si escludono reciprocamente, ma evidenziano come pretese presumibilmente identiche siano in realtà profondamente antagonistiche. Egalitarismo significa la stessa esatta ricchezza (comunque la si misuri) per tutti? Significa, nell’ambito astratto delle relazioni, uguaglianza giuridica o sociale davanti al Popolo o alle leggi dello Stato? Significa la stessa opportunità di impegno economico o la stessa possibilità di accedere ai granai? L’uguaglianza sostituisce altre virtù come la libertà? È meglio che tutti siano ugualmente oppressi o che qualcuno sia più libero? Non faccio dello spirito. Noi insabbiamo queste questioni serie dicendo che vanno lasciate al “buonsenso”, o sperando che i compagni affronteranno i dettagli così come faremmo noi, valutando i pro e i contro, mentre sappiamo per esperienza che non è così. Siamo in disaccordo costante.


Si parla di “democrazia diretta collettiva” come se qualcosa che rappresenta il volere pressoché unanime di un qualche organismo costituisse una condizione egalitaria. Certo, per certi versi è così. Ma se un qualche organismo collettivo decide della mia vita, io non voglio “partecipare”, gli lancio una bomba. C’è gente di sinistra che usa slogan come “potere al popolo” o “aboliamo il potere”, e questo dovrebbe essere un forte segnale d’allarme per tutti: parliamo di sistemi concettuali e valori completamente diversi. È una grossa illusione pensare che se ci si siede a discutere alla fine ci si ritrova tutti dalla stessa parte. Il presupposto di un obiettivo comune o di una solidarietà che abbraccia tutta la sinistra è una rassicurante bugia.


La sinistra non è una serie di assiomi etici su cui accordarsi per poi dibattere sulle conseguenti pratica e strategia. La sinistra è una coalizione storica assemblata per caso. Come nelle rivoluzioni, noi tendiamo ad identificarci con i vinti, formiamo le nostre coalizioni con le classi che reputiamo perdenti in opposizione alle classi che reputiamo di governo, ma così facendo confondiamo le cose. Siamo per l’aborto perché vediamo nelle donne il lato perdente del patriarcato. Ma stiamo anche dalla parte dei vegani perché gli animali sono (a volte letteralmente) i perdenti del dominio dell’uomo. Ma attribuiamo lo stesso valore a tutte le forme di vita? E cos’è una forma di vita? Valutiamo tutte le forme di vita allo stesso modo o secondo il loro grado di coscienza? O secondo il rapporto che hanno con noi? Il nostro giudizio cambia secondo che i perdenti siano nostri famigliari o altri.


Non sto dicendo che non c’è un filo conduttore che unisce queste dinamiche diverse, o una guida etica di fondo, una pratica attenta e sfumata; anzi, credo nella sua esistenza (anche se quando dico che esiste un ampio spettro di coscienza tra zigoti o nematodi e chiunque abbia una coscienza anche lontanamente umana molti a sinistra pensano che non sono egalitario). Voglio dire che il nostro atteggiamento nei confronti dei vinti è spesso una risposta istintiva a ciò che ci appare più che il risultato di un’analisi etica. La sinistra è raramente una filosofia, più spesso è una coalizione tenuta assieme da una dottrina. Possiamo immaginare un mondo diverso in cui, in seguito a un percorso storico diverso,

l’illegalità

 dell’aborto è una delle basi della sinistra, in linea con la lotta contro l’omofobia, il patriarcato, l’abilismo …

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Denied Education, Denied Choice: The Rise of Child Marriage in Afghanistan
content:
Five years after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, reports of child marriage are increasing. Globally, more than 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 every year. UN Women identifies education, legal protections, and social support as critical measures for preventing child marriage. Yet in Afghanistan, the Taliban have systematically dismantled these very protections. By banning girls from education beyond the sixth grade, restricting women’s participation in public life, and eliminating pathways to independence, the Taliban are leaving Afghan girls increasingly vulnerable to early and forced marriage.

The Taliban have created an environment in which women and girls are cut off from opportunities, resources, and support systems that would allow them to shape their own futures. With secondary schools and universities closed to girls, millions have lost access to higher education, professional opportunities, and the possibility of financial independence. Restrictions on women’s employment further compound this vulnerability, limiting their ability to support themselves and exercise control over decisions affecting their lives. In addition to these restrictions, the Taliban have issued over 160 decrees and directives affecting all aspects of Afghan girls’ and women’s lives.

The consequences of child marriage extend far beyond economic hardship. Marriage at an early age often forces girls into adulthood before they are physically, emotionally, or socially prepared. It can end their education, increase their exposure to domestic violence, and put them at greater risk of early pregnancy and serious maternal health complications. These risks are especially severe in Afghanistan, where women’s access to healthcare is increasingly threatened and limited by restrictions on female healthcare workers, women’s freedom of movement, and international aid organizations.

The loss of education is particularly consequential because schools provided far more than academic instruction. They offered girls a sense of community, a degree of protection, and access to trusted adults who could recognize abuse and intervene when necessary. Without these spaces, girls have fewer opportunities to seek help, build support networks, or challenge decisions made about their futures. The Taliban’s dismantling of legal protections, including the Ministry of Women’s Affairs and the removal of women from judicial positions, has further weakened the systems through which women and girls could seek protection and justice.

For Afghan girls, the fundamental right to decide when and whom to marry is increasingly constrained by circumstances beyond their control. The closure of schools, restrictions on employment, and dismantling of legal and social protections have steadily narrowed their choices. What should be decisions about their own lives and futures are increasingly shaped by a system designed to deny them agency and independence.

Preventing child marriage requires more than addressing individual cases. It means restoring the conditions that allow girls to remain in school, women to achieve financial independence, and all women and girls to exercise their rights and make decisions about their own lives. Until Afghan girls regain access to education, opportunity, and meaningful protection, the Taliban’s policies will continue to leave them increasingly vulnerable to early marriage and rob them of the freedom to grow and to determine their own futures.

Sources: Kabul Tribune, UNICEF, Afghanistan International, OHCHR

author: Valerie Anne
title: Liv Hewson Opens Up to Drew Barrymore About the Early Parts of Their Career
content:
feature image photo by The Drew Barrymore Show/Ash Bean via Getty Images

Yellowjackets star Liv Hewson reunited with their former Santa Clarita Diet co-star Drew Barrymore on Drew’s talk show this week.

In the interview, they discuss all sorts of topics, including but not limited to Yellowjackets, of course. Drew presents Liv with gifts for what she thought was their engagement, but Liv reveals that actually they got married already. (There are actually really cute pics that pop up behind them of the couple as well in the clip, so you should check it out.) Drew’s now-wedding gifts are two beautiful candlesticks Drew said represents the two of them living together in harmony.

Liv talks about meeting their now-spouse on the set of Yellowjackets when they were AD, and recounts seeing them for the first time and having a “who IS that” moment immediately.

Drew shows Liv a clip of another of their Santa Clarita Diet co-stars, Skyler Gisondo, asking Liv to share dating advice, and their advice boils down to the fact that people want to feel safe and that should be a priority in any relationship, not just romantic. (This is not really here nor there but I could listen to Liv talk for hours. They have such a calming presence and such a thoughtful way of speaking and you can tell, even just from little clips and interviews, that they are a deeply intelligent person, both intellectually and emotionally, and I just really love hearing them talk about pretty much anything.)

The pair also talks about Molly Ringwald coming on Yellowjackets to play Van’s mother, and Liv says they really hit the jackpot when it came to fictional moms, having now had two legends (Molly and Drew herself) play their mom on television.

Liv also talks about how they felt like they were living in a “defensive crouch” for a long time; they came to the US to work when they were 20 and felt like they had to go back in the closet as nonbinary when they started working in Hollywood, but that Drew and the cast of Santa Clarita Diet became a soft place for them to land and they are really grateful to her for that.

It’s a very sweet interview and as sad as I am to see Yellowjackets come to an end, I’m really excited to see what Liv will get up to next, mostly because they are extremely talented and should be cast in whatever the hell they want, but also because, selfishly, I want to watch them on more press tours.

+ Miley Cyrus also got married, to drummer Maxx Morando

+ Cynthia Erivo will be hosting the Rockefeller Center tree lighting and Christmas special, alongside special guests that include Alanis Morrisette and Kelly Clarkson

+ A wild Lea DeLaria popped up in the show CIA playing someone named Marbles and it was such a bit part but I am already obsessed and hope we see more Marbles in the future

+ Hunter Schafer is kicking ass and taking names in her new series, Bladerunner 2099

+ Speaking of Hunter Schafer, she said she tried polyamory but is more into monogamy; she supports it of course but says there’s too much scheduling for her

+ Tennis legend Billie Jean King hopes her documentary Give Me the Ball! will help “any gay kid or trans kid”

+ Jennifer Love Hewitt is going to reunite with I Know What You Did Last Summer costar Ryan Phillippe in an upcoming 911/911: Nashville crossover (I know this is a stretch to include here but both shows do have queer women on them and also J.Love was one of my roots so LET ME HAVE THIS)

+ There’s something fruity going on with Venita and Salley on the reality show Southern Charm

+ Also: YELLOWJACKETS IS BACK which means so are Kayla’s recaps so be sure to check those out

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: a14 – What’s fermenting underground – Jazz Dance with today’s zine scene
content:
Our collective can barely process all the correspondence coming our way. The least of which comes with scrappy limited edition zines. We endeavor to highlight them here when we can. Thankfully we have found a bright and wise ally who, when not tending to the garden warmly sits and reads deeply and widely freaky shit on paper. Maybe you will find a new life of reading zines, reviewing or even making them to thicken the plot we’re in.

Ear of Corn #66 24 pages – $2 foodfortunata@hotmail.com

It’s really endearing that even after 18 years, Ear of Corn still uses pasteup for the design, even as it’s moved to glossy paper. You can see on every page that Ear of Corn is still assembled old school and copied like we all used to do at Kinkos with glue sticks. The glue had a mild starchy taste, slightly sweet with a bitter finish; not unlike bad cheese pizza.

I have this conspiracy theory about this zine. I usually write reviews in batches, and I’ll often have multiple issues of Ear of Corn on my desk at a time. But I’ve never had any sequentially numbered issues. I’ve begun to suspect issues are not numbered non-sequentially or perhaps they are sequential, but aren’t printed in that order. Their practice of reviewing old and new releases side by side makes it impossible to know for sure; but they’re definitely up to something other than eating the glue.

Out From The Void #8 $5 – 70 pages outfromthevoid@yahoo.com

This issue goes places Out From The Void hasn’t gone before. The new topics are mostly adjacent to the core topic: the missing. So it’s the CAHOOTS program, police records requests, suicide, and police killings. But on page 51 begins a 6 page essay about Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It’s sober, historical and philosophical without trumpeting statistics.

In the middle of Issue #8 is a photo essay reprinted from the zine Here’s What I’ve Hidden Under My Tongue. Writer DJT was visiting an abandoned and mostly collapsed mental institution. In the introduction Brenton Gicker comments that he didn’t write any of the stories in this issue. I appreciate that Gicker puts his mission ahead of his ego to spread awareness of these topics but I do miss his voice as a writer. But until next time, we get more tales of the missing, the lost and the found.

The story of James B. Hunt and Fluke goes back to issue #16 of the infamous Fluke fanzine in 2018. Kudos if you kept that issue, it’s now a fine collectible. Even Maximum RockNRoll said so. They saw the future, perhaps even more clearly than I did. Gina Murrell always had a sixth sense for such things. But if you wake up feeling a bit goth, have a soft spot for monsters, or just like dead stuff, NXOEED might be for you.

If you don’t recognize his art that tells me you don’t skate bruh. His art appears on show flyers, album covers, websites, rad stickers and other greasy places. But among all that ephemera this issue is special. Usually Mr. Hunt lets the ink speak for him, but this time we actually get a few precious pages of text; our first sense of the man himself. He’s a geezer, like me, trying to do punk rock things, but to also go to bed on time. I feel that in my soul.

$20 – 192 pages inequitypress@hotmail.com

It’s hard to say that many poets are famous today. But as poets go, some of those published in Big Hammer are highfalutin people now like David Cope, Donald Lev, Chris Stroffolino, Ken Greenley, and Enid Dame (RIP). Others, like Michael Pingarron, are still writing for Big Hammer. They’ve found their layer of strata, and one would hope some sense of belonging.

The first issue of Big Hammer rolled off the press in 1988. That was 38 years ago, kids. Statistically most of you reading this weren’t even born yet. That zine was way underground, like the Lincoln Tunnel; like the FDR Train Car in the pitch blackness of Track 61 marooned below Grand Central since 1945. But Dave Roskos is still out there in the tunnels, in the darkness, still editing and publishing Big Hammer. He’s doing it his own way, and accountable to no one. Doesn’t it sound grand?

Zine content from the eighties makes more sense in the context of its contemporary punk 7-inches” like “Too scared to be queer,” “Be a Fag,” and “Forbidden Love.” So I queued up the Homocore Hit parade cassette, and pondered its place in history. Homocore ran for just 7 issues between 1988 and 1991. If you didn’t catch my drift, it tapped into two communities which still remain the core of the underground today: queers and …

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Officer who shot Neqotkuk First Nation man six times not charged
content:
The police watchdog for Atlantic Canada has cleared the officer who fatally fired six shots at a man in Neqotkuk First Nation in January.

In the final report, released Friday, the Serious Incident Response Team (SIRT) determined that based on evidence which included interviews, bodycam footage and an autopsy, the RCMP officer who pulled the trigger on 40-year-old Bronson Paul had “reasonable grounds to believe there was an imminent threat to his life and others.” SIRT also found that the “force was proportionate, necessary and reasonable in the circumstances.”

Police arrived at the family’s residence on the evening of Jan. 18 after receiving a call about a “domestic disturbance,” from a youth within the residence, according to the report.

He was shot six times in the chest after approaching a police officer with two halves of a broken toilet plunger.

The New Brunswick community, also known as Tobique First Nation, gathered in the local town hall to receive the news at noon Friday, where “representatives from various support programs” were on-site.

“This has been a very difficult year that has weighed heavy on the hearts of the community, which started with Bronson’s death in January 2026,” the Nation’s leadership stated Tuesday, when it announced the report would be made public within the week. “In this time of grieving, please show compassion to one and other.”

The results were not taken lightly, according to councillor Jasmine Eve Pirie, who posted a statement to Facebook.

She said the final decision was “deeply disappointing and heartbreaking.”

“A finding of no criminal wrongdoing does not erase the loss of a life, the trauma inflicted upon a family, or the pain that continues to resonate throughout an entire community,” Pirie wrote.

“Bronson was more than the subject of an investigation. He was a father, a son, a loved one and a member of our community. His life mattered, and it will always matter. As Indigenous people, we are all too familiar with the feeling of being failed by the very systems that are entrusted to protect us. Today’s findings only deepen the hurt and mistrust that already exists.”

Jessica Paul, Bronson’s partner, told APTN Investigates in May that “everyone knows where they were” when Paul died.

At the time of the interview, she had been fighting to view the police bodycam footage from that night, and had been wondering why it was necessary to use “such lethal force.”

She said she remembered the events differently than it had been described by police, prior to the completion of SIRT’s investigation.

According to the report, written by SIRT director Erin Nauss, Paul told investigators that following a nap in the afternoon leading up to the incident, she woke up to find Bronson drunk and “a little bit agitated.”

He would not let her leave the back room for an hour, according to the report, where he yelled at her and held her to the floor.

After he left to go take a shower, Paul asked their two kids to make the 911 call “just to be safe, to have him taken to the drunk tank.”

“She noted that the AP [Bronson] had been tased several times in the past, and that she had previously called police to take him to the drunk tank. Her goal was to have him leave the house peacefully,” the report continued. “She stated that, although this would be a challenge, he had always gone before.”

When police arrived, the kids were barricaded in the back room so they “wouldn’t have to see anything,” Paul said.

According to bodycam footage, she told police that he had been “yelling at her” for an hour, and he can be “very scary when he’s drunk,” and “very violent.”

RCMP New Brunswick knew of Bronson, Nauss noted, and that “he had a history of being violent.”

At the time of the incident, he was “subject to a release order arising from charges of assaulting a police officer and resisting arrest,” SIRT wrote. “He was on conditions to keep the peace and be of good behaviour toward CW1 [Paul].

“The AP [Bronson] had a history of police interactions, including violence, domestic disputes involving CW1 [Paul], and allegations that he had harmed her and others.”

The officer who eventually shot Bronson had called him “a fighter” during a communication with dispatch, the report continued.

According to the RCMP Subject Behaviour Officer Response (SB/OR) report made after the fact, the pair had labeled Bronson’s “risk assessment” as “high.”

author: Ricardo Sangiovanni
title: O coelhinho não existe
content:
Num dia, você é pai de uma bebezinha careca; no outro, é informado de que ela já não acredita no Coelhinho da Páscoa.


– Mamãe, o coelhinho existe ou são os pais que compram os ovos?


– Os pais que compram, minha filha.


– E por que você nunca me contou?


– Porque você nunca tinha perguntado.


É isso: num belo dia, você se dá conta de que sua bebê já tem sete anos e começou a indagar o mundo, irreversivelmente desperta para o desígnio humano de querer descobrir as coisas como elas são.


Ela então estende, por analogia, o princípio ativo do Coelhinho da Páscoa ao Papai Noel e à Fada do Dente. Essa arriscada hipótese requer confirmação, e eu faço que sim com a cabeça. Vem a pergunta irresistível: posso contar para meu irmão?


Respondo que não, que ele ainda tem cinco anos e cada criança descobre essas coisas no seu próprio tempo. Comprometida a proteger a fantasia do irmãozinho, ela agora se diverte ao se referir àqueles seres outrora encantados usando aspas manuais e um sorriso maroto, discreto de orelha a orelha, ao qual acrescenta um olhar cúmplice aos adultos.


Cruzar o umbral do mundo adulto implica, contudo, desafios. Papai e mamãe, até então imaculados, revelam-se terrivelmente imperfeitos, e agora são objeto não só do amor transbordante de sempre, como de um novo e incontrolável impulso de correção – oh, terrível conflito! Os sentimentos se complexificam, e o éden escolar de repente virou um terreno de relações multifacetadas, que passa a requerer difíceis tomadas de posição. As telas revelam uma infinidade de riscos bizarros – de acidentes, abandonos e inseguranças de toda ordem.


Aos sete anos, o mundo já nos apresenta uma lista enorme de contradições e nos coloca, pela primeira vez, o imperativo de ecoar os pensamentos bons e silenciar os malignos, para se manter positivo na vida. Cinco setênios adiante de minha filha, retorno aos meus sete anos em busca de alguma palavra útil.


Lembro-me do medo-pânico de meus pais sofrerem um acidente de carro e nunca mais chegarem; lembro-me da TV dando uma enchente calamitosa na cidade de Alagoinhas; da fuga insana do assaltante Leonardo Pareja; do interminável sequestro de Abílio Diniz. Tudo isso ao som tenebroso do canto das cigarras quando a noite caía no bairro da Federação.


Meus medos infantis, como os de minha filha, são medos de crianças bem cuidadas, hipotéticos, bem distantes dos medos reais que alcançam crianças desprotegidas planeta a fora. Mas medos, ainda assim. Que não suplantam, felizmente, as memórias divertidas, como a de quando comprovei que Papai Noel não existia ao notar, no Natal de 1992, a evidência inconteste de que suas unhas eram as unhas pontudas e vermelhas da minha avó, fantasiada de um bom velhinho vanguardista.


Outro dia minha filha perdeu um dentinho de leite e me disse: – Papai, eu sei que a Fada do Dente não existe. Mas eu quero colocar meu dentinho debaixo do travesseiro mesmo assim. Porque eu sou criança e adoro me divertir com essas coisas!


Nada tenho a lhe ensinar. Crescer deve ser isso: enxergar a realidade do mundo e escolher a nossa própria fantasia. Ah, filha, o tempo passou depressa; e andou mexendo com a gente, sim.

author: Rizomatica
title: Violenta expulsión por parte de gendarmería a comunidades que esperaban audiencia autorizada con la directora regional en Temuco
content:
La mañana del jueves 26 de noviembre se registró una violenta expulsión por parte de gendarmería y fuerzas especiales de carabineros hacia los familiares del Preso Político Mapuche Matías Ancalaf y de pu lof en resistencia que se encontraban a la espera de una reunión con la directora regional de Gendarmería Denise Melgarejo.


De acuerdo a los testimonios de los familiares de Matías Ancalaf, la coronel Melgarejo habría autorizado esta audiencia, sin embargo habrían negado la participación del Lonko Víctor Queipul, autoridad tradicional mapuche. El objetivo de la audiencia buscaba tratar una situación referente a la salud de familiares respecto al uso de body scan que maneja gendarmería, que es de uso obligatorio para el ingreso de visitas al penal de Angol.


Posterior a ser expulsados de las dependencias de gendarmería, algunas de las personas que asistieron a apoyar esta instancia, denunciaron controles de identidad realizados por carabineros en el transporte público.


Declaración de Janet Marilaf, azkadi de Matias Ancalaf.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Caída del consumo: en dos años cerró un tercio de los kioscos del país
content:
En Argentina 21 kioscos por día cerraron sus puertas en los últimos 2 años.


Foto: Noelia Guevara, Anccom


Escuchar el reporte de Radio Estación Sur de La Plata.


La Unión de Kiosqueros de la República Argentina (UKRA) advirtió que el sector atraviesa una crisis terminal: en todo el país, 21 kioscos cierran por día y los puntos de venta activos cayeron un 33,3% en dos años.


En diálogo con Radio Estación Sur, Cristian Loureiro, kiosquero y representante de UKRA, explicó: “En el 2024 había 86 mil kioscos a nivel país, hoy hay 64.500 puntos de venta a nivel país, es decir que 21 kioscos por día cerraron sus puertas en toda la Argentina”.


La caída del poder adquisitivo, la retracción de las ventas, el aumento de los alquileres y las tarifas de los servicios públicos son algunos de los factores que dificultan la continuidad de los pequeños comercios. Este año, durante el mundial, con la venta de las figuritas de los jugadores, tuvieron una suba de consumo, pero luego volvió a caer.


En ese sentido Loureiro explicó que esto se debe a que las familias no tienen dinero para gastar en ciertas cosas  y repercute en los kioscos que no venden productos de primera necesidad.


“A nuestro rubro le afecta que la gente no tenga plata en el bolsillo”, resaltó.


Para poder sobrevivir, muchos kioscos tuvieron que implementar otras modalidades de comercialización, como recibir envíos de plataformas online pero Loureiro explicó que esa modalidad no deja dinero a los comerciantes. “Como negocio mismo perse no sirve, no es rentable. Por ejemplo te digo, paquetes de Mercado Libre, no te deja plata eso pero hace que la gente venga, te conozca”.

author: anred
title: Criminalizar la solidaridad: denuncian las condiciones de detención y exigen la libertad de Betti, Chana y Moni
content:
Bettina Köpcke durante su detención.


Familiares, amistades y organizaciones de militancia denuncian la persecución judicial y las condiciones inhumanas de detención de Bettina Köpcke, Chana Boekle Yarza y Mónica Mellid Cañiza, privadas de su libertad desde el 18 de noviembre en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, en el marco de la causa por la búsqueda y extradición de Leonardo Bertulazzi, exintegrante de las Brigadas Rojas italianas. Advierten sobre las consecuencias del encierro en su salud integral y exigen la inmediata liberación y el sobreseimiento de las seis personas detenidas.

Por ANRed


A través de un comunicado, familiares, amistades y compañeras y compañeros de militancia denunciaron la arbitrariedad y el abuso de poder en el accionar de la jueza federal

María Servini

, en el marco de la investigación por la fuga de

Leonardo Bertulazzi,

 ocurrida el pasado 10 de noviembre.


Los operativos fueron ejecutados por efectivos del Departamento Federal de Investigaciones (DFI), dependiente del Ministerio de Seguridad de la Nación, a cargo de Alejandra Monteoliva, en el marco de una investigación en la que interviene la fiscal Alejandra Mangano.


Las personas detenidas integraban una red de solidaridad y cuidados que acompañaba a Bertulazzi durante su arresto domiciliario. En su mayoría, se trata de mujeres, migrantes, militantes y defensoras de derechos humanos.


Desde su entorno denuncian que los allanamientos fueron realizados durante la noche y la madrugada, mediante procedimientos policiales intimidatorios y violentos.


Condiciones de detención y vulneración de derechos


Bettina Köpcke, Chana Boekle Yarza y Mónica Mellid Cañiza permanecen detenidas en la alcaidía de la calle Cavia, luego de que la jueza Servini rechazara los pedidos de excarcelación presentados por sus defensas.


Según denunciaron en el comunicado, se encuentran hacinadas en celdas colectivas, con colchones en condiciones insalubres, agua contaminada, vigilancia permanente y severas restricciones para recibir visitas.


«La investigación se transforma en una condena con el castigo del encierro y la presión psicológica», expresaron.


Las defensas sostienen que las detenidas reúnen las condiciones necesarias para afrontar el proceso judicial en libertad.


Bettina Köpcke

 es médica, de nacionalidad alemana y compañera política y de vida de Bertulazzi. Según sus allegados, fue ella misma quien dio aviso a la policía de la fuga.

Chana Boekle Yarza,

 de nacionalidad española y alemana, es artista y gestora cultural, mientras que

Mónica Mellid Cañiza

 es trabajadora, militante y ciudadana paraguaya.


En el marco de la misma causa también fueron detenidos Marcos Rodríguez González, Ethel Villalta de Rodríguez y una persona identificada en el comunicado con las iniciales L. D.


La situación, según informaron sus allegados, ya fue puesta en conocimiento de Naciones Unidas, ACNUR y las representaciones diplomáticas de España y Alemania.


El caso de Leonardo Bertulazzi


Leonardo Bertulazzi, de 74 años, es un exintegrante de las Brigadas Rojas, organización política armada que actuó en Italia durante las décadas de 1970 y 1980. En 1987 fue juzgado en ausencia y condenado a 27 años de prisión, en un proceso judicial cuestionado por sus allegados por la falta de garantías para ejercer su derecho a la defensa.


Tras vivir en El Salvador, se radicó en Argentina, donde en 2004 obtuvo el reconocimiento como refugiado político por parte de la Comisión Nacional para los Refugiados (CONARE).


En aquel momento, la jueza María Servini había rechazado su extradición debido a que la legislación italiana no garantizaba la realización de un nuevo juicio.


Sin embargo, en 2024, en el marco del acercamiento político entre los gobiernos de Javier Milei y Giorgia Meloni, Bertulazzi perdió su condición de refugiado en Argentina y se reactivó el proceso de extradición.


El 1° de julio de 2025, la Corte Suprema de Justicia habilitó su extradición. Desde entonces permaneció bajo custodia policial hasta su fuga, el pasado 10 de noviembre.


Criminalizar a quienes cuidan


Familiares y allegados cuestionaron también el tratamiento mediático del caso, al considerar que contribuye a la estigmatización y criminalización de las personas que integraban la red de acompañamiento y cuidados.


Denunciaron que la exposición de sus rostros y trayectorias de vida busca presentarlas como integrantes de una organización delictiva, invisibilizando el contexto político y las …

author: Darío Aranda
title: El embrujo extractivista del progresismo uruguayo
content:
Por Raúl Zibechi


El gobierno de Yamandú Orsi parece empeñado en profundizar la carrera extractivista que inició Tabaré Vázquez con Botnia y continuó José Mujica con la minera Aratirí (que tuvo que detener por la amplia oposición que despertó). Ahora se están multiplicando los emprendimientos extractivos, entre los que destacan nueve barrios privados en la costa de Canelones, gobernado durante décadas por el Frente Amplio, que amenazan los últimos pulmones verdes de ese departamento. Puertos sobre ríos y sobre la costa atlántica, el lujoso barrio "+Colonia" frente a Buenos Aires y la desregulación ambiental, son algunos de los síntomas de este creciente contagio del progresismo de la cepa desarrollista que conocemos como extractivismo.


También se suman los centros de datos, uno en construcción por Google, y otro aprobado por el Presidente, que lo anunció el 14 de octubre en rueda de prensa como la “mayor inversión en la historia” del país, 5.700 millones de dólares para construir un campus de centros de datos por la española Solaria.


Abierto el grifo, se prevé un total de nueve centros de datos en los próximos años. Se trata de una iniciativa de la empresa española Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente, que ya firmó con el gobierno y la empresa estatal de electricidad (UTE), para desarrollar el mega proyecto. Además del centro datos se construirá un hub tecnológico de hasta 500 Megavatios (MW) bajo el régimen de zona franca y un parque fotovoltaico para generar 350 MW de energía solar. Se instalarán en los departamentos de Canelones, San José y Florida y la promesa del gobierno es de crear 1.500 empleos permanentes.


Foto: Solaria


Solaria ya tiene dos plantas solares en Uruguay de 9,5 MW cada una. Ahora ocupará unas 700 hectáreas de UTE en régimen de comodato. El periodista y activista ambiental

Enrique Amestoy

semanario Brecha

 que la empresa tiene un valor en bolsa de 2.080 millones de dólares, algo más de un tercio de la inversión anunciada, por lo que “grandes operadores internacionales de servicios en la nube financiarán el proyecto”, pero en realidad se trata de “inversores desconocidos”.


La planta consumirá una enorme cantidad de energía. Estima que llegará a 4.400 gigavatios al año, más que el consumo total de Montevideo donde habita la mitad de la población uruguaya

.


Amestoy recuerda que los centros de datos operan con unas 50 personas, por lo cual los datos sobre empleo suenan más a campaña publicitaria que a realidad Pero lo más significativoses que en este negocio “el país aporta energía, terrenos, conectividad y obras de red, mientras los servicios se venden al exterior”. Al operar en zona franca, está exenta de tributos.


Las críticas surgieron en el mismo momento en que se anunció el proyecto, y se multiplican, incluso entre aliados del progresismo gobernante.

La Diaria

, periódico de claro cuño frenteamplista, recoge el análisis de la economista argentina Cecilia Rikap, quien advirtió que un espacio destinado a los centros de datos no equivale a un parque tecnológico y sostuvo que podría convertirse en “un cementerio en el cual Uruguay entierra sus posibilidades de desarrollo”.


“

U

ú

ltimo son centros de I+D, empresas de base tecnológica. Nada de eso habita en un parque lleno de centros de datos

”

, sostuvo


Rikap

. Más aún,


consider

a que este tipo de emprendimientos profundiza la matriz extractiva ya imperante en el país.


“Abrirle los brazos a inversiones predatorias como esta es profundizar la dependencia, abrir más el espacio a las inversiones que cada vez más comunidades del mundo rechazan. Es cristalizar un rol subordinado en el capitalismo global en lugar de buscar un camino propio para el desarrollo”, dijo Rikap. Difunde la imagen del “cementerio” porque los centros de datos no sólo sobre utilizan el agua y la energía sino que generan contaminación auditiva, visual y del aire.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Urgente: Nelson Llempi, PPM de Caso Grollmus en huelga de hambre, es trasladado al hospital de gendarmería del Cp Biobío
content:
Durante esta jornada el prisionero político mapuche Nelson Alonso Llempi, quien se encuentra en huelga de hambre desde hace 5 días en el Cp Biobío, es trasladado al hospital de gendarmería, del recinto.

Nelson Llempi, quien tiene diabetes y es insulino dependiente, se encuentra en delicado estado de salud tras iniciar el lunes 23 de noviembre, junto a otros presos del Caso Grollmus, una huelga de hambre líquida, exigiendo la nulidad del juicio racista que los condenó a mas de 1050 años.

La situación de salud de Llempi es hasta ahora la de mayor gravedad debido a su enfermedad base, por lo que la falta de alimentación ya tiene consecuencias graves en su cuerpo.

Desde las redes de apoyo llaman a acompañar a su familia este viernes desde las 16:00 horas, a las afueras de la cárcel empresa Cp Biobío y a exigir su traslado al Hospital Regional donde puede revibir mejor atencion medica acorde a su actual estado.

A estar atentxs al desarrollo de esta información.

title: Gebet und Tanz für eine gute Reise.
content:
Gebet und Tanz für eine gute Reise.

In den zapatistischen Caracoles und Gemeinden – und auch in den Gemeinden der Partei-Anhänger*innen – haben die Tuneles [der anzestralen Spiritualität der Pueblos] und Katechet*innen [der katholischen Kirche von unten] zu einem Gebet zusammengerufen, um für die Delegation, die sich mit den Familien Sucherinnen in Mexiko-Statt treffen wird, [für eine gute Reise] zu bitten. Es wurde für deren Wohlergehen gebetet, sowie für das Wohlergehen der Familien, die diesen Schmerz und Jammer tragen, nichts mehr von einem geliebten Menschen zu wissen. Damit es ihnen im Herzen die Kraft gibt, nicht nachzulassen, bis sie ihn*sie gefunden haben.

Danach folgte das Tanzvergnügen mit Sonidero-Musik. Und in der Morgendämmerung fuhren dann die Fahrzeuge aus den 12 Caracoles zum CIDECI in San Cristóbal de las Casas los. Einige kamen nach bis zu 8 Stunden Fahrt – hin- und hergestoßen auf den Ladeflächen der Pritschenwagen und bei leichtem Regen, der den Weg säuberte und die Müdigkeit wegwischte – heute am 25. November gen Mittagszeit an.

Morgen, am 26. November, werden tausende Hände sticken, um zu versuchen, die Geschenke für die Mütter Sucherinnen zu vervollständigen. All das wegen des Capitán, der zuerst sagte, es geht um 100 Geschenke, dann 200, später auf 400 erhöhte und jetzt meint er, es sind [Geschenke für] mehr als 700 Familienangehörige Mexikos, die suchen [und mit denen sich getroffen wird]. Also geht es auf die Kappe des Capitán, falls die Geschenke nicht vollständig werden sollten.

Und tausende bereiten sich vor, um zuzuhören und zu umarmen.

Aus den Bergen des Südosten Mexikos.

Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés.

PS. Hier ein Video mit [Aufnahmen] einer Gebetszeremonie in einem Caracol, vom Tanz, der Ankunft im CIDECI sowie der gesamten Delegation im dortigen Auditorium. Diejenigen, die während des [Parole-]Rufens Misstöne verbreiten, sind die vom Comando Popcorn. Sie gehen nur bei Süßigkeiten und Schokolade koordiniert vor.

Zapatistische Tuneles, Katechet*innen, Keyboarder, Chauffeurologen, vollständige Delegation.

author: Comunizar
title: Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria
content:
¿Qué está pasando?


            En las últimas semanas hemos visto una serie de eventos que parecen abrir la esperanza de un cambio en la dirección de las luchas sociales. Estamos pensando en primer lugar en las protestas en las calles de Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países. También hemos visto la derrota de la derecha en una serie de elecciones: Hungría, Serbia, Brasil, Estados Unidos. Pero al mismo tiempo y, sobre todo, sigue el genocidio en Gaza. ¿Qué está pasando?


            ¿Cómo entender la serie de protestas de las últimas semanas en Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países? ¿Hasta qué punto se está abriendo, sobre todo entre lxs jóvenes, una perspectiva o una forma de organización que va contra-y-más-allá del capitalismo? ¿Es la rabia -volcánica- la conexión entre todas esas luchas actuales y pasadas?


            ¿Cómo entender la derrota de la derecha en las elecciones? ¿Pensamos que hay una diferencia significativa entre un gobierno de extrema derecha y uno de centro-izquierda? ¿Pensamos que el descontento expresado en esas elecciones podría desbordar la forma-Estado?


            ¿Cómo entender las luchas actuales en el marco del genocidio en Gaza? ¿En la virulencia de las recientes protestas en varios países de Europa, no estará escondido también un grito de impotencia/desahogo por el genocidio impune de Gaza? ¿Hay una rabia que esté tratando de salir del encierro que este sistema genocida nos impone? ¿Es posible sostener la esperanza crítica de un mundo otro no capitalista en un mundo que no ha logrado impedir ni detener el genocidio en Gaza?


Call for Papers


What’s Going On?


           

 In recent weeks we’ve seen a series of events that seem to open hope for a change in the direction of social struggle. We are thinking in the first place of the protests in the streets of France, Italy, Portugal, Germany, Albania, India and many other countries. And we have also seen the defeat of the right in a series of elections: Hungary, Serbia, Brazil, the Unites States. But at the same time, and above all, the genocide continues in Gaza. What’s going on?


            How do we understand the protests in all these countries? To what extent can we see, especially amongst the young, a perspective that goes against-and-beyond capitalism? To what extent are these protests breaking with the state-form and creating communising or other forms of organisation? Is volcanic rage the connection between all these struggles of the present and the past?


            How do we understand the defeat of the right in the various elections? Do we think that there is a significant difference between a government of the extreme right and one of the centre-left? Do we think that the discontent expressed in these elections could overflow from the state-form?


            How do we understand these struggles in the context of the genocide in Gaza? Does the virulence of these protests reflect a scream of hopelessness or fury in the face of the unpunished genocide in Gaza? In the violence of these protests is there a rage that is trying to break the enclosure that this genocidal system imposes on us? Is it still possible to maintain the hope of a world beyond capitalism in a world that has not succeeded in stopping the genocide in Gaza? In this context, of what significance are the elections in the USA or the visit of the Pope to Argentina and other countries of South America?


The post

Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria

 first appeared on

Comunizar
