title: Turkish troops remove two checkpoints in Serêkaniyê countryside
content:
Turkish troops have removed two checkpoints on secondary roads in the countryside of Serêkaniyê.


One of the removed checkpoints was located in the village of Um-Ushba, west of Zirgan district, while the other was in the village of Sefeh, northeast of Serêkaniyê.


Despite the removal of the checkpoints, the main roads providing access to Serêkaniyê city center from the east remain closed.


The checkpoints on the main roads connecting Dirbêsiyê to Serêkaniyê and Til Temir to Serêkaniyê remain closed. The Alya checkpoint on the international highway, which is under the control of Turkish troops, remains open to civilian vehicle traffic.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: ‘Alkansya’ for a family’s future
content:
By Viggo Sarmago

Bulatlat.com


TARLAC – On the way to Monasterio De Tarlac, bamboo-made

alkansyas

 (piggy banks) line up along the road. They were crafted by hands that dream of a stable life. 


Juvy-Ann, 29, an Ayta Abelling, spends most of her day drawing and designing

alkansyas

 in her house in Sitio San Pedro, San Jose, Tarlac. Making

alkansya

 is a family business; her partner, Erron Santos, her sister-in-law Rosa and Rosa’s husband, Junior, help in the production. 


Their inlaws would first harvest bamboo poles from the nearby forest and inspect their quality before transporting them back home in sacks in a tricycle. Once they arrive back home, they would cut the bamboo into the correct length and clean them thoroughly before attaching a handle. After drying, they would then lather it in varnish to help protect it from the environment. After the varnish settles, Juvy-Ann and Erron would then start hand drawing each design using stencils and mixing acrylic paints to add vibrance to their product.   


For the family, producing these is their main source of income.


“Before, we would make charcoal and sell

puso ng saging

(banana heart or banana blossom), but after being inspired by

alkansyas

 crafted by vendors from Zambales, we thought of improving it, which ended up being a hit among visitors and neighbors,” Juvy-Ann said. Through this business, she and her partner are able to support their family and their four children; three of whom are in elementary school, and the other, a highschooler. 


Despite their business showing some success, the family still struggles financially. Juvy-Ann thinks it’s partly because of insufficient local government support, and for Erron, it is because the business is showing signs of dwindling. “We were doing better before I think, because our products were novel at the time. Now that it’s getting old, not as many people are buying it anymore,” he explained. To help ease financial burden, Erron also takes bikers up the mountain for P100 (1.62$) to nearby biking routes in the area. 


The couple and by extension the family, continue to do their craft for the next generation. Even with concerns over the construction of the Balog-Balog Dam that can potentially make nearby communities flood prone, they are thankful to have a space to sell alkansya, so that they can save money for a future still left uncertain.

(CAM, RVO)


A long line of alkansyas made by Juvy-Ann and her family, that are being sold by their neighbor for 40 pesos ($0.65), on the road leading to Monasterio De Tarlac. They send their products for sale every weekend, so they spend the weekdays making the alkansyas.


Juvy-Ann and Erron Santos with their children in their balcony, while Juvy-Ann continues designing an alkansya. They have expressed wanting to teach their children their craft, but are concerned over health concerns from breathing in varnish and scented paint.


Freshly harvested bamboo and years worth of layered varnish stuck on a wooden table. The family started this business about 5 years ago, and had many influencers visit them, most notable of which was SepTV, who wanted to learn more about them and their products.


Juvy-Ann draws the line art of an alkansya design. The alkansyas use many colors, and lineart is applied using nail paint bottles with small nozzles to ensure thin but vivid lines.


Juvy-Ann inscribes the final touches on an alkansya that has a drawing of Luffy from One Piece. Their business also accepts commissions where customers can ask for a specific design. This One Piece design in particular, is popular amongst their youth because of the rebellious nature of the character.


Erron takes over drawing on an alkansya as Juvy-Ann takes care of their youngest son Erron Cable. The couple usually switches duties so that they can take care of family matters.


Erron Santos carefully puts the line art on an alkansya. While he does not draw as much as his wife, he enjoys the process of drawing the line art, and mixing paint, and pasting stencils.


Judy-Ann taking out some alkansyas from inside their home. On their walls is a tarpaulin of her and her partner’s wedding day, and the honors certificates their children have received in school–a motivation to keep creating alkansyas.


Juvy-Ann stares at her son Elrond playing outside their house.


Their son Elrond walks on stilts next to their house as a way to pass the time. While Juvy-Ann and Erron Santos are occupied with …

author: Brian Hioe
title: Win Or Lose, What Comes After the “Ocean Current”?
content:
TAIWAN WILL GO to the polls tomorrow to vote for a series of nine different government positions, hence the name nine-in-one elections. Most focus is on city/county councilor elections, as well as mayoral elections.

The predominant theme of the elections is local governance. This became the case after the meteoric rise of Puma Shen as a DPP mayoral candidate in Taipei. Before the rise of Shen, in what came to be termed the “Ocean Current” phenomenon, the election was one that seemed characterized by familiar, stale issues, in which there was seemingly no real difference between the two parties except for their stance on cross-strait issues.

Taiwanese politics has long faced the issue that both major parties largely agree on what the issues facing Taiwanese society are–that young people are paid low salaries, work long hours, and Taiwan’s population is increasingly elderly. Both parties do not fundamentally differ on any of the solutions that they offer, in that no party is willing to make structural changes to Taiwanese society, for fear of offending big business interests. That being the case, the two political parties largely only differ on their position on cross-strait politics.

The “Ocean Current” phenomenon represents a desire for alternatives, especially from the youth. This is especially visible in the backlash against the KMT, given that Shen is up against Chiang Wan-an, who is increasingly perceived as someone who comes from a powerful political family and may be handsome, but who has little concrete knowledge of policy and has stumbled his way to a high political office.

Nevertheless, before the rise of Shen, the DPP, too, was struggling. Shen is of the political generation that entered politics after the 2014 Sunflower Movement and if someone as young as him manages to become Taipei mayor, that represents another benchmark in this generation’s ascent up the political ladder. But even if the youthful politicians who entered electoral politics after 2014 were fresh faces, many have simply entered the DPP’s familiar rotation of cast members every election–whose main asset is that they are not aging or geriatric, as the DPP’s political leadership is.

What explains the rise of Shen, then, was his ability to project competency in offering policy that was formulated based on assessing and consulting the needs of the citizenry, and grasping social reality through data analytics. This sharply differed from the familiar cycle of the DPP and KMT simply seeking to one-up each other in terms of the policy they offer, but without any true difference in the kind of policies that were put forth.

But Shen was not a data analytics technocrat either, instead emphasizing how formulation of policy should be an open, transparent process. Through the survey results he collected and analyzed in the course of his campaign, he was also able to identify policy needs that were not previously recognized–for example, Taipei residents’ concern with the declining amount of greenery in Taipei. In this sense, Shen has excited the public because he seems to offer the promise of participatory decision-making that would restore agency to the citizenry.

Yet, in spite of the frequent comparisons to New York’s Zohran Mamdani, Shen is not exactly Mamdani because he has not called for structural changes to society. A message of good governance can be sufficient for addressing issues of decaying urban infrastructure, perhaps, but still proves insufficient to address deeply-rooted socioeconomic inequalities.

And if the DPP and KMT have proven reluctant to rock the boat, for fear of offending big business interests, it is to be seen whether Shen would be able to if elected mayor. If so, Shen would face opposition not only from the KMT but also from elements of his own party.

After all, one notes how in the wake of the Sunflower Movement, activists desired alternatives from the DPP and KMT alike–with the view that the DPP had become equally corrupt to the KMT in the course of its many years in office. It was fears of a split vote leading to a KMT victory that led many activists to join the DPP after the 2018 elections.

In 2018, the KMT proved unexpectedly resurgent, with the KMT unexpectedly making inroads into the DPP’s heartland in southern Taiwan through Han Kuo-yu’s victory in Kaohsiung. Han’s victory was seen as marking the ascendancy of the “Han wave” phenomenon, later propelling him to become the KMT’s presidential candidate in 2020 …

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Rights groups condemn killing of farmer organizer, tricycle driver in Batangas
content:
Jane Lee (middle) with other relatives of victims of extrajudicial killings join a protest in front of Camp Aguinaldo July 21, 2019 demanding accountability to the death of their loved ones. (Photo by Kodao Productions)

The group said the incidents reflect a recurring pattern in which civilians killed in military operations are subsequently presented as members of armed groups.

On November 17, Gilbert Orr was on his way to meet farmers. Jayson Cortas was driving a rented tricycle, earning a living for his family. Neither would make it home that night.

The two civilians were killed in an alleged military-police operation in Barangay Bataan, San Juan, Batangas, at around 9 p.m. that day, according to human rights groups in Southern Tagalog.

Elements of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and Philippine National Police (PNP), led by the Regional Mobile Force Battalion (RMFB), reportedly opened fire on the two while they were traveling.

Karapatan Southern Tagalog condemned the killings. According to the group, Orr had previously worked in the labor movement, organizing workers through a union. He later chose to serve farming communities, helping organize peasants in their struggle for land and livelihood.

On the night he was killed, he was reportedly heading to a farming community to help unite residents opposing mining operations in San Juan.

Cortas, meanwhile, was simply earning a living. He drove a rented tricycle to provide for his children and his pregnant partner.

“He was only driving a tricycle. And now he will never come home to me,” his partner said in a video post of Karapatan Timog Katagalugan.

Following the killings, PCOL Gerry Laylo, chief of the Mimaropa Police Regional Intelligence Division, reportedly claimed that the two were members of the New People’s Army (NPA). Laylo also cited supposed warrants of arrest for murder and alleged violations of the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Karapatan Southern Tagalog and Tanggol Batangan rejected the claims, maintaining that Orr and Cortas were civilians.

The groups questioned the police account, particularly the attempt to associate the victims with the armed movement despite their identification as a community organizer and an ordinary driver.

For human rights defenders, the allegations cannot serve as justification for the deaths of the two men. They called for accountability from the state forces involved and demanded that the circumstances of the killings be established.

Tanggol Batangan also recalled the killings of nine-year-old Kyllene Casao in Taysan and Maximino Digno, a farmer with psychosocial disabilities, in Calaca in 2022. Both were reportedly tagged by the military as casualties of armed encounters.

The group said the incidents reflect a recurring pattern in which civilians killed in military operations are subsequently presented as members of armed groups.

Orr’s killing also raises concerns over the risks faced by community organizers opposing development projects in Southern Tagalog.

Before his death, Orr had been working among farmers, helping them organize against mining operations in San Juan.

Progressive groups have raised concerns over the Luzon Economic Corridor, citing their potential implications for communities, the environment, and national sovereignty.

Karapatan Southern Tagalog linked the killings to the government’s intensified efforts to suppress opposition to these projects, particularly amid the ASEAN Summit and the visit of US President Donald Trump.

The group argued that those organizing communities to defend their land, livelihood, and environment have increasingly become targets of state violence.

The killings also came amid the recent arrest of 276 participants of the Timog Katagalugan Lakbayani delegation in Manila. Although subsequently released, the participants continue to demand accountability for the arrests and alleged abuses committed by state forces.

Karapatan Southern Tagalog called for assistance to ensure the safe retrieval of the victims’ remains and appealed for legal and financial support for their families.

Tanggol Batangan joined the victims’ relatives and the people of Batangas in demanding truth, justice, and accountability from the AFP and PNP.

For their families, the loss cannot be reduced to police allegations or official accounts of an operation. Two men were killed while one was working to organize farmers and the other was earning a living for his family.

Their deaths demand answers …

author: rti_admin
title: Brutality and Caste: The Murder of Rohit Anil Pathare
content:
What does the recent brutal murder of Rohit Pathare by a dominant caste group show? Here, it is inevitable to know the caste identity of the victim. A young ‘Ambedkari’ man from Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, and his killing in a hospital after a mob of dominant caste group brutally wounded him, exposes a grim reality of the caste system in India. If we understood it just as an act of violence against an individual, we may miss the social and structural underlying causal factors behind the kind of brutality it witnessed. This is a disturbing reflection of how caste hatred is deeply embedded in the social structure of Indian society, which continues to resurface time and again. This hatred appears at times in the form of Dalit youth like Somanath Suryawanshi, who was subjected to custodial torture and death in police custody, and at other times through incidents such as Khairlanji (2006), Mirchpur (2010), Bhima-Koregaon (2018), and Hathras (2020), alongside countless other cases of caste-based violence that remain unreported.

When a person is dragged out from his own house, in a broad daylight pulled through the streets and brought across a public square; when his wife is kicked in the stomach; when mob directs casteist slurs at him on his caste; when he is tied to a tree in a nearby agriculture field and brutally beaten by an iron rod; when wounds are made on his body by a screwdriver; when stones are used to crush his legs; and when, writhing in agony, he begs for water, urine poured over his face — such an inhuman and barbaric crime cannot remain confined to the individual victim alone. It casts a stain on the claims of so-called civility made by Indian society, the moral foundations of democracy, and the values of humanity at a global level. It also constitutes a grave affront to the universal principles of human dignity and fundamental human rights.

What kind of social system produces such inhuman violence and grants one human being the power to exercise domination and supremacy over another? This question leads us to Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar’s critique of the caste system. In Ambedkar’s intellectual framework, the question of human dignity cannot be separated from the complete annihilation of caste. According to him, caste is not merely a system of social stratification; it is a hierarchical structure of social and institutional inequality based on birth that denies individuals equal social recognition, freedom, and human dignity. Within such a system, caste-based violence does not manifest itself merely through physical assaults. It continuously reproduces through the humiliation of individuals, their systematic exclusion from society, the persistence of different forms of untouchability, and the systematic denial of their equal humanity.

Caste Hierarchy and Relations of Power

The caste system regulates the distribution of human dignity, power, and social rights, creating a hierarchy in which the humanity and dignity of some are systematically subordinated to the social privileges of others. Within this hierarchical order, violence is not merely a form of punishment; it becomes an inhuman lesson intended to remind the oppressed of their supposedly assigned ‘place’ in society. More importantly, caste-based violence cannot be separated from misogyny. When Rohit’s wife was kicked in the stomach by members of the mob, it exposed how caste supremacy employs patriarchy as a weapon of domination. Within the caste system, the bodies of women belonging to marginalised communities are often treated as instruments through which the collective morale of an entire community can be crushed and its members are subjected to collective humiliation.

This hierarchy also exposes a deep contradiction between the equality promised by the Constitution of India and the social inequality of everyday life practices. As long as a marginalised or Dalit individual remains within the conventional social boundaries and silently endures injustice, society appears to have no objection. However, when that very individual takes education, begins to advance, becomes conscious of their rights, and starts questioning the existing social order, the established social mindset becomes deeply unsettled. At such moments, social inequality and casteist arrogance become active forces, attempting to undermine that individual’s confidence and reassert their supposedly assigned ‘place’ in society.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Dismissal of petitions challenging Duterte’s arrest major step towards justice – Bayan Muna
content:
Bayan Muna (BM) welcomed the Supreme Court dismissal of the habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte and his turnover to the International Criminal Court (ICC).


Bayan Muna chairperson Neri Colmenares said on Wednesday said the decision is “another nail in the coffin of impunity” during the Duterte administration and is a major step in the victims’ search for justice and accountability.


“We support the decision of the Court because the warrant of arrest and surrender of Duterte has legal basis under Republic Act 9851 (the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity of 2009) and our obligations in the Rome Statute of the ICC,” Colmenares said.


In a November 11 decision released on Tuesday, the high tribunal voted 9-4 with one dissenting vote to deny the petitions filed by Duterte’s children, Sebastian, Veronica and Paolo.


The Court said the petitions are “moot” and that Philippine courts “cannot enforce the writ since he is already in the custody of the ICC in The Hague, the Netherlands.”


Duterte was on March 11, 2025 and flown to The Hague, awaiting the formal start of crimes against humanity trial at the ICC on Monday, November 30.


Duterte’s children filed the habeas corpus petitions the day after his arrest, arguing that the ICC arrest warrant could not be enforced in the Philippines because the country had already withdrawn from the Rome Statute.


The SC decision, however, said a writ of habeas corpus is a domestic remedy enforceable only within the country. “Significantly, [Duterte] is not just beyond the Court’s coercive powers, but also stands accused before an international tribunal that has assumed jurisdiction over his person,” the SC said.


The Court likewise noted that Duterte is already participating in ICC proceedings and has pursued remedies available under the international tribunal rules, even challenging – albeit unsuccessfully – the basis of his detention.


Colmenares said all that remains now is for Duterte to defend himself during the trial, likewise urging the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government to arrest Senator Ronald dela Rosa, Duterte’s co-accused in the alleged killings of thousands of suspected drug dependents as well as political critics.


“His (dela Rosa) arrest is not merely an issue of law but also an issue of justice for thousands of victims who were killed in the drug war conducted when Dela Rosa was Chief of the Philippine National Police,” the human rights lawyer said.


“He should be tried together with Duterte for the atrocious crimes committed when they were in power,” Colmenares added. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles. 


Our criteria for partnership were therefore not primarily based on size, institutional recognition, or formal representativeness. We were interested in organisations with real connections to workers’ struggles. This frequently meant working with small but independent unions and grassroots NGOs rather than established national trade union centres.


While building a network of such organisations, the network operated through collaborative research, education, organising, and advocacy. Activities involved …

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

author: Michael Cooke
title: Vale Suriyan 1948-2026: Tamil activist who lived by his socialist principles
content:
Suriyan was born in Sri Lanka in 1948, the year the country was granted independence by Britain, leaving it in the safe hands of the indigenous elite.

Sri Lanka was and still is a plantation economy, not producing enough of a surplus to both support the lifestyle of the elite and provide jobs with a liveable wage for the masses. Scapegoats had to be found; initially they were the plantation Tamils, imported as indentured labourers in the 19th century, who lost their citizenship at the time of independence.

It was the fruits of their labour that generated the wealth of the country.

At the time of independence, there was a militant anti-colonial left which supported workers’ rights regardless of their ethnicity and exposed the political bankruptcy of colonial rule.

The labour movement could bring the economy to its knees, as it did in the 1953 hartal (national strike). It fought for workers’ welfare rights, universal health care, education for all and the rationing of essential foodstuffs like rice.

Suriyan became active during this period. His understanding of oppression was deepened when anti-Tamil riots erupted in 1958, the first of many pogroms.

Suriyan was also aware of caste prejudice within his own community. When canvassing for votes for the left in Tamil-dominated regions, he was given tea in the finest bone china, while his lower caste comrade was served tea in an earthenware mug in the balcony. Suriyan would have none of it and let the household know in no uncertain terms.

Like many offspring of the South Asian elite, Suriyan was sent to London to further his education. While he dressed in a suit, he was strip searched on arrival. After that, he had an aversion to wearing suits.

In the 1970s, the National Front thugs were attacking Asian, African and Caribbean communities in Britain. Many were beaten up; homes and businesses were fire bombed.

Suriyan had shit shoved into his letter box and was often beaten up and harassed. He participated in coalitions of community groups, left-wing parties, trade union groups and civil society activists to defend homes and businesses from fascist hate marches.

Suriyan saw the importance of mass action and working in united fronts of progressive people, regardless of their ethnicity.

This lesson was reinforced by the many progressive individuals and political parties he mingled with, who were agitating against colonialism in South Africa, Rhodesia (Zimbabwe), Angola and Mozambique and Northern Ireland. He also flirted with left-wing parties, in particular the Workers Revolutionary Party.

One of his abiding convictions, reinforced by Leon Trotsky’s work, was the need for an international perspective and for alliances between progressive elements. That is why he supported the People’s Liberation of Tamil Elam (PLOTE), whose central aim was an alliance with progressives, regardless of their ethnicity, for a socialist Lanka.

While his support for the Tamil cause never wavered, he became increasingly disillusioned with the Tamil Tigers’ brutal tactics in their quest to be the sole voice of the Tamil struggle.

He was shocked when PLOTE leaders in good faith went to mediate a truce with the Tigers, which ambushed and killed them all. His disenchantment with deepened with the Tigers’ eviction of 70,000 Muslims from the Northern Provinces.

Nevertheless, Suriyan was tireless in his support of the Tamils when he came to Australia. He buttonholed progressive trade union officials, spoke to church groups, left-wing office holders and anybody he could get to listen.

After the 1983 pogrom, in which around 3000 Tamils were killed, many of whom were burnt alive and many women raped, Suriyan worked tirelessly to help Tamils escape, including members of his family, and to highlight these atrocities.

After 30 years of bloody civil war, the Tigers were defeated in 2009. The government’s victory was accompanied by a massacre of Tamil civilians. The Tamil’s demands for self-determination were ignored.

Suriyan, now with a burgeoning family, was working in the Australian Taxation Office when the anti-worker Prices and Incomes Accord was brought in by Labor. He and his close comrade, the late Gaetano Greco, were always pushing workers’ rights and vigorously opposing anything that would cut their conditions.

Notwithstanding powerful entrenched forces, from within the union and the bosses, they were elected to senior union positions and held in high esteem by rank-and-file members …

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: German Left Party expels pro-Palestine politician
content:
German pro-Palestine politician Vanessa Emde has been expelled from 

Die Linke’s 

(the Left Party’s) parliamentary group in Berlin.

On Tuesday 24 November, 33 out of 44 representatives of the party’s Berlin parliamentary group voted to oust Emde, overcoming the two-thirds requirement.

Emde, a theatre director associated with the Left Party’s Trotskyist Marx21 wing and co-founder of Neukölln’s Palestine solidarity working group, won her Neukölln constituency directly with 46.2 percent of the first preference vote in September’s Berlin state election. Like many supporters of Palestinian freedom, she has been falsely slandered as an antisemite.

For months, a hysterical campaign has been waged against Emde. Major German news outlets—from conservative Axel Springer publications (

Bild

, 

Welt

) to centrist and centre-left papers (

Der Spiegel

, 

Die Zeit

, 

Tagesspiegel

)—have united in denouncing her. They have repeatedly decried her statement that “nations don’t have a right to exist, people have a right to exist” and her criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza as antisemitic.

This campaign intensified with the prospect of a Berlin coalition government led by the Left Party, which won the most votes in September’s election. The Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) made Emde’s expulsion a prerequisite for any coalition with the Left Party. “We are of one opinion”, Berlin SPD leader Steffen Krach told the ZDF 

heute

television network. “We do not want to work with antisemites, and we will not work with antisemites.” Berlin Green parliamentary leader Werner Graf told the media they “will not be dependent on people with antisemitic attitudes”.

In November, coalition negotiations in Berlin broke down when the SPD and Greens walked out, demanding Emde’s expulsion before talks resumed. On 6 November, the Left Party’s Berlin state co-chairs, Kerstin Wolter and Maximilian Schirmer, demanded Emde surrender her parliamentary seat. She refused. She has now been expelled in order to restart negotiations.

This is a disgraceful turn of events. It is obvious why the pro-Israel German media, the Greens and the SPD would slander Emde. Uncritical support for Israel is sacrosanct in the German political establishment, where hostility to Palestinian solidarity is fiercer than in any other Western country. The SPD is even more cravenly pro-Israel than Australia’s Albanese government, while the German Greens define Germany’s responsibility for Israel’s security as “non-negotiable” and denounce other European Green parties as antisemitic.

Why, though, would a left-wing socialist party expel Emde?

The Left Party leadership cares far more about forming government than advancing the struggle of the oppressed and exploited. They are willing to do whatever it takes to enter the halls of power, even if it means facing down a backlash from their own membership.

This is not a new problem. Formed from a fusion between a left-wing split from the SPD and former East German Stalinist politicians, the Left Party has always attracted grassroots activists while remaining firmly controlled by career bureaucrats committed to moderate progressive politics.

From 2002 to 2011, the Left Party—and its predecessor, the PDS—served as junior partners in an SPD-led Berlin government. That administration sold off 100,000 state-owned apartments, laying the groundwork for the city’s current housing crisis. Left Party ministers also signed off on wage freezes, public-sector job cuts, higher public transit fares and cuts to social and cultural programs, alienating unions and working-class voters. The party’s vote fell from 22.6 percent in 2001 to 11.7 percent in 2011.

The Left Party also led the Thuringia state government from 2014 to 2024. During that decade, Left Party Minister-President Bodo Ramelow oversaw budget cuts and deportations of refugees. When his coalition ended in 2024, the party’s vote plummeted from 31 percent in 2019 to 13.1 percent, creating space for a dramatic surge by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

More recently, the Left Party experienced a revival, drawing in tens of thousands of new left-wing members as it campaigned against the far-right.

September’s Berlin state election was a historic victory. Finishing first with 25.7 percent of the vote, the Left Party more than doubled its previous Berlin result. This followed a broader resurgence in early 2025, when membership doubled to 123,000 and national polling …

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Bizzi Lavelle
title: Young Women, Pain, Mobility Aids
content:
Stories Contributors Pitch an Idea

To be sick, or have a health condition of any kind is not a moral failing. I know this and I hope that you do too. However, every time I find myself staying in or leaving something early because I’m in pain or I’m fatigued, I can’t help but feel the people around me are disappointed.

People wish they had a friend who could come to their fortnightly event like they said they would. They wish they could book a performer to MC an event without them withdrawing due to spending that week pain ridden in bed. They wish the friend they extended a birthday party invite made it instead of sending through an apologetic message. They wish their friend would be in the room cheering them on at their weekly drag comp or production show.

A common online talking point echoes in my head as I send my latest “I’m sorry” message; you have to inconvenience yourself a little for the sake of your community. You have to be someone’s villager if you want to have a village.

With the weeks or days I spend hidden away, inside, barely leaving the house I often ask myself, do I deserve to be in anyone’s village? Do I deserve my own villagers?

The words to Rina Sawayama’s ‘Bad Friend’ circle my mind as I spend another Saturday night in my pajamas, watching anime in bed: “So don’t ask me where I’ve been, been avoiding everything.”

As I’m lamenting my woes to my notes app and the friends who get it, an article from The Times UK comes across my feed. “Why are young women using walking sticks?” by Katherine Stock. And then another, this time from The Telegraph, “How having a disability became cool” by Poppy Coburn.

The themes of these pieces are misogyny and ableism, with sprinkles of transphobia and ageism.

In both of these pieces, the authors seem to believe that young women in increasing numbers are faking to be disabled for social clout. In the first piece, Stock declares young women using mobility aids and posting about being ill are victims of “social contagion” deems the pain they’re in as “unclear” and therefore “unclear” if these women “really have” disabilities.

It’s wild to me, that in 2026, anyone would partake in such ableist vitriol. Despite what both authors think, there are a wide range of ways to be disabled. Disability and chronic illness don’t always look like a wheelchair user. Sometimes disabilities and chronic illnesses are invisible. Sometimes they’re dynamic. The only criteria to being disabled is having a condition, injury or alike that impedes you and your ability to do day to day tasks.

Disability is the only minority group a person can become part of at a moment’s notice, and is the only minority group we will all be part of at some point in our lives. As my friend, Protect our NDIS rally organiser and activist Oriela says “You will become disabled. That’s a promise not just a threat”.

That one influencer you follow could one day be surfing and the next using a wheelchair or cane. You aren’t able to discern how much pain someone is in by simply looking at them. If that were the case, women wouldn’t be waiting years for their pain to be believed and diagnosed.

For Aboriginal women, seeking medical care has an extra layer of stress. Racial bias in medicine historically saw beliefs that bla(c)k people, particularly women, have a higher pain tolerance than their white counterparts. This, along with classic medical misogyny has led to Aboriginal women being mistreated, ignored or treated as though they’re only ‘drug seeking’.

In Allanah Hunt’s 2024 piece ‘The Good Patient’, she details her experiences of medical racism as she navigates dealing with endometriosis. Despite Allanah’s attempts to present to hospitals as the best and most polite patient, her pain was still disbelieved and she was still treated as a drug seeker. “Because the truth is, no matter how much I’m ‘the good patient’, I will never escape the racial judgement from healthcare providers” Allanah writes.

Similarly, Colleen Lavelle (my mother) discusses her experience of medical racism in her 2017 piece. “Death by racism: bigotry in the health system is harming Indigenous patients’”.

She notes from her own experiences and other First Nations people whose medical experiences she’s listened to that a common thread is wondering if you’ve been overly sensitive.

One memory I have from my teens is when I was at the shops with my mum and younger sister. I went out to the car to put some bags in the car and a man …

author: Mat Ward
title: 10 new albums that sum up the state of the world
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for November.

At the start of November, Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a huge wipeout in the US midterm elections. One reason was voters' disgust with his war on Iran, which has increased inflation worldwide. Three days later, Canadian rock star Bryan Adams - who has broken records with the length of time his songs have topped the charts - released his new LP, which repeatedly attacks Trump. On its song "Lake Ontario", he reminds listeners that Trump was facing accusations related to late paedophile Jeffrey Epstein when he started the war. "Things weren’t going his way in Iran," sings Adams. "So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram, he may have thought it best to throw a low blow, and create a real dog and pony show. But it feels like another distraction, while the Epstein files are gaining traction." On November 17, a forensic expert told the media that autopsy photographs suggested Epstein was killed. LISTEN>>>

Also addressing voters' disgust with the war is new LP from Ai Tsuno, released a fortnight later. Ai Tsuno is the side project of US protest singer David Rovics, who uses artificial intelligence to generate the music. Talking about its title track, he said: "Those trying to make sense of the voting habits of US citizens have noticed a pattern: we tend to vote against whoever started the most recent war." The elephant in the room is that the midterms wipeout was also fuelled by voters' hatred of AI, which is championed by Trump and tech billionaires. They include Elon Musk, who spent $US445 million on an AI slop-assisted election campaign in an apparent bid to stay out of jail. On November 19, musicians at Australia's ARIA awards attacked AI and the government's failure to stop AI firms stealing their work. "Roses are red, violets are blue," pop star Tash Sultana said. "If you support AI music, fuck you." LISTEN>>>

Anonymous New York hip-hop artist Lucy Be also takes aim at Trump on her new album. “Someone needs to do something about what’s going on in our country, and this is my way of doing that," she said in a Music Talkers article on November 6. On its opening track, she blasts: "Ay yo, fuck Donald Trump and the GOP. It's the Ku Klux Klan, with our eyes we can see. Epstein files you release but redact from the world, makes it crystal clear you were raping young girls. Ay yo, fuck Donald Trump and the GOP, represent rich and powerful, you don't represent me." The irony? Lucy Be also generates her music with AI. It also sounds almost identical to Ai Tsuno, which is perhaps inevitable if similar prompts are being typed into the same software, trained on the same artists' work. Hitting back three weeks later, Brisbane band Will Remedy & The Influencers released their new anti-AI album, Made By Humans. LISTEN>>>

Famously outspoken industrial music pioneers Ministry also use AI on their 17th and final album, which targets Trump, politics, authoritarianism, disinformation, social media and the AI industry itself. But they manage to keep their musical identity by using AI only to synthesize mock speeches by Trump and others. Discussing the LP on November 19, bandleader Al Jourgensen said using the controversial technology is "a very dichotomous feeling for me” as "Trump puts out his little AI videos every day". “We’re fighting fire with fire,” he said. Not that he thinks they're making much progress, which is why this is Ministry's last album. “We’ve been yabbering about the same stuff for 45 years,” he said. “Nothing’s changed. It has gotten worse, and so it’s time for a new generation to carry the torch because they’re not listening to our message.” LISTEN>>>

And the new generation are slamming AI in protests worldwide. Their anger is summed up by AI sceptic Ed Zitron: "No industry that demands everything from us - our land, our energy, our water, our jobs, our art, our writing, our attention and every dollar we have - should ever be treated with anything but revulsion." Yet Trump celebrated the reinstatement of Jensen Huang - the boss of the world's biggest AI firm, Nvidia, who had been sacked for an affair with an alleged Chinese spy - by posting an AI image of Huang holding up a bra on November 23. His move came after The New York Times said the emissions of the biggest US …

title: Palestine activists protest Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce lunch
content:
Sixty members and supporters of the Palestinian community protested outside the Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce (AICC) business luncheon on November 27 demanding that Israel end its genocide on Gaza.

The AICC is deeply embedded in Australian collaboration with Israel on arms production, much of which is centred in this city.

Organisations taking part included Adelaide University Students for Palestine. The university was a sponsor of the event and its Vice Chancellor was the guest speaker.

AICC promotes business with Israel’s military-industrial complex, including Elbit Systems and Rafael, and corporations involved in weapons, surveillance and illegal settlements.

The protesters demanded an end to the normalising of war crimes; an end to Adelaide University sponsorship of AICC; and an end to apartheid.

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: The irrationality of the AI bubble is the irrationality of the market
content:
The AI investment boom is one of the largest bets in the history of capitalism. Money is pouring into the tech industry. Global AI spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $10 trillion cumulatively by 2032. The priorities of the system are obscene. Ending world hunger, according to the United Nations World Food Programme, would cost $40 billion per year. Amazon is spending over four times this on AI infrastructure this year.

In Australia alone, $150 billion is committed to building AI infrastructure over the next five years. That money could be life-changing for workers if it was used for almost anything else. Diverting the money from the data centre buildout could fund Australia’s health and Medicare budget for one year. Imagine the improvements we could make to an over-stretched and under-funded hospital system. With $150 billion, we could house the 200,000 households on the public housing waiting list at an average cost of just under half a million dollars and still have $50 billion left over. 

The $150 billion committed to data centres could also be used to pay for the Labor government’s aged care expansion package 38 times over. Or we could fund a significant chunk of the green transition needed to limit runaway climate change. The Australian Energy Market Operator places the cost of decarbonising the National Electricity Market by 2050 at $122 billion.

​Alas, the ever-rational invisible hand of the market has decided that we need more data centres to power Elon Musk’s Grok AI and its

 epic, vulgar roasts

.

​That the AI boom is socially destructive is irrelevant to investors. Data centres guzzle fossil fuels and water and are a significant source of noise pollution, emitting a constant low, droning hum. Most of the data centre buildout is happening in working-class and poorer communities in Western Sydney, not in Mosman or Toorak.

In recent weeks, the AI stock market boom has faced a sharp downturn. This is not because the world’s capitalists have taken notice of the socially and environmentally destructive nature of the industry, but because they are concerned that future windfall profits may not materialise.

​AI is now integrated into the militaries across the world, the result of an AI arms race. The results are terrifying. Take Russia’s

 

ZALA Lancet drone

, which uses AI to spot and dive bomb targets free from human oversight.

​Bosses are using AI as an excuse to sack workers. In the past few weeks alone, Qantas, NAB and Canva have announced over 4,000 redundancies cumulatively. Moreover, the data centre buildout is pushing inflation upwards, which the Reserve Bank is using as an excuse to raise interest rates, pushing unemployment higher. It is yet another way the AI boom is coming at the expense of the working class.

​The insanities of the AI boom are the insanities of the market. It is only in a capitalist society driven by profit and competition that it makes sense for trillions of dollars to be ploughed into AI while working-class needs are neglected. For anything that would benefit the working class, governments and capitalists across the world cry poor. Yet when there’s a share market boom, trillions find their way into it with no thought for what society actually needs. 

It’s not like people are crying out for data centres. In the US midterm elections, when data centres were on the ballot, voters rejected data centre expansion or approved local restrictions in 40 out of 41 ballot measures. AI data centres are unpopular yet continue to be imposed on ordinary people. Genuine democracy and the capitalist market are incompatible.

Under capitalism, production occurs to enrich the capitalist class, not to meet human needs. Karl Marx wrote in Capital: “Accumulate, accumulate! That is Moses and the prophets!” In a market economy, maximising shareholder value counts for more than the cries of hungry children or the plight of the homeless. 

​The AI boom is making many capitalists astronomically rich. Tech billionaires gained a combined $845 billion through the first nine months of this year. The stock market has reached record highs multiple times in 2026. The benefits of the AI bubble concentrate at the top, in the hands of corporate executives, financiers and the rich more generally. Workers, on the other hand, receive almost nothing. There is no boom in wages. Huge speculative wealth sits alongside stagnant or falling living standards.

​No boom, however, can last forever …

author: Wendy Bacon
title: CAMouflage: Antisemitism conference for councils
content:
Several hundred people gathered at Martin Place on November 24 to oppose this week’s national Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM) Local Government Summit that will urge councils to impose the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism on communities.

The protest was organised by a number of pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist Jewish groups, including Palestine Justice Movement and Jews Against the Occupation ‘48 (JAO48), who defiantly vowed to continue fighting against Israel’s genocidal war and apartheid.

If the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition is enforced, the six speakers would face allegations of antisemitism. Those holding banners stating “Globalise the Intifada” and “Readers and Writers against Genocide” could be arrested if proposed laws, that CAM supports, are passed. All the speakers rejected CAM’s claim that anti-Zionism is antisemitism.

The protest included an absurdist theatre performance — CAM-ou FLAGE — created by the JAO ‘48. It effectively called out CAM, which purports to be about building social cohesion but which is more likely to add to social division, censorship and hierarchies of social discrimination.

By contrast, the conference itself quietly kicked off with welcome drinks and speeches at Bondi Surf Club, not far from the site of the Bondi massacre.

The first speaker was Sheina Gutnick, whose father, Reuven Morrison, was killed by the gunmen. Not long after the massacre, CAM appointed her as its public affairs officer.

Other opening night speakers included Tahli Blicblau, former director of strategic intelligence and capabilities at the NSW Crime Commission, now CEO of the Dor Foundation, which was established by ex-Liberal Treasurer Josh Frydenberg.

Another was David Solsky, who organised a hugely successful memorial Paddle Out after the massacre. He also spoke at last week’s Jerusalem Post Summit, encouraging investment in Israel.

The opening attracted about the same numbers as those who attended the protest. The conference organisers seem to have gone out of their way to avoid attention by keeping its locations secret, or perhaps to amplify the sense of threat. The newly-formed Armed Response Command attended.

Whereas the protesters issued a media release, which was ignored by mainstream media, CAM issued no such thing in the lead-up to its conference.

The silence stands in stark contrast to last year’s conference. That was organised in collaboration with PR agency Agenda C, which boasted that it achieved 972 media mentions.

This year’s media strategy was executed around Gutnick’s story, about turning the loss of her father into a constructive purpose. Gutnick told the Daily Telegraph: “If anyone were actually open to having a conversation with us, understand the work that we’re doing and what we are trying to achieve against the background of the horrific antisemitism that has exploded, unfortunately, within Australia.”

She also attacked lawyer Nick Hanna who, in a video, drew attention to CAM’s association with the extremist pro-Israel and Trump supporter Congressman Randy Fine for spreading “disinformation”. He responded with a second video.

In rejecting Hanna’s focus on CAM’s global connections, Gutnick failed to mention that her work for the conference included a trip to New York, where she consulted with two Zionist members of New York City Council, who are opponents of the Muslim Mayor Zoran Mandami.

Gutnick was quoted as saying: “We find ways to come together and address [challenges] with unity and strength. CAM offers an amazing and unique international platform.”

The protest groups, including JAO48, Palestine Justice Movement, Coalition of Women for Justice and Peace, initiated a letter-writing campaign to councils and promoted this week’s protest.

CAM’s CEO in Tel Aviv, Sacha Roytman, sprang into action with an open letter calling on councillors to attend. Roytman, who was busy in the United States meeting with 150 leaders to launch a tracker to monitor CAM progress, didn’t see the contradiction in arguing that critics are unfair, while highlighting his past IDF connections and/or the activities of the Zionist lobby.

He went further, suggesting: “To me, some of the rhetoric around this campaign echoes narratives I have seen promoted internationally by actors in Iran, Qatar, China, and Russia. That resemblance is not evidence that any of those governments organised or paid for this campaign. I am …

author: Unknown
title: AKP’li Savcı Sayan’dan Mehmet Şimşek’e: “Geldiğiniz günden beri hedefinizde çiftçi, işçi ve memur var”
content:
Eski Ağrı Belediye Başkanı AKP’li Savcı Sayan, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada Hazine ve Maliye Bakanı Mehmet Şimşek’i eleştirdi. Sayan, “Geldiğiniz günden beri hedefinizde köylü, çiftçi, esnaf, işçi ve memur var. Vatandaşın cebini boşaltmak ekonomi yönetmek değildir”

Sayan açıklamasında şu ifadeleri kullandı:

“Mehmet bey, aldınız da aldınız, peki neyi başardınız.

Üç yıldır ekonomi yönetiminin başındasınız.

Geldiğiniz günden beri hedefinizde köylü, çiftçi, esnaf, işçi ve memur var.

Berberin koltuğuna vergi müfettişi oturttunuz, çiftçinin pulluğuna vergi müfettişi bindirdiniz, esnafın kasasının başına vergi müfettişi diktiniz.

Aldınız da aldınız, ceza kestiniz de kestiniz.

Motorlu taşıtlardan çifte vergi aldınız, vergileri artırdınız.

Ancak enflasyon sorununu çözemediniz, vatandaşın belini doğrultacak bir ekonomi politikası ortaya koyamadınız.

Küçük esnafa yaptığınız denetimi MASAK’a, SPK’ya ve BDDK’ya da yaptırsaydınız bugün yüz binlerce vatandaşımız mağdur olmayacaktı.

Borsadaki manipülasyonların, fonlardaki usulsüzlüklerin ve milyarlarca dolarlık kayıpların önüne geçebilirdiniz.

Para toplayacağım dediniz, topladınız.

Elimizdeki rakamlara göre Sayın Nebati görevden ayrılırken 54 milyar dolar olan net döviz rezervimiz bugün

2 milyar dolara gerilemiş durumda.

Başarı dediğiniz buysa, alkışlamak lazım.

Vatandaşın cebini boşaltmak ekonomi yönetmek değildir.

Dışarıdan kurtarıcı diye getirdiklerimizin hikâyesi nedense hep aynı.

Kemal Derviş döneminde bankacılık krizinin ağır bedelini millet ödedi. Bugün de Sayın Mehmet Şimşek’in ekonomi politikalarının bedelini millet ödüyor.

Sizlerden son ricam; fon ve borsa mağdurlarını unutmayın, unutturmayın.

Bu vurgunlarda parmağı olduğu tespit edilen siyasetçileri, bürokratları ve iş insanlarını affetmeyin, hesap vermelerini sağlayın.

Berberin üç kuruşunun hesabını soran devlet, milyarlarca doların hesabını da sormalıdır.

Binmişiz bir alamete, gidiyoruz kıyamete.

NOT: Dün ekonomi kurmaylarımızın basın toplantısında yaptıkları “net değer” açıklaması, daha önce dile getirdiğim “Ana paralar ödenmedi, Sayın Cumhurbaşkanımız yanıltılıyor” sözlerimi doğruladı.

Hisselerin değer kaybetmiş son hâlini ana para kabul edip kelime oyunuyla “Ana paralar ödendi” dediler.

Böylece ana paraların gerçekte ödenmediğini ekonomi kurmaylarımız kendi ağızlarıyla teyit etmiş oldular.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: CMI Argentina
title: En lo que va de 2026 se iniciaron 232 procedimientos preventivos de crisis en empresas y ya es la cifra más alta en una década
content:
Multiplicó por 6 el número de 2023 y superó instancias de crisis como las de 2018 y 2019. Son cifras oficiales que el Ministerio de Capital Humano informó al Senado.


Los Procedimientos Preventivos de Crisis (PPC), instancia en la que las empresas negocian con los sindicatos ante posibles despidos o suspensiones, sumaron 232 casos en lo que va de 2026, según datos oficiales de la Secretaría de Trabajo de la Nación del Ministerio de Capital Humano. La cifra supera el total de trámites de cada año en la última década.


La serie de PPC pasó de 42 expedientes en 2023 a 131 en 2024 y 158 en 2025, según datos de Trabajo publicados por La Nación. Durante la pandemia, cuando el Gobierno puso en marcha el programa de Asistencia de Emergencia al Trabajo y la Producción (ATP), se iniciaron 26 procedimientos en 2020 y 24 en 2021. En 2018 y 2019, dos años que cerraron con caída del PBI, los PPC habían llegado a 158 y 184, respectivamente.


La información fue presentada por Capital Humano en el informe de gestión que envió el Poder Ejecutivo al Senado. El documento consignó que, al 4 de noviembre, 22 de los 232 trámites habían derivado en acuerdos homologados y otros 22 tenían un proyecto de homologación.


Según informó Capital Humano, las medidas aprobadas en los 22 acuerdos homologados alcanzaron a 7905 trabajadores. Entre los compromisos asumidos por las empresas, la cartera mencionó “garantizar la fuente de trabajo” y, cuando se pactaron suspensiones al amparo del artículo 223 bis de la Ley de Contrato de Trabajo, “no reducir la nómina de trabajadores”.


El procedimiento se tramita ante la Secretaría de Trabajo cuando una empresa prevé despedir o suspender, por razones económicas, tecnológicas o de fuerza mayor, a una proporción de su personal que supera el umbral fijado por ley: del 15% en las firmas de menos de 400 empleados, del 10% en las de entre 400 y 1000 y del 5% en las de más de 1000. La firma debe respaldar la situación que invoca con documentación.

author: Ed Pomfret
title: On Black Friday, Amazon Workers in Over 20 Countries Demand Their Fair Share
content:
A worker on Amazon’s $20 starting rate needs to work about 8.7 million years to earn as much as Bezos’s personal wealth.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The promotions started weeks ago. Fridges, sports shoes, air fryers — every one a deal of the day, every one ending at midnight, every one ending again tomorrow. Adobe expects Americans to spend $12.9 billion online on Black Friday alone. Shoppers are expected to have to use short-term credit plans to purchase more than $800 million in goods that day.

When wages can stretch no more, the corporations sell you the stretch.

The biggest deal is the one Amazon and Jeff Bezos get every day of the year through exploiting their workers. On Friday, the people who pack and drive those parcels will try to take some of it back.

Make Amazon Pay is a coalition founded in 2020 of more than 80 unions and campaign groups, led by UNI Global Union, the global union for service workers, and Progressive International.

The campaign’s demands: decent wages, safe work, union rights, fair taxation, and climate justice. This year, unions and campaigners in more than 20 countries are expected to take part in strikes and protests from November 27 to November 30.

In response to last year’s actions, an Amazon spokesperson called the campaign “intentionally misleading” and said Amazon offers “great pay, great benefits, and great opportunities.” Then the company published its numbers.

Amazon made $20.7 billion in profit between July and September 2026, on an operating margin of 13.9 percent, the highest in its history. That is about $225 million a day. Or $156,000 a minute, if you like your outrage in smaller change.

Amazon’s own press release puts U.S. warehouse starting pay at $20 an hour, or $41,600 for a full-time employee before tax. They do not reveal pay levels for their many part-time employees.

If that makes you angry, add your name to our petition to tax extreme wealth.

The company plans to spend about $220 billion this year, much of it on AI data centers. The company’s internal plan is to use robots to avoid hiring more than 600,000 U.S. workers by 2033. So the “great opportunities” come with an expiry date for many employees.

Forbes says Jeff Bezos, Amazon’s founder and executive chair, had a net worth of $361 billion on November 1, 2026. That makes him the second-richest person alive. The richest, Elon Musk, had a bad week earlier this month and didn’t notice.

A worker on Amazon’s $20 starting rate would need about 8.7 million years of full-time shifts to earn as much as Bezos’s personal wealth. Clock on 8.7 million years ago and you’d be finishing about now, if the scanner gun lets you take your break.

Bezos would like you to think he built his fortune himself. In reality, he built it with warehouse workers, delivery drivers, public roads, and every customer who ever paid extra for next-day delivery. Profits soared. The people holding the scanners got a $1 an hour rise in September.

Black Friday has gone global. So have the bills. In Nigeria, delivery-app Black Friday deals trended on X on November 20. The same week, the national statistics office put food inflation at 19.13 percent, and 31.43 percent in Lagos.

In Pakistan, the government’s weekly price index shows cooking gas up 111 percent in a year and tomatoes up 79 percent. In Brazil, the basic food basket in Fortaleza has risen 21.52 percent since December.

Nobody is running a Black Friday sale on rice.

The same rules produce both numbers. Big companies set the prices, pay trails behind, and the winners keep what they bank. That is a choice made by people with names, and governments can change it.

Six years in, Make Amazon Pay can point to concrete victories. In Italy, workers won a nationwide Amazon agreement curbing surveillance. In India, they won social-security protections for delivery workers. In Canada, warehouse workers have won union recognition. And across Germany, they’ve formed Amazon works councils, legally protected bodies through which employees elected by their peers represent worker interests before management.

On November 19, Brazil’s President Lula signed a decree ending the six-day workweek. Starting December 16, 14.8 million workers on six-day rotations get two days off a week with no pay cut. The maximum week drops from 44 hours to 42, then 40 in December 2027.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Public hearing set for Canadian North flight attendants’ potential strike
content:
There will be

a public hearing in Iqaluit next week to determine which Canadian North services must continue if the airline’s flight attendants go on strike.


The Canada Industrial Relations Board is holding the hearing next week at the Iqaluit Cadet Hall. It starts at 10 a.m. Nov. 30 and runs until Dec. 2,

Jean-Daniel Tardif, the board’s senior director of alternative dispute resolution services, said in an email.


The public can attend in person or remotely through Zoom

.


About 200 flight attendants, who are represented by the Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 8111,

could strike

 as early as Dec. 19 if they do not reach a new collective agreement with the airline.


The hearings will determine which of the airline’s services are essential, and therefore can’t cease, in the event of a strike or lockout.


The board previously invited the public to submit information about how a potential work stoppage could affect health and safety. The deadline for submissions was Nov. 20.

author: anred
title: El futuro del manejo del fuego se debatió en la Patagonia
content:
Foto: Gentileza UTT


Este fin de semana la Comarca Andina del Paralelo 42° fue escenario del Primer Congreso Nacional de Combate, Prevención, Políticas Públicas y Restauración Forestal, un encuentro nacional que fue el escenario para compartir experiencias, fortalecer capacidades y debatir cómo enfrentar los incendios forestales y sus impactos en los territorios.

Por Violeta Moraga (Equipo de Comunicación Popular Colectivo Al Margen).


Organizado por ATE y la Unión de Trabajadores de la Tierra Patagonia (UTT PATAGONIA), el Congreso reunió a brigadistas nacionales y provinciales y comunitarios, bomberos voluntarios, trabajadores forestales y de conservación, especialistas, técnicos, investigadores, productores, organizaciones y comunidades.


“A la hora de la tragedia, frente a un Estado que se va podando, achicando, desfinanciando, la comunidad se organiza e irrumpe. Las brigadas comunitarias son un claro ejemplo de eso”, dice Juan Pablo Acosta, coordinador general de la UTT Patagonia en diálogo con Al Margen y señala que, en la emergencia, también las organizaciones desarrollan sus propuestas, como es el curso de restaurador y restauradora forestal de la UTT.


“Frente a esa irrupción se generan instancias de coordinación con brigadistas institucionales. Para nosotros no hay una dicotomía: brigadas comunitarias sí, brigadas comunitarias no. Las brigadas comunitarias existen y van a seguir estando, sobre todo con un Estado que se retira de los territorios”, continúa Acosta.


Es en este marco es que se tomó la iniciativa de pensar este espacio: un momento donde encontrarse y construir articulaciones para que, al momento de la emergencia, haya algunos puntos que estén previamente discutidos. “El congreso tuvo esa impronta, tanto con la cuestión del combate del fuego como en la prevención y la restauración”.


“Los trabajadores enfrentamos un tiempo complejo y necesitamos respuestas urgentes. Los combatientes demandan un suplemento salarial de emergencia que se incorpore con carácter permanente al sueldo, pase a planta permanente y estabilidad, incorporación de más personal y que se impulse una ley que establezca un régimen jubilatorio diferencial por tareas de alto riesgo, como así también un régimen integral para los combatientes de incendios forestales”, expresó por su parte Rodolfo Aguiar, secretario general de ATE Nacional presente en el congreso.


“Si algo quedó claro es que no nos van a regalar nada, que vamos a tener que pelear. Aquellos que piensan que van a sobrevivir haciéndoles concesiones al Gobierno están perdidos. Sobreviven los que resisten, sobreviven los que luchan y nosotros vamos a luchar. Avanzaremos en una medida de fuerza de carácter nacional. Fueron dos días a puro debate que consolidan nuestro crecimiento y unidad. Las instituciones son los hombres y mujeres que la representan, y son ellos los que hacen la historia todos los días”, volcó el dirigente en sus redes.


“Avanzaremos en una medida de fuerza de carácter nacional. Fueron dos días a puro debate que consolidan nuestro crecimiento y unidad”, dijo Aguiar. Foto: ATE


“El congreso superó las expectativas, hubo una participación muy amplia de distintos sectores de la sociedad, de brigadas comunitarias, de brigadistas de Parques Nacionales, algunos provinciales, gente del Servicio Nacional de Manejo del Fuego y representantes de 13 provincias que estuvieron pasando por el congreso en distintas mesas propuestas”, dijo a Al Margen Marcelo “Chelo” Rojas, delegado de ATE en Parques Nacionales.


“Se pudieron abordar muy bien diversas cuestiones, algunas más relacionadas con el combate de incendios, con la prevención, con la necesaria articulación entre las instituciones y los vecinos, las brigadas, abordando este paradigma relativamente nuevo: las brigadas comunitarias y cómo pueden articular y colaborar con el laburo de las instituciones, cómo darles un marco en específico con respecto a la legislación, enfrentando también la problemática de las instituciones con sus prioridades y las de la comunidad organizada en sí misma, enfrentando este tipo de desastres que hoy en día se nos acercan a las ciudades con la noción de interfase”, continuó.


“Hubo un panel mucho más político el sábado, en el cual intervinieron diputados, senadores, legisladores provinciales. Estuvo Adriana Serquis, Ana Marks, José Glinski, Magdalena Odarda, Leandro García, vino Matías Oberlin del Observatorio de Tierras también para dar una mirada con respecto a lo que …
