author: Rose Nneoma Abba
title: Labors of liberation
content:
Ricci Shryock’s

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 is marketed as an account of the women who helped win the 11-year guerrilla war for independence from Portuguese colonial rule in Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Shryock’s book delivers on that promise with hyperrealistic scenes that drop you into mangrove forests where female teenagers and young adults shoot and dodge bullets, manage makeshift clinics, become mothers, devise new cooking technology, teach, gossip, and boil water for breakfast. 

It also exposes prejudice that women in the struggle faced at the hands of their fellow African men. A funny scene in the book exemplifies both the prejudice and the women’s handling of it. Shortly after Joana Gomes, a nurse and the book’s protagonist, joins a new base, the commander, who is also her distant cousin, threatens her that if she gets hurt, he will have to kill her. She replies that “as a nurse. . . .  even you, if you are injured and no-one can carry you I can give this medicine to you [to kill you].” As Carmen Pereira, a prominent guerrilla fighter with the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), nurse, and later acting head of state, famously observed: “In Guinea-Bissau, we say that women must fight against two colonialisms. One against the Portuguese, the other against men.”

But beyond illustrating women’s agency in the struggle, the book also offers timely provocations on our relationship with nature, the labor that sustains revolutions, elite-led movements, and the individual costs of collective struggle.

One of the book’s greatest strengths is its exploration of how the PAIGC’s vision of a future state manifested in practice long before victory was formally declared. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 to achieve independence for Guinea and Cape Verde from Portuguese colonial rule. For the party, building for the future state was just as vital as tearing down Portuguese colonial rule. 

This state-building effort is most visible in the book’s heartwarming scenes of education. We witness it when Joana’s father goes out of his way to secure teachers for his daughters. And again when 11-year-old Joana and her friends are instructed by Amílcar Cabral to teach the other teenagers on a boat trip from Guinea-Bissau to Guinea-Conakry. We learn that the PAIGC built 156 primary schools during the war across liberated territories compared to 11 created under Portuguese neglect. We also see the PAIGC send young Guineans to the Soviet Union and Cuba to master guerrilla combat tactics as well as medicine, engineering, agronomy, and teaching for the nation they were bringing into existence.

The book takes a firm stand: The success of a liberation struggle depends on the viable, egalitarian alternative structure you build to ground your sovereignty while you fight the oppressive power. As Shryock writes in the introduction, it is “a story worth knowing as a universal lesson in the undeniable courage it takes to imagine a new world, the way creation rather than destruction is integral to that new world.” Through Joana’s story, Shryock holds a steady lens on women’s central role in designing and executing that vital labor of building Guinean sovereignty from the ground up.

Shryock opens the book with a scene that haunts the entire reading experience: 22-year-old Joana inside a dry-season mangrove forest, where she had gone to retrieve a commander who was recovering from a lung infection. “Gnarly, bare mangrove branches protruding from the muddy riverbed stare back at [Joana],” setting the tone for the book from the very first page. 

The land, its trees, and its waters are alive. At times angry, at times hungry, mostly gracious, and systematically exploited by the Portuguese regime. And it was precisely this ecological exploitation that precipitated the revolution. Cabral, the founder of the PAIGC, was an agronomist by training, and his radicalization took root while he was conducting an agricultural census commissioned by the United Nations and the colonial Portuguese government. There, he saw firsthand how Portuguese land policies and price controls were squeezing the life out of both the land and the people tilling it.

As the Guineans fought for the land, the land protected them. Whether it is Joana tripping over an exposed root and narrowly dodging a bullet or people abandoning their towns to seek shelter in the forest, “besides the Soviets and the Cubans, the land [proved] to be the liberation …

author: Gastbeitrag
title: Die Spur der Roten Lunte – Aus dem Gerichtssaal: Über die revolutionäre Kontinuität
content:
– In der Geschichte revolutionärer Klassenkämpfe, in der Geschichte internationalistischen Kämpfe ist die Konfrontation mit der Konterrevolution ein Muss, denn es wird nun mal die Machtfrage gestellt. –


„

Bitte stell mir keine Fragen zum Gerichtsprozess“, stellt die Genossin im Gespräch nach der Bekanntgabe ihrer Verurteilung klar. „Das interessiert uns wirklich nicht.“ Lieber mag sie sich über die revolutionäre Perspektive und den aktuellen Widerstand austauschen. Widerstand ist notwendig, wenn die herrschenden Verhältnisse unerträglich werden. Doch wo Widerstand ist, ist die Repression nicht weit. Der Prozess gegen unsere Genossin Andi ist dafür ein Beispiel: Wegen ihrer Beteiligung an antifaschistischen, klimapolitischen und antimilitaristischen Protesten wurde sie jüngst zu mehreren Monaten Haft verurteilt. Dabei geht es längst um mehr als eine einzelne Angeklagte. Es geht um den politischen Umgang mit all jenen, die sich gegen die herrschenden Zustände organisieren und zur Wehr setzen. Doch wie wird aus einem bürgerlichen, konterrevolutionären Gerichtsprozess eine Stärkung der revolutionären Perspektive? Und was hat es mit dieser Lunte auf sich?


Von der Prozessgruppe „Spieß umdrehen“ Zürich


Von Beginn weg war klar, dass uns die konterrevolutionäre Seite eigentlich nicht interessiert. Wir haben eine lange Erfahrung in den Auseinandersetzungen zwischen Revolution und Konterrevolution. Die Position, die wir dazu haben, ist seit Jahren immer die gleiche: Wir sagen, Revolution und Konterrevolution, das ist ein dialektisches Paar. In der Geschichte revolutionärer Klassenkämpfe, in der Geschichte des Internationalismus, ist die Konfrontation mit der Konterrevolution ein Muss, denn darin wird die Machtfrage gestellt.


In diesem dialektischen Prozess liegt sehr viel Potenzial, sich auf die Fragen zu konzentrieren, die heute auf der Tagesordnung der Revolutionär:innen, egal ob kommunistischen, antifaschistischen, anarchistischen oder internationalistischen Linken, stehen.


Wir sind uns bewusst, dass die Beschäftigung mit der Konterrevolution immer mit einer Selbstverteidigung einhergeht. Dabei verstehen wir die Selbstverteidigung keineswegs als passive Verteidigung, sondern als ein Moment der Konfrontation. Indem wir unser Eigenes, unsere Kultur, unser Erkämpftes im Kleinen und Großen verteidigen, stärken wir die eigene, innere, revolutionäre Seite.


Selbstverteidigung im Sinne der Verstärkung der eigenen Seite und Konfrontation gegenüber der Konterrevolution.


Wir konzentrierten uns in der Kampagne auf den revolutionären Prozess, die revolutionäre Perspektive und die Frage, wo wir heute darin stehen. Auch mit einem Blick auf die Geschichte: Diese verläuft in Etappen, welche alle ihre Besonderheiten beherbergen. Darin müssen wir uns die Frage der Kontinuität des revolutionären Prozesses stellen, denn in ihr liegt die eigentliche Sprengkraft. Wie an diese Kontinuität anknüpfen? Wie verläuft die rote Lunte? Wir sind uns bewusst, dass die historischen Etappen und Phasen in der heutigen Zeit sich viel schneller entwickeln und wir uns schwertun, rechtzeitig antizipieren zu können. Deswegen haben wir den Prozess als Anlass genommen, uns auf unsere Seite zu konzentrieren, und analysiert, was wir für Erfahrungen und Kräfte auf unserer Seite haben.


Der Blick in die Geschichte bringt uns nach vorne


Es gibt einen revolutionären Strang der Geschichte. Wir haben als Bild dafür die Zündlunte gewählt. Dies ist wichtig zu sehen, um zu erkennen, was der revolutionäre Prozess war, wie er sich zusammengesetzt hat und was das aufs Jetzt übertragen heißt.


Dabei haben wir viel Wissen und Erfahrungen, sei es jetzt durch unsere lange Zeit der revolutionären Klassenkämpfe im eigenen Land wie international, aktuell u.a. der

Roten Hilfe International

oder der

Widerstandsvernetzung Schweiz

, und können daraus sehen, welche Errungenschaften und historischen Erkenntnisse wir zur Verfügung haben, um darauf aufzubauen. Dabei fragen wir uns natürlich in erster Linie: Was ist ein revolutionärer Prozess, und woraus setzt er sich zusammen?


Auch hier führt uns die rote Lunte zu unseren heutigen Fragen der Kontinuität. Der Revolutionäre Prozess ist nicht irgendwie einfach qualunquistisch

(Anm.d.Red.: apolitisch, jenseits des Handelns einer politischen Partei)

 oder an die eigene Wahrnehmung gebunden, sondern funktioniert nach revolutionären, marxistischen Gesetzmäßigkeiten. Es geht darum, mit welchen Methoden und Analysen wir eine …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Americans also don’t like Pax Silica nor Trump
content:
By Viggo Sarmago


People from abroad visited the three day campout (kampuhan) in Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila as part of the progressive group’s campaign against Pax Silica and protest against the visit of US President Donald Trump. 


Landon Little is an American who stumbled upon the campout. It was his first protest, and was initially curious as to why Filipinos were angry at Pax Silica. For him, their frustrations are as clear as day.


A portrait of Little during the first day of the encampment. Photo by Viggo Sarmago


Indigenous Peoples and progressive organisations have been condemning the Pax Silica Initiative, and the Luzon Economic Corridor as it threatens to displace farmers and indigenous communities, destroy and poison its surrounding environment, and undermine national sovereignty, deepening U.S. intervention in Philippine soil. 


“It’s all motivated by money. And if we look back at history, this has happened thousands thousands of times…For example, Europeans, when they came and immigrated to America, they kicked out Native Americans. It’s the same exact thing that’s happening right now to the [Indigenous Peoples]. So I think that it is just history repeating itself,” Little explained. 


Christopher Teixeira is an American-Brazillian who has been living in the Philippines for over a year. He saw posts about the campout circulating online, and decided to join in solidarity. As someone with Guatemalan descent, he says that he is acutely aware of the adverse effects of U.S. intervention and war. 


He adds that his fight is also personal, as American communities are currently dealing with data centers that have been documented to poison the local water supply, raise the temperatures of nearby areas, and are disruptively noisy making it extremely difficult for communities to live peacefully near them.


A portrait of Teixeira during the first day of the encampment. Photo by Viggo Sarmago


For Teixeira, these data centers and AI infrastructure were promised by big tech giants to bring many “jobs and opportunities” in the same way Pax Silica is being vaguely framed as a project geared to progress national development. 


He strongly believes that the fight against these data centers is the same fight against Pax Silica especially in a globalized world.  


“We live in a [crumbling] neoliberal order…With that interconnectedness, what it leads me to think is that nothing happens in isolation. If Pax Silica passes here, where else might the U.S. want to expand? Will it be more in the Philippines? Will it be in other nations that might rely on U.S. funding? Who knows?”, Teixeira asked. “So anything that the U.S. touches that isn’t inherently ours, I don’t think we should touch it. I think that’s it.”


Renewed hope through international solidarity

 


Despite it all, Teixeira remains hopeful for a better future. He cites the recent “blue wave” during the U.S. midterm elections, referring to votes heavily swinging toward Democratic Senators and Representatives, who as of writing is projected to take the majority of seats in Congress. 


For Tiexiera, this shows America’s clear distaste for Trump’s actions in his second term as President, notably the wars he waged on Iran and West Asia that saw the extreme spike of oil prices from around the globe. 


Dev Pillai, of International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines (ICHRP), shared the same sentiments, and joined the campout because “We hate Trump too.”


 “[The blue wave] is a referendum for the American people on Trump. So we’re seeing that more and more people are hating the war agenda. And that is what the Filipino people have been fighting for many, many years… So we as US citizens have a responsibility to build link arms with the Filipino people in their fight against war,” Pillai stated.


“[Trump] is just coming here out of the midterm elections and thinking that he can hash out more unequal agreements with Filipino people but also other Southeast Asian peoples,” he added.


Pillai underscored the necessity of international solidarity to fight against the plundering of nations like the Philippines because of the greed of imperialists like Donald Trump, and asserted that there is no other choice but to join the struggle. 


“We’re seeing that the crisis is getting worse and worse. It’s having a serious devastating impact on the people, on workers and peasants across the world. And so we really have to tackle the root cause here and link arms …

author: Keston K. Perry
title: The imperialism of progressive economics
content:
Progressive economics has an imperial problem. It is possible to denounce inequality, defend redistribution, and criticize neoliberalism while preserving a deeper hierarchy: the presumption that experts, often based in powerful institutions in the Global North, can determine what justice should mean for societies shaped by slavery, colonial extraction, and imperial rule. The issue is not simply whether their intentions are good or their proposals sufficiently radical. It is who has the power to define the problem, decide which histories count and prescribe solutions after short field visits or, worse, on conference calls, before those most affected have determined the terms of repair.

This contradiction is particularly visible in debates about reparations and climate finance. Universal basic income, public ownership, cheaper credit, and expanded development finance can all be useful demands. None, however, returns stolen land, reverses accumulated colonial wealth, repairs ecological destruction, or restores collective authority over political and economic life. Redistribution and reparations can reinforce one another; they are not interchangeable. When the former is offered as a substitute for the latter, progressive universalism becomes a way of setting aside historically specific claims.

I encountered this argument during a debate about reparations in 2020. A senior economist asked where reparative claims should begin and end, questioned the feasibility of identifying descendants of enslaved people, and suggested universal income or shared dividends funded by wealth taxes as more practicable responses. The framing exposes an asymmetry: Why must restitution meet an exceptional test of feasibility while universal redistribution is treated as a reasonable starting point? Who decides which demands are too complicated to count as politics?

The point is not to dismiss universal social provision. It is to insist that the injuries of empire cannot be reduced to unequal household incomes. Colonialism reorganized property, labor, public finance, land tenure, and the authority to govern. Repair must be capable of transforming those relationships, not merely compensating people for living within them.

At a conference on African economic sovereignty in Dakar in 2022, I heard related arguments from progressive economists who treated nationalization or the green developmental state as ready-made alternatives to reparations. State ownership and planning can be indispensable instruments of transformation. Yet our meeting in the Museum of Black Civilizations was a striking setting in which to overlook the intellectual traditions and struggles through which African peoples have articulated their own visions of sovereignty. A model developed in one context does not become universal because its advocates consider themselves anti-neoliberal. The question is who defines the political horizon, and whose knowledge is allowed to unsettle it.

A similar dilemma runs through the international sustainability industry. Island and African societies confronting climate disasters are surrounded by consultants, conveners, investment platforms, and intermediaries promising innovation. International collaboration is not inherently objectionable. What matters is who controls the agenda, data, networks, and resulting resources. When communities supply experiences while outsiders translate them into fundable or bankable projects, an old division of labor survives under the language of partnership.

The Bridgetown Initiative brings these contradictions into focus. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has rightly drawn attention to the global financial system’s unequal treatment of climate-vulnerable countries. The initiative has pushed sovereign debt, liquidity, Special Drawing Rights, and multilateral development bank reform onto an international agenda that too often marginalizes small states. Yet recognition of an unjust financial architecture is not the same as transforming the relations of ownership and creditor power that sustain it. Expanded access to finance can leave the underlying distribution of wealth, risk, and power largely intact.

Consider what financial innovation means when disaster strikes. After Hurricane Beryl in 2024, Grenada activated a disaster clause that deferred debt-service payments. This created fiscal breathing room, but deferred payments were added to principal: relief in the timing of repayment, not cancellation of the …

author: Unknown
title: Mangelhafte Recherche als Kritik verpackt
content:
Nach der Demo gegen Imperialismus vom 11. Oktober 2026 schrieb Noctua Rosa Moser einen Meinungsartikel bei "Dilemma" (ehemalig "Das Lamm). Statt einer differenzierten Perspektive oder einer solidarischen Kritik, setzte die Redakteur*in auf einen Kahlschlag gegen die Demo und die dahinterstehende Bewegung: Eine Gegenkritik.


Wir sind zwei der Bewegung vom 11. Oktober gegenüber solidarisch eingestellten Genoss*innen. In dieser Replik werden Inhalte des Textes von Noctua auf den Prüfstand gestellt. Ursprünglich war geplant, die Gegenkritik bei "Dilemma" selbst zu publizieren: das hat jedoch nicht geklappt, jedenfalls nicht so, dass die Bedürfnisse beider Seiten befriedigt gewesen wären. Das ist mitunter ein Grund, warum dieser Beitrag nun etwas verspätet erscheint. Unser Text sollte ohne Vorwissen verständlich sein: eine Auseinandersetzung mit der Ursprungskritik ist aber von Vorteil. Zugleich soll unser Beitrag auch eine Vertiefung in vielerlei Fragen bieten, die nicht immer direkt mit der Kritik zusammenhängt bzw. sie mancherorts nur streift.


Bereits im ersten Abschnitt liest sich ein Punkt, der so nicht stehen gelassen werden kann. In der Aufzählung zur angemessenen Militanz vom 11. Oktober letzten Jahres – wie die Autorin es selbst nennt – wird mit den durchaus nachvollziehbaren zerlegten Bankgebäuden und dem Trotz gegenüber den Polizeisperren dann auch gleich die Brandstiftung eines Restaurants in einem Atemzug genannt. Doch wer diese Flamme gelegt hat und aus welcher Überlegung heraus, ist bis heute ungeklärt – ein Agent Provocateur ist nicht auszuschliessen. Unabhängig davon, möchten wir der Autor*in dennoch widersprechen, dass diese angemessen war. Unser Widerspruch dazu soll nicht moralistisch gelesen werden: Was ist schon ein Feuer vor einem Restaurant – wo kein Mensch physisch zu Schaden kam – im Kontrast dazu, dass dieser Staat einen Völkermord unterstützt und breite Teile der Bevölkerung diesem gleichgültig bis unterstützend begegnen? Natürlich ist es geheuchelt, wenn ausgerechnet da plötzlich alle möglichen Nutzniesser*innen des Imperialismus die Frage der Gerechtigkeit aufmachen, diesen Vorfall in den Fokus nehmen und dabei nicht selten den Protest als Ganzes delegitimieren. Wenn in unseren aktuellen Verhältnissen aber zur Militanz gegriffen wird, dann sollte sowohl das Ziel der Militanz, das Ausmass und die inhaltliche Begleitung davon aus revolutionärer und klassenbewusster Perspektive heraus möglichst einleuchtend sein: das sehen wir bei diesem Feuerlegen alles als nicht gegeben an.


Anschliessend wird der Demotag diesen Jahres folgendermassen beschrieben: «Dieses Mal ohne grossen Demonstrationszug und ohne Gewalt: Kleingruppen verteilten sich in der Stadt, färbten Brunnen, malten mit Kreide und kleisterten vereinzelt Plakate.» Damit werden zentrale Facetten der Demo ausgeklammert, die dann auch im restlichen Text vergeblich gesucht werden. Um das Bild also wieder gerade zu rücken, ist folgendes festzuhalten: Die Bewegung ist in der ganzen Stadt präsent gewesen – trotz Hunderte von Bullen aus der ganzen Schweiz. Es gab verschiedene Blöcke und nicht nur "diesen einen" oder "Kleingruppen", wie es die Leitmedien – und nun auch das Lamm – darstellen und die Bewegung damit kleinreden. Eine Velodemo fuhr entschlossen vom Eigerplatz bis zum Bundesplatz durch alle möglichen Strassen und Gassen. Über 250 Menschen, die im Demoticker die Aufrufe mitverfolgten, haben sich bei der Zytglogge, auf dem Waisenhausplatz und in der gesamten unteren Altstadt die Strasse genommen. Zu guter Letzt kam dann auch der Demozug, der sich durch den Breitsch und die Lorraine bewegte, zum Banhofsplatz hoch. An all diesen Orten wurden gehaltvolle Reden gehalten – etwa zur medialen Komplizenschaft von Tamedia im Genozid, zum kurdischen Befreiungskampf oder eine Rede zu Palästina und imperialer Besatzung generell. In allen Demos wurden laut und entschlossen Parolen geschrien. Auch Aktionen wie bpsw. der Bannerdrop am Bahnhof und die Trumpfigur auf dem Bubenbergplatz oder, dass sich ca. 1'000 Leute den Bahnhofsplatz nahmen, ist der Autor*in keine Erwähnung wert. Die Autor*in bringt die Demo also um eine Menge Inhalte und Formen, zeichnet das Bild einer umkämpferischen, beinahe kindlichen Bewegung und streicht jegliche Informationen heraus, die diesem Zerrbild zuwider laufen. Zu einer ernsthaften und solidarischen Kritik würde an dieser Stelle die Erwähnung aller Akzente der Demo dazugehören – gerade, wenn diese mit dem Inhalt der …

author: ROAPE
title: Statement of the Finishers Revolutionary Movement
content:
At the beginning of this year, young Ugandans (activists, researchers, academics and lawyers) came together under one roof to confront a question that could no longer be postponed: what becomes of Uganda after the sham elections of January 2026?


With the possibility of Muhoozi Kainerugaba succeeding his father, we gathered around a simple conviction: Uganda must not be handed from one generation of the same ruling family to another. Succession is not liberation. Changing the face at the top while preserving the same machinery of patronage, militarism and corruption is not the future Uganda deserves.


Under the name Finishers Revolutionary Movement, we committed ourselves to organizing Ugandans to reject this succession project and to take up the unfinished work of national democratic liberation.


What we stand for


The Finishers is more than a name. It is an idea: that Uganda’s liberation cannot remain an unfinished historical promise, and that our generation has a responsibility to finish the task. That means we will:


End dictatorship.


Dismantle systems of patronage and impunity.


Reclaim democratic power for the people.


Build a country capable of true economic independence.


What have we done


Since the beginning of the year, we have been organizing, teaching and rallying people to confront injustice and corruption and to recover the spirit of resistance that every generation of Ugandans has inherited. We have reminded our people that oppression survives not only through the violence of the state, but also through fear, silence and the belief that nothing can change.


Because political freedoms in Uganda have been brutally restricted, we have had to organize with caution. Much of our work has been quiet and covert, because even the ordinary act of bringing Ugandans together has become dangerous.


Why we write in mourning


In the last month, the state has descended on the Finishers with an iron hand. Three of our comrades have been arrested or disappeared.


Praise Aloikin 

was arrested, later released on court bail, and continues to face the state through an ongoing court case.


Byakika Abubaker 

and 

David Musiri 

have been taken, and their whereabouts remain unknown.


We mourn them. We fear for them. We are angry.


Yet we refuse to let their disappearance become the disappearance of an idea. The state may arrest a Finisher. It may abduct a Finisher. It may intimidate a Finisher. But it cannot arrest the hunger for freedom that brought us together.


We are Finishers. We are not terrorists. We are young Ugandans who looked at the country we are inheriting and decided we cannot remain spectators to its destruction. We chose to organize. We chose to resist. And we choose to continue.


Our demands


That the state immediately disclose the whereabouts of Byakika Abubaker and David Musiri, and return them safely to their families.


That the state end enforced disappearances and abductions of Ugandans for their political beliefs and organizing.


That the state stop criminalizing the right to organize, assemble and hold political ideas.


That Praise Aloikin be afforded a fair process, and that the case against her be dropped.


Our appeal to the people of Uganda


Do not leave the Finishers alone. Protect your own. Protect the people who are standing up for the country we all claim to love.


When a Finisher is taken, ask where they are. When a family is left searching for a disappeared son or daughter, stand with that family. When the state attempts to criminalize an idea, refuse to repeat its lies. When fear tells you to look away, remember that the person taken today could be your neighbour, your child, your brother, your sister, or you tomorrow.


The Finishers belong to the people, and so does the idea. You do not have to carry our name to carry it. You do not have to stand where we stand to believe that dictatorship must end. You do not have to be an activist to understand that Uganda cannot be inherited like a family estate


Our resolve


We do not know what the state will do next. We know only that repression is meant to make us disappear one by one, to isolate us from each other and to convince Uganda that resistance is futile. We refuse that outcome.


The disappearance of our comrades has deepened our grief, but it has also clarified our resolve. We will remember those who have been taken. We will stand with their families. We will demand their return. And we will continue the …

author: ROAPE
title: Africa’s green stewardship
content:
“First we were dispossessed in the name of kings and emperors, later in the name of state development, and now in the name of conservation” –Indigenous delegation, Fifth World Parks Congress (2003)


I remember that familiar anecdote beneath email signatures during my brief time within the United Nations (UN) system. It read, “please consider the environment before printing this email.” Similar reminders far beyond the UN invoke a familiar ethic of environmental responsibility, particularly around the use of paper and the depletion of natural carbon sinks, namely trees.


Such institutional gestures are largely unobjectionable and even function as legitimising paraphernalia for highly corporatised entities, including NGOs. Much like ethical sourcing labels attached to coffee, clothing and other consumer goods, they can furnish institutions and businesses with the symbolic credentials of environmental stewardship, leaving the structures of production and accumulation seemingly untouched and, by implication, legitimate.


This also speaks to a broader ‘bandwagonism’ within international development, and to the insularity of development professionals when it comes to interrogating the political questions embedded within such global framings. In hindsight, the email footnotes reveal not only symbolic expression of environmental responsibility within development practice, but also the moralising and legitimising weight attached to green stewardship and, more broadly, sustainable development.


Yet this moral vocabulary leaves largely unexamined how sustainability is defined, whose interests environmental policies serve, who bears their disproportionate costs, who captures their benefits, and whose lands and livelihoods become subject to environmental governance. These political-economic questions are also bound up with the knowledge systems through which nature and sustainable development are understood and governed.


Don’t take this the wrong way. I am not suggesting that climate change is a hoax, nor am I opposed to greening development. Rather, I am concerned with how proponents of market-led development, including the UN, IMF and World Bank, predominantly sidestep the profit motives embedded within contemporary environmentalism. In doing so, my UN email footnote risks becoming little more than a LinkedIn hashtag, a symbolic display of environmental virtue within a corporatised world.


Yet the market, understood here in its neoliberal capitalist form, is neither benign nor guided by an invisible hand capable of resolving ecological crises. Its constellation around profiteering and accumulation has historically subordinated human and ecological wellbeing to the imperatives of capital. Situating climate change within the history of global capitalism makes legible how the extraordinary wealth enjoyed by many countries in the Global North was built through centuries of fossil-fuelled expansion, resource extraction and colonial dispossession.


What is particularly troubling today is the transformation of this historical contradiction into a new environmental frontier, where the mechanisms of accumulation that have contributed to ecological crisis are increasingly mobilised and legitimised as means of resolving it.


This logic takes shape in multiple guises, including banking nature, green capital, carbon trading, biodiversity credits, ecosystem payment services,

REDD+

, conservation finance and nature tourism. Put simply, forests become carbon sinks, biodiversity becomes natural capital, ecological processes become ecosystem services, and landscapes become financial and tourism assets capable of generating economic value.


Nature is thus increasingly rendered legible through the language of capital, where its ecological functions can be measured, priced and incorporated into circuits of global investment and accumulation. Environmental protection is consequently framed not as a challenge to capitalism, but as a new frontier for investment, accumulation and market expansion.


Once these concepts enter the vocabulary of global development, and more specifically the language of institutions such as the UN, they acquire considerable moral and institutional authority. They travel from donor conditionalities into national policy frameworks, where market-based approaches to environmental protection become normalised as legitimate and even necessary pathways to sustainability. author: ROAPE
title: Who gets to make Ethiopia’s peace?
content:
Ethiopia’s newest opposition alliance contains a remarkable contradiction. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the main party in northern Tigray, now shares a coalition with the Amhara Fano National Movement, although their forces fought on opposite sides of the devastating 2020–2022 war.

[1]

 The Oromo Liberation Army and organizations rooted in Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz also appeared in its founding declaration.

[2]


Announced on 20 September 2026 as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, the coalition seeks Abiy’s removal and an inclusive transitional administration. Its advertised seven-member composition was soon disputed: the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement denied membership on 26 September.

[3]


Removing a government requires agreement about an adversary. Constructing the political order that follows requires agreement about something much harder: who may exercise power, how that power will be limited, what happens to rival armies, how disputed territory will be governed, which crimes from the previous war will be investigated, and who has the authority to write the rules of a transition.


Opposition to Abiy may be sufficient to create a wartime coalition. It is not, by itself, a postwar settlement. Events have since altered the military balance. Tigrayan forces seized the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire in September, actions the African Union described as inconsistent with the Pretoria Agreement.

[4]

 Britain condemned the seizures and rejected the alliance’s objective of overthrowing the government, while calling for an end to hostilities and renewed dialogue.

[5]


By early October, federal and allied forces had retaken Mekelle after the TPLF withdrew. Their allies include the Tigray Peace Force, composed of former TPLF fighters.

[6]

 On 16 October, Abiy announced a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, tasked with restoring services, facilitating displaced people’s return and preparing elections.

[7]

 Fighting nevertheless continued: ACLED reported clashes in northwestern Tigray on 19 October.

[8]


These reversals change the immediate question. Alongside the alliance’s claim to determine a transition stands the federal government’s ability to reshape Tigray’s administration through military success. Neither battlefield control nor an electoral timetable, by itself, establishes that civilians can freely determine their political future. Military power can determine who cannot be ignored. It does not automatically determine who is entitled to rule.


A coalition united by a common opponent


The alliance presents itself as an answer to a profound political crisis. Its members accuse Abiy’s government of centralizing power, producing insecurity and restricting political space.

[9]

 Some concerns overlap with independent findings. Human Rights Watch has documented arrests of journalists, newsroom raids and regulatory pressure on independent outlets.

[10]

But opposition to the federal government does not erase the histories separating the coalition’s members.


Fano forces fought alongside the federal side against Tigrayan forces during much of the 2020–2022 war, before entering their own confrontation with the federal government in 2023.

[11]


The TPLF, which dominated Ethiopia’s ruling coalition

 before Abiy took office in 2018, signed the Pretoria Agreement and subsequently alleged federal failures to implement it; the Oromo Liberation Army has pursued a separate insurgency in Oromia.

[12]


Their present cooperation rests chiefly on agreement about what they oppose. Reuters reported when the coalition was announced that its members remained divided over territorial and political questions.

[13]

 These disagreements concern how the Ethiopian state itself is organized. Ethiopia’s constitution links regional boundaries to language, identity, settlement patterns and consent, while protecting communities’ right to self-government.

[14]


The clearest example is the territory commonly called Western Tigray by Tigrayans and Welkait-Tegede by many Amhara claimants. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented competing claims, earlier abuses under TPLF-led rule against Amhara and Walqayte communities, and wartime ethnic cleansing of Tigrayans under Amhara-controlled authorities.

[15]

 Hundreds of thousands of displaced Tigrayans remained unable to return when Human Rights Watch reported continuing persecution in April.

[16]

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: A place to call home, but only for six months: Yellowknife Housing First secures temporary housing
content:
Marlena Francis and her boyfriend, Preston Beaulieu, spent nights in Yellowknife shelters, never knowing if they would be turned away.


Becoming Housing First residents brought some stability, but it did not end the uncertainty. A fire forced them out of their first apartment at Sunridge. After two weeks in a hotel, they moved into a unit in Norseman, where they stayed for a little more than a year before facing another displacement.


“They [YKWS] didn’t really have a place for us to go for a while and I was losing a lot of sleep,” Francis said. “I really thought that we were going to be back on the streets.”


This summer, six downtown apartment buildings were sold by property management giant Northview Residential REIT to Montreal-based Balto Capital Inc.


As part of the sale, Northview moved to evict tenants in all 23 units rented by Housing First clients by Oct. 31.


At the eleventh hour, the society reached an agreement with the new property owners, allowing Housing First residents to live together in one building at Dorset Apartments.


Francis and Beaulieu are among 20 clients now receiving services in one centralized location.


Francis said she has already started settling into the space.


“I actually got my creativity back, and I’m actually enjoying drawing,” Francis said. “I love cooking and I have a working oven again.”


But the new arrangement is guaranteed for only six months. The lease with Balto Capital ends April 30, 2027, leaving the society with another deadline to find somewhere for residents to live.


The limits of scattered housing


Becky Broderick Basil, executive director of Yellowknife Women’s Society (YKWS), says the previous model made it difficult to provide the consistent support the program was designed to offer.


For more than a decade, YKWS has delivered its Housing First program by renting individual units scattered across the city. The society was responsible for supporting residents but had limited control over the conditions in the buildings where they lived.


Residents described apartments with poor upkeep, longstanding repair requests, and disruptive conditions.


Beaulieu, who lived with Francis at Norseman, recalled a bathtub that was plugged and leaking for about two weeks.


“We couldn’t use the tub and it was leaking and plugged,” he said. “We had to sit there and scoop water and make sure it didn’t overflow, for like forever.”


Over the years,

APTN News

 has


reported on tenant complaints about maintenance and safety in Northview buildings

, while reporting by


Cabin Radio has documented legal rulings

 involving basic upkeep and repairs.


Myles Nelson, another Housing First resident, described the noise and activity outside his former apartment at Fort Gary. He said he would watch from his balcony and see what he described as unsavoury foot traffic and drug deals.


“At Fort Gary, the doors would smash and crash just outside my apartment,” Nelson said. “You didn’t even pay attention anymore because it was just natural, but now we’re here [Dorset], you don’t hear anything.”


Myles Nelson, another Housing First resident, described the noise and activity outside his former apartment at Fort Gary. Photo: APTN News/Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs


When being housed doesn’t mean being treated like a tenant


For Housing First residents, the challenges of scattered-site housing went beyond maintenance. Broderick says residents also faced discrimination and scrutiny from people responsible for managing the buildings where they lived.


She says the stigma attached to homelessness and the Housing First label could follow residents into their homes, affecting how landlords, security personnel and contractors treated them.


“When you’re used to scattered market rent and you’re discriminated against and you face security and landlords and even contractors and mechanical people coming in and out of your unit like you’re not even there or being treated badly by security just trying to go home,” Broderick said.


Broderick says the society saw how that scrutiny played out through regular reports from private security contractors.


In 2022, Northview hired Equity Security to address complaints about unsafe conditions in and around its properties. Broderick says YKWS began receiving weekly reports from the company, known as “trouble tenant” reports.

author: infolibre
title: Υπό κατάληψη το 1ο ΕΠΑΛ και το 2ο ΓΕΛ Νεάπολης – Σοβαρές καταγγελίες για τη θέρμανση και ελλείψεις σε εκπαιδευτικούς και εξοπλισμό
content:
ΦΩΤΟ-ΡΕΠΟΡΤΑΖ Ανθή Κ.


Σε κατάληψη βρίσκονται δύο σχολεία στη Νεάπολη, το 1 ΕΠΑΛ και το 2 ΓΕΛ, που βρίσκονται στο ίδιο κτιριακό συγκρότημα με σοβαρά προβλήματα που αφορούν την κατάσταση των σχολικών εγκαταστάσεων και την υποχρηματοδότηση, την έλλειψη εξοπλισμού και τα κενά σε εκπαιδευτικό προσωπικό αλλά και για την έλλειψη θέρμανσης.


Στο πλαίσιο του ρεπορτάζ συνομιλήσαμε με μαθητές και με εκπαιδευτικούς και μας ενημέρωσαν για τα αιτήματα της κατάληψης . Σύμφωνα με τον πρόεδρο του 15μελούς, το σχολείο στερείται καθηγητή ηλεκτρολογίας για το μάθημα των ηλεκτρικών εγκαταστάσεων, ένα μάθημα πανελλαδικώς εξεταζόμενο, γεγονός που προκαλεί ανησυχία στους μαθητές ενόψει των εξετάσεων. Έκανε λόγο και για fan coil που είναι γεμάτα σκόνη και βρωμιά, επισημαίνοντας ότι η κατάσταση αυτή δημιουργεί ανησυχία για τις συνθήκες υγιεινής και ασφάλειας μαθητών και εκπαιδευτικών. Ιδιαίτερα σημαντικό είναι και το ζήτημα των ελλείψεων σε εκπαιδευτικό προσωπικό και υλικών στα εργαστήρια του σχολείου εξαιτίας της υποχρηματοδώτησης.


Ο πρόεδρος υπογράμισε οτι ο ίδιος επισκέφτηκε τον δήμαρχο της Νεάπολης Συκεών ζητώντας την παρέμβασή του για την επίλυση των προβλημάτων. Όπως αναφέρουν, ωστόσο, η ευθύνη για ορισμένα από τα ζητήματα μεταφέρεται στη Διεύθυνση Δευτεροβάθμιας Εκπαίδευσης. Από την πλευρά τους, ζητούν άμεσες παρεμβάσεις και ουσιαστικές λύσεις, ξεκαθαρίζοντας ότι δεν θα επιστρέψουν στα μαθήματα εάν δεν υπάρξουν συγκεκριμένες δεσμεύσεις.


Την ίδια ώρα, υπό κατάληψη βρίσκεται και το διπλανό σχολειο 2ο ΓΕΛ Νεάπολης για τεταρτη ημέρα, με τους μαθητές να διαμαρτύρονται για την κατάσταση των κτιριακών εγκαταστάσεων και τις ελλείψεις στις βασικές υποδομές του σχολείου. Σύμφωνα με όσα καταγγέλλουν οι μαθητές, υπάρχουν καλώδια που κρέμονται, σοβάδες που πέφτουν ενώ προβλήματα καταγράφονται και στη λειτουργία των τουαλετών. Ιδιαίτερη αναφορά κάνουν στο ζήτημα της θέρμανσης, περιγράφοντας χαρακτηριστικά τις αίθουσες ως «ψυγείο», καθώς όπως υποστηρίζουν, οι χαμηλές θερμοκρασίες δυσκολεύουν την παρακολούθηση των μαθημάτων.


Για τα προβλήματα στο 2ο ΓΕΛ Νεάπολης τοποθετήθηκε ο δήμαρχος Νεάπολης – Συκεών, Σίμος Δανιηλίδης, αναφέροντας ότι έχει ήδη δρομολογηθεί η επισκευή του κυκλοφορητή του συστήματος θέρμανσης, προκειμένου να αποκατασταθεί η λειτουργία του καλοριφέρ τις επόμενες ημέρες. Παράλληλα, όπως σημείωσε, έχουν δρομολογηθεί και άλλες εργασίες αποκατάστασης στις σχολικές εγκαταστάσεις.


Από την πλευρά του, ο αντιδήμαρχος Τεχνικών Έργων και Μικροέργων, Στέλιος Γκατζές, ανέφερε ότι έχει κατατεθεί πρόταση για την ένταξη του σχολείου στο πρόγραμμα «Μαριέττα Γιαννάκου», με στόχο την εξασφάλιση χρηματοδότησης για την υλοποίηση εκτεταμένων εργασιών αναβάθμισης κατά τη διάρκεια του καλοκαιριού.


Την ανησυχία της για την κτιριακή και λειτουργική κατάσταση των σχολείων έχει εκφράσει και η Γ΄ ΕΛΜΕ Θεσσαλονίκης. Σε ανακοίνωσή της κάνει λόγο για περιστατικά πτώσης σοβάδων, προβλήματα θέρμανσης και παλαιωμένες ηλεκτρολογικές εγκαταστάσεις, ζητώντας, μεταξύ άλλων, άμεσους τεχνικούς ελέγχους, αποκατάσταση των φθορών και επαρκή χρηματοδότηση των σχολικών μονάδων.


Το ζήτημα που αναδεικνύεται μέσα από τις κινητοποιήσεις των μαθητών δεν περιορίζεται, επομένως, σε μεμονωμένες τεχνικές βλάβες. Αφορά συνολικά τις συνθήκες μέσα στις οποίες καλούνται να λειτουργήσουν τα σχολεία, αλλά και το κατά πόσο υπάρχουν οι απαραίτητοι πόροι για τη συντήρηση των εγκαταστάσεων, την ανανέωση του εξοπλισμού και την κάλυψη των εκπαιδευτικών αναγκών.


Στο πλευρό των μαθητών τάσσεται και η δημοτική παράταξη της αντιπολίτευσης «Πόλη Αλλιώς», η οποία επισημαίνει ότι τα προβλήματα δεν είναι μεμονωμένα, αλλά εντάσσονται σε μια ευρύτερη εικόνα εγκατάλειψης των σχολικών υποδομών. Η παράταξη είχε ήδη αναδείξει στο Δημοτικό Συμβούλιο τα προβλήματα θέρμανσης που προέκυψαν από καθυστερήσεις στη συντήρηση των καυστήρων. Η «Πόλη Αλλιώς» ζητά άμεση αποκατάσταση των προβλημάτων θέρμανσης και ασφάλειας, τεχνικούς ελέγχους στα σχολικά κτίρια, επισκευή των εγκαταστάσεων υγιεινής, συγκεκριμένο χρονοδιάγραμμα εργασιών και ουσιαστική αύξηση της χρηματοδότησης για τη συντήρηση των σχολείων.

author: anred
title: Encuesta Inquilina 2026: seis de cada 10 hogares del AMBA se endeudan para pagar el alquiler y solo uno de cada 10 puede ahorrar
content:
La ACIJ, el CELS, el CEUR-CONICET, el IEALC-UBA y la EIDAES-UNSAM, presentaron la Encuesta Inquilina 2026, un relevamiento sobre las condiciones de vida de las familias que alquilan en el Área Metropolitana de Buenos Aires. Los resultados arrojan que el 59% pidió dinero prestado durante el último año, el 72% de quienes se endeudaron usó esos recursos para pagar el alquiler y apenas el 10% logró ahorrar. El informe también revela que el 53% destina más de la mitad de sus ingresos al alquiler, el 70% recortó consumos y el 49% gastó sus ahorros. A tres años de la derogación de la Ley de Alquileres, aumentaron los contratos más cortos, las actualizaciones trimestrales y la informalidad: el 30% alquila sin contrato escrito y el 46% paga en efectivo. Tras el conocido caso de la jubilada Maricarmen Abascal, que desató movilizaciones y acampes en diversas ciudades españolas: ¿cuándo podrá convertirse este malestar extendido en una movilización colectiva por el derecho a la vivienda? ¿Habrá que esperar a que una historia individual se convierta en emblema para que la crisis habitacional ocupe las calles?

Por ANRed.


La

Asociación Civil por la Igualdad y la Justicia (ACIJ)

, el

Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS)

, el

Centro de Estudios Urbanos y Regionales del CONICET (CEUR)

, la

Escuela Interdisciplinaria de Altos Estudios Sociales de la Universidad Nacional de San Martín (EIDAES-UNSAM)

 y el

Instituto de Estudios de América Latina y el Caribe de la UBA (IEALC)

 presentaron la

Encuesta Inquilina 2026

, un relevamiento sobre las

condiciones de vida de los hogares que alquilan en el Área Metropolitana de Buenos Aires (AMBA)

. Los resultados muestran un escenario de creciente precarización habitacional:

el 59% pidió dinero prestado

 durante el último año, frente al 37% en 2025; entre quienes se endeudaron,

el 72% utilizó esos recursos para pagar el alquiler

. Además, el

70% recortó consumos

, el

49% gastó sus ahorros

 y apenas el

10% pudo ahorrar

.


El endeudamiento aparece como una estrategia para sostener el pago de la vivienda aun cuando eso implique postergar otras necesidades

. El 31% de los hogares se atrasó en el pago de gastos corrientes o deudas, casi el doble que en 2025, cuando ese porcentaje había sido del 16%. Entre quienes recurrieron a préstamos,

el 35% pidió dinero a familiares o amistades, el 32% acudió a billeteras virtuales, el 22% tomó préstamos personales o pidió adelantos de haberes y el 13% recurrió a financieras o prestamistas

. Aunque el 91% se encuentra al día con el alquiler, los datos muestran el costo que implica cumplir con esa obligación:

endeudarse, consumir menos y agotar los ahorros

.


Foto: Federico Imas.


La presión sobre los ingresos también es cada vez mayor:

el 53% de los hogares destina más de la mitad de sus ingresos al alquiler, frente al 38% registrado en 2024

.

La situación es todavía más grave entre quienes dependen principalmente de jubilaciones o pensiones: allí la proporción alcanza el 74%

. Apenas el 6% de los hogares destina un cuarto o menos de sus ingresos a pagar la vivienda. A esto se suma el deterioro de la situación laboral:

la desocupación entre los hogares inquilinos llegó al 10,1%

, frente al 7,4% de 2025, mientras que quienes tienen trabajo pero quisieran trabajar más horas pasaron del 17,3% al 24,8%.


El informe señala que,

desde la derogación de la Ley Nacional de Alquileres en diciembre de 2023, se consolidó una tendencia hacia contratos más cortos y actualizaciones más frecuentes

. Los contratos de tres años cayeron del 30% al 7% entre 2024 y 2026, mientras que el 52% de los acuerdos vigentes tiene una duración de dos años. En cuanto a los aumentos,

las actualizaciones trimestrales pasaron del 23% al 46%

, mientras que los incrementos anuales descendieron del 17% al 2%. El 19% de los contratos, además, no tiene un índice de actualización definido de antemano.


La informalidad también forma parte de este escenario:

el 30% de los hogares inquilinos no cuenta con un contrato escrito, frente al 22% registrado en 2025, y el 46% paga el alquiler en efectivo

. El relevamiento también expone los abusos vinculados a la intermediación inmobiliaria:

el 83% de quienes alquilaron mediante una inmobiliaria pagó una comisión

. En la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, donde está prohibido cobrarla a la parte inquilina, el porcentaje llegó al 76%. Además, los contratos gestionados por inmobiliarias son, en promedio, un 15% más caros …

author: Daron Letts
title: Kugluktuk welcomes 10 new modular housing units
content:
Kugluktuk’s housing stock increased by 10 modular public housing units this week.


Built by Arctic Modular Homes out of Cambridge Bay, the dwellings are a mix of three duplexes and two-, three- and four-bedroom units.


“It’s nice to finally see we are getting development in our community,” said Dettrick Hokanak, the hamlet’s deputy chief administrative officer who, in his previous role as the planning and lands administrator, approved the project.


The modular homes stem from an agreement

reached in January

 between the federal and territorial government and Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. to build up to 750 homes across the territory, including public, affordable and supportive.


Build Canada Homes is providing up to $250 million, and the territorial government is contributing up to $230 million under the agreement.


Construction and development is underway on an additional 139 homes in other communities including Iqaluit, Cambridge Bay, Arviat, Baker Lake and Rankin Inlet.


Housing Minister Cecile Nelvana Lyall and other territorial ministers attended a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Tuesday for the modular homes.


Nunavut MP Lori Idlout said in a news release on Tuesday that the development won’t solve overcrowding in the hamlet, but it’s a start.


“Ten new public housing units will not solve our housing challenge overnight,” she said. “But for 10 families, everything changes. They soon will have a safe and comfortable home to raise their families.”


Hokanak said he expects families to move in this week.


In addition, a 12-plex and two other units are under construction, headed by Concentric Associates International Inc., which has offices across Canada, including Iqaluit.


In light of Nunavut’s

housing crisis

, those units can’t come fast enough, Hokanak said.


“There could be 15 people in a three-bedroom house and 12 people in a two-bedroom house. People move from house to house,” he said.


The overcrowding takes a toll on family relationships, he said.


“It causes tension and leads to many different negative aspects of life,” he said. “I really want my community to succeed, and I really want my community members to succeed. Housing is vital.”

author: C.J. Polychroniou
title: Affordability Worries Go Beyond Prices. Addressing Them Demands Systemic Change.
content:
We must increase workers’ resources and limit capitalists’ and elites’ political power, says economist Gerald Epstein.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

“Affordability” was the buzzword of the 2026 midterm elections, echoed often by Democrats as they scored a massive victory and captured both chambers of Congress. Indeed, the cost of living was the top issue on the mind of voters as they headed to the ballot box, according to polls. But the increasing economic pressure on working-class people is also inextricably linked in voters’ mind with corruption and the war on Iran. Now, as Democrats get ready to put forth new policies under their new majorities, it still isn’t exactly clear what a focus on “affordability” actually means.

As renowned progressive economist Gerald Epstein points out in the interview that follows, “affordability” is more than prices. The “affordability crisis” points to a plethora of economic and political ills facing the contemporary United States that need to be thoroughly addressed in order to make average citizens thrive. These include extreme wealth concentration, government corruption, corporate greed and unaccountability, an out-of-control health care system, unfair tax policy, and bloated military spending. Epstein argues that the policies to address these economic and social ills are already well-known, and only political will is needed to fix the broken system.

Epstein is professor of economics and co-director of the Political Economy Research Institute (PERI) at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of the project called Game Changers: Economic Policies for a Working America.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

C. J. Polychroniou: The 2026 midterm elections have been interpreted as a referendum on President Donald Trump as voters worried about the state of the economy under his administration. In fact, “affordability” was the dominant issue in the election cycle as many people in the U.S. are struggling with the cost of housing, groceries, and health care, and worry about their financial prospects, all while the rich continue to get richer. Do you agree with this interpretation of the midterm elections? Moreover, what do we mean by “affordability” and how is it to be addressed?

Gerald Epstein: I do agree. The 2026 midterm elections could indeed be dubbed the “affordability” midterms. Poll after poll, both before and after the elections, identified the rise in the cost of living due to Trump’s Iranian adventure and romance with tariffs as the top concerns of voters. And close to the top was voters’ dissatisfaction with the corruption of Trump, his family, and his minions. In fact, corruption did not rise to the top of voters’ priorities until Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff effectively tied Trump’s corruption to American families’ affordability problems. And now that Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, they seem to be converging on a two-pronged strategy: promote legislation that will improve “affordability” and investigate the Trump administration’s corruption.

All of this raises several questions: What is meant by “affordability?” What are the policy tools available to the government at the federal but also state and local levels that could make life more affordable for Americans? And, finally, is this “affordability agenda” sufficient to address the multiple challenges facing U.S. workers?

There are many “affordability” agendas to choose from. The Congressional Progressive Caucus released a “New Affordability Agenda” in April. According to the caucus: “The New Affordability Agenda is a slate of creative new bills to help families get ahead by making things cheaper, putting money in pockets and getting big money out of politics.” The agenda includes policies such as making prescription drugs cheaper by making it easier to produce generic drugs; reducing grocery prices by reducing grocery chain monopolies; making housing more affordable by increasing rental assistance and assistance for down payments; levying windfall profits tax on oil to be returned to consumers; limiting AI’s use in dynamic pricing of products; setting a minimum of two weeks paid vacation for workers; raising federal overtime pay; and getting money out of politics by limiting super PACs.

Clearly, this is not a comprehensive agenda, but it …

author: Ana Naomi De Sousa
title: ‘No Dignified Way to Live’: Why Portugal Is Rising up Over Housing
content:
Edmilson Tavares Fonseca didn’t join the thousands of people who marched through Lisbon last Saturday to protest against Portugal’s rising living costs and unaffordable housing. Saturday is the only day he gets to spend with his partner and their baby. The rest of the week, he works two jobs, trying to make ends meet. Still, he identifies strongly with the protesters. “The people in the streets right now are demanding what most people in Portugal want,” he says. “The government have shut their eyes to reality – but we don’t have a dignified way to live right now.” 


Fonseca grew up in the Lisbon suburb of Cova da Moura, known for its precarious self-built housing. He still works full-time in the area, supporting marginalised young people, but goes home to a different part of the city, where he lives in a rented apartment with his partner. They can afford it, for now, but since becoming parents, and with average rents in the city having almost doubled since 2017, Fonseca and his partner long for the security of owning their own home. Fonseca took a second job as an Uber driver to supplement his income, but, despite this, he has been refused a mortgage four times. “Sometimes it feels as if all the sacrifices I’m making are for nothing,” he says, “it’s so demoralising”.


Fonseca’s story shows what Portugal’s housing crisis means for ordinary people. Since 2015, house prices

have outstripped wage growth by 60%

 – by far the widest gap in the EU, where the average is 6.8%. Meanwhile, public housing makes up less than 2% of the country’s housing stock.


Last weekend’s protest marked five weeks of people in Portugal taking to the streets over the housing crisis. Spontaneous

encampments have sprung up from Porto to Lisbon

, and tens of thousands have turned out to weekly demonstrations,

defying violence

 and disparagement from the authorities. As the gaping discrepancy between house prices and wages pushes both renting and buying far beyond what most can afford, people in Portugal are starting to question where all the money has gone – and who really owns the cities they live in.


“What we’re seeing now is the failure of public policies to respond to national housing needs over several decades, resulting in a deep-rooted crisis,” says Ana Cordeiro Santos, an economist at Coimbra University. 


After property prices crashed during the 2011 debt crisis, the government responded to a shortage of capital and widespread urban decay by courting foreign investment in real estate, Cordeiro Santos says. A central pillar of this strategy was the Golden Visa scheme, which offered residency – and eventually a route to citizenship to non-EU nationals who invested at least €500,000 (£420,000) in property.

 Between 2012 and 2023, it brought in €6.5bn in property investment, with most visas going to Chinese (43%), Brazilian (10%) and United States (6%) nationals, fuelling further speculation in real estate.


The flood of global capital has generated huge profits for investors, but

 made the housing market

completely unaffordable

 for ordinary Portuguese people. In Lisbon, the average net salary is currently €1,405 (£1,190) a month – while the average one-bedroom flat rents for around €1,450 (£1,230).


Frederico Ascensão da Natividade Prazeres, a 24-year-old software engineer, says he “made all the sensible choices” – and now feels “deeply betrayed”. Despite earning €2,200 (£1,860) a month, a high salary in Portugal, especially for his age, he can’t afford to live alone in the Lisbon neighbourhood where he grew up. Instead, he rents a room in a shared three-bedroom apartment with no living room, splitting his time between his bedroom and the kitchen. “I live like a rat,” he says.


He checks property websites every couple of weeks, but would have to move at least 80km away to buy. Now he’s thinking of going further – to Switzerland. Portugal’s Emigration Observatory estimates that around 65,000 people left the country in 2024. “There is an urban exodus of people of my generation,” Prazeres says. “We really don’t want to leave, but we feel we have no choice.”


So many young people are leaving Portugal just as it has become one of Europe’s most desirable destinations. Tourist overnight stays have more than doubled since 2012, helped by the deregulation of the rental market, tax breaks for short-term lets on platforms such as Airbnb, and budget airlines like easyJet and Ryanair. “Tourism has boosted the economy, but it has had …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Ley de Tierras: vía libre para desalojos exprés y un Congreso a medida del extractivismo
content:
OPINIÓN


Por Silvina Ramírez*


Finalmente, se sancionó la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada. El Senado la convirtió en ley, luego de múltiples avatares que tuvieron su epicentro en la extranjerización de la tierra. La derogación de un artículo del polémico DNU 70/23, que eliminó la Ley de Tierras Rurales —la que impuso un límite a la extranjerización— fue el punto de partida de un enorme debate público que culminó con esta última sanción.


El bochornoso papel de la

Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación

, que en el lapso de diez días puso en vigencia el artículo en cuestión suspendiendo una medida cautelar, y luego en un golpe de timón volvió a establecer dicha medida prohibiendo otra vez la extranjerización, concluye en un acto final de sanción de una ley que incluye la restitución de la Ley 26.737 de tierras rurales.


Sintetizar en un párrafo las idas y vueltas parlamentarias y las decisiones de la Corte Suprema no fue una tarea fácil. Sí traduce el nivel de “tironeo” político, las negociaciones desenfrenadas, decisiones judiciales de la máxima instancia del país inexplicables, y la relevancia de

la movilización

 de diversos sectores sociales que presionaron para preservar la soberanía. En pocas palabras,

se logró la restitución de una ley que protege el territorio de la injerencia externa

.


Sin embargo, la movilización popular no alcanzó para frenar los desalojos exprés y la restricción para las expropiaciones, que subsisten en el texto de la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la propiedad privada aprobada. Estas medidas perjudican a vastos sectores de la sociedad, entre ellos las comunidades indígenas.


Los desalojos apuntan tanto a inmuebles urbanos como rurales. Al agilizar el proceso y acortar los plazos, la fragilidad de aquellos potenciales desalojados se agudiza. En el caso de las comunidades indígenas, la seguidilla de desalojos o intentos de desalojos que se dieron en los últimos meses —algunos de ellos pudieron ser suspendidos—, bajo la vigencia de esta ley, adquieren mayor gravedad.


Es el caso también de las expropiaciones. Aquellas comunidades indígenas que tienen expectativas de recuperar sus territorios a través de un procedimiento administrativo como lo es la expropiación, van a encontrar ahora muchas más dificultades, por lo que una de las vías posibles de titulación colectiva encuentra nuevos obstáculos. Nada es fácil para las comunidades indígenas que pretenden gozar de sus derechos territoriales reconocidos.


Esta ley debe leerse a la luz de otras medidas de este Gobierno que privilegian no sólo la propiedad privada, sino las inversiones extranjeras, despreciando e invisibilizando el reclamo legítimo de las comunidades indígenas, campesinos y trabajadores rurales, entre ortos. El

Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI)

, la derogación de la

Ley 26.160 (Emergencia Territorial Indígena)

, el

desguace de la Ley de Glaciares

, el rol nefasto del Instituto Nacional de Asuntos Indígenas (INAI), son

piezas de una maquinaria al servicio de la explotación de los bienes comunes naturales y el despojo

, otra vez, de los territorios indígenas.


Es cierto que se logró frenar la extranjerización de la tierra, debido principalmente a la presión ciudadana. No obstante, los objetivos de esta gestión de gobierno son claros. Muchas veces se retrocede para avanzar con mayor fuerza. Es imprescindible estar alertas frente a potenciales avances que pretendan erosionar aún más la ya débil institucionalidad pública y seguir socavando derechos que costaron tanto obtener. Que la arena (o la cal) no tape la cal (o la arena).


*

Especialista en Derechos Indígenas. Docente de la Facultad de Derecho de la UBA. Miembro de la Asociación de Abogados/as de Derecho Indígena (AADI).

 se publicó primero en

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

author: Mag
title: „Die Kürzungen sind unerträglich“: Ein breites Bündnis hat den Kampf zur Verteidigung des öffentlichen Bildungswesens in Madrid aufgenommen
content:
Dossier


„

Mehr als 20 Organisationen haben sich zusammengeschlossen, um zu versuchen, das, was sie als Plan der Regionalregierung zur Dekapitalisierung des öffentlichen Bildungswesens zugunsten des privaten Bildungswesens ansehen, rückgängig zu machen. Mit dem Ruf „Bildungsqualität oder unbefristeter Streik“ haben Tausende von Menschen heute Morgen im Zentrum der Hauptstadt mehr Mittel für die öffentliche Bildung in Madrid gefordert. An der von mehr als 20 Organisationen, darunter Gewerkschaften, Universitätsversammlungen und verschiedene soziale Gruppen, organisierten Demonstration nahmen Vertreter und konkrete Forderungen aus allen Bildungsbereichen, von den 0- bis 3-Jährigen bis zu den Studenten und der Berufsausbildung, sowie politische Parteien teil. Nach Angaben der Organisatoren nahmen etwa 120.000 Menschen an der Demonstration teil

…“ So beginnt der umfangreiche span.

Artikel von Guillermo Martínez vom 23. Februar 2025 in elDiario.es


 (maschinenübersetzt) mit schönen Fotos der Transparente – siehe mehr Infos:


Die Lehrkräfte in der 7. Woche des unbefristeten Bildungsstreiks in Madrid kämpfen nach Verschärfung der Mindestdienstvorschriften auch für das Streikrecht


Madrid: Sechs Wochen Bildungsstreik, Stehversammlungen und Proteste auf der Straße gegen die Zensur


„

Die Lehrkräfte beenden die Woche vom 16. bis 20. November mit dem Einsatz für Verhandlungsrechte und das Streikrecht angesichts der Verschärfung der Mindestdienstvorschriften und der Anweisungen des Bildungsministeriums. Die Organisation an den Schulen sowie die Zusammenarbeit mit den Kindergärten und der Universität tragen einen Kampf aus, der sich nicht auf die Wände des Klassenzimmers beschränken lässt. Die sechste Woche des unbefristeten Streiks im öffentlichen Bildungswesen Madrids hinterlässt ein Bild, das den Konflikt auf den Punkt bringt: Lehrkräfte versammeln sich vor dem Bildungsministerium, einige mit Aufklebern über den Lippen, um gegen die Einschränkungen ihres Protests zu protestieren; dabei beteiligen sich auch Schüler und es wird gefordert, dass Mercedes Zarzalejo Verhandlungen aufnimmt.


Zwei Wochen nach der

in LoQueSomos veröffentlichten Bilanz der vierten Woche


 bleiben die Kernpunkte des Konflikts bestehen: Senkung der Schüler-Lehrer-Verhältnisse und der Unterrichtsbelastung, Aufstockung des Personals und stärkere Berücksichtigung der Vielfalt, Wiederherstellung der Kaufkraft sowie die Bereitstellung angemessener Schulgebäude. Es gibt keine Einigung, die den am 14. Oktober begonnenen Streik beenden würde. Doch diese Woche kommt ein Thema hinzu, das untrennbar mit diesen Forderungen verbunden ist: die Verteidigung der kollektiven Mittel, mit denen die Lehrkräfte diese Forderungen durchsetzen. (…)


Die Versammlungen – die Arbeit, die die Straße am Laufen hält


Die Mobilisierung lässt sich nicht allein durch ihre Demonstrationen erklären. Es gibt ein Netzwerk der täglichen Organisation, das die Aktionen vorbereitet, die nächsten Schritte bespricht und die Probleme der einzelnen Zentren mit einem gemeinsamen Forderungskatalog verknüpft. „Menos Lectivas“ beschreibt seine Struktur anhand souveräner Zentrumsversammlungen, die im Konsens oder durch Abstimmung entscheiden und über Verbindungsleute verfügen, um ihre Positionen an die Generalversammlung weiterzuleiten. Die territorialen Versammlungen ermöglichen die Koordination von Schulen innerhalb desselben Stadtviertels oder Gebiets; die Gruppen nach Schulstufen und Fachbereichen machen unterschiedliche Bedürfnisse sichtbar. (…)


Vom Haushalt in Vallecas bis zum Druck auf die regionalen Behörden


Am Dienstag, dem 17., versammelten sich Hunderte von Lehrkräften vor dem Regionalparlament von Madrid, während Zarzalejo den Haushalt seines Ministeriums verteidigte. Die Sprecherinnen des Komitees legten in der nahegelegenen Buchhandlung Muga ihre Sicht auf den Haushalt dar: Die Gesamtsteigerung reicht nicht aus, wenn sie sich nicht in mehr Lehrkräften, geringeren Schülerzahlen pro Klasse, öffentlichen Stellen und Infrastruktur niederschlägt. Angesichts der offiziellen Präsentation von Rekordzahlen stellte der Protest die entscheidende Frage: Was kommt tatsächlich in den öffentlichen Klassenzimmern an?.

author: By Konstantinos Zilos, Contributor
title: Frontline Voices of Albania’s Gen Z Uprising
content:
Tirana, Albania — Gen Z is at the forefront of a new wave of social and political protests in different parts of the world, seeking to change the existing situation. From Nepal and Serbia to India and France, young people are taking to the streets demanding political change, transparency and a better future. Social media plays a crucial role in organizing and spreading these movements, creating new forms of collective action.


In Albania, young people are giving new momentum to the protest movement known as the “Flamingo Revolution,” which began as an

environmental protest

 earlier this year and evolved into a broader anti-government movement. Youth are gathering across the country and demanding a different future.


In Tirana, protesters Arlinda, Jesmina, Ani and Jurgen, along with many other young people, shared with Unicorn Riot the uncertainty they experience in a country where the rising cost of living, corruption scandals, the lack of professional opportunities, and distrust in political leadership have fueled the frustration of a generation that refuses to remain silent.


Issues such as housing, the declining quality of education, unemployment, low wages, limited employment opportunities and social inequalities are among the main problems facing young people, who are no longer willing to tolerate impunity.


“

The rents are high. The education system is falling apart. And most of all, the corruption has gotten so out of hand.

“


The protests emerged as a result of all these social and economic inequalities. For the young people who have taken to the streets, demanding a dignified life is no longer simply a request, but an ongoing struggle.


The unity of young people is what has brought this struggle this far, and it is what will keep it going. Many of the young people we met want to have a future in their country, to stay there and contribute to its development.


Youth lead protests against the government in Tirana, Albania in November 2026. Photo contributed by Konstantinos Zilos.


A large number of the young people taking part in the demonstrations believe they are living under a regime that restricts democratic freedoms. Kristina, in particular, described the situation in her country as a dictatorship.


One of the protesters’ main demands is the resignation of the country’s Prime Minister, Edi Rama, as they believe that the political promises he has made for the country have come to nothing. What they are demanding is a better future, with a government that cares about its people and its country.


There is widespread distrust of the country’s politicians and, for many, the challenge is to find an alternative political proposal that can put an end to the dilemma of “Rama or Berisha.”


On the one hand, Edi Rama calls for dialogue, while on the other, allegations of police violence remain at the center of the protests. At the same time, he announced a €2,500 bonus for each police officer on the front line of the demonstrations, as well as salary increases for police officers. 


Meanwhile, according to a testimony we received, plainclothes police officers visit the homes of families of young people identified as participants in the demonstrations and who have experienced police violence, in order to deliver fines to them.


The protesters believe that the government cares neither about their living conditions nor about the future they can have in their own country. This is closely linked to one of Albania’s biggest challenges: the emigration of young Albanians to other countries in search of greater opportunities and a better standard of living.


A protester walks through tear gas during youth-led protests against the government in Tirana, Albania in November 2026. Photo contributed by Konstantinos Zilos.


*The people we met and who spoke to us about the protests were between 20 and 33 years old.


Cover image contributed by Konstantinos Zilos.
