author: Unknown
title: Soma ve Kangal termik santrallerinde üretim durdu: İşçiler alacakları için Konya'da eylem yaptı
content:
Konya — Soma B Termik Santrali’nin üretiminin durması ve kamuya devredilmesinin ardından yaklaşık bin 100 çalışanın maaş ve kıdem tazminatı alacakları gündemdeki yerini korurken, Sivas Kangal Termik Santrali’nde de kömür tedarikinin kesilmesiyle üretim durdu. Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şubesi ile TES-İş’in öncülüğünde Konya’da bir araya gelen maden ve enerji işçileri, milyarlarca liralık alacaklarının ödenmesini istedi. İşçiler, kamulaştırma ve üretimin yeniden başlaması çağrısı yaptı.

Manisa’nın Soma ilçesinde yıllarca kömür üreten maden işletmelerinin, termik santral işçilerinin ve kent ekonomisinin geleceğini etkileyen sorun, bu kez Konya’da Torku ve Konya Şeker’in önünde verilen mücadeleyle gündeme geldi. Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şubesi temsilcileri ile Soma B ve Sivas Kangal termik santrallerinin işçileri, ödenmeyen alacakları ve iş güvencesi talepleri için şirketin merkezi önünde bir araya geldi.

TES-İş Sendikası Genel Merkezi öncülüğünde, Soma ve Sivas şubelerinin koordinasyonuyla gerçekleştirilen eyleme, Soma’daki maden işçileri de destek verdi. İşçiler, yalnızca bireysel ücret ve tazminat alacaklarının değil, işletmeler arasındaki birikmiş borçların ve üretimin durmasının yarattığı ekonomik sonuçların da çözülmesini istedi.

Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şubesi İş Yeri Temsilcisi Emin Kara, eylem alanında yaptığı açıklamada, maden işletmelerinin milyarlarca liralık alacakları bulunduğunu belirterek Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’a, İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi ve Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanı Murat Kurum'a çağrıda bulunarak, “Memleketinizdeyiz. Devletin gücünü iliklerimize kadar burada hissettik; aynı gücün, aynı iradenin masada da Torku'ya karşı verilmesini istiyoruz" dedi.

Eyleme katılan maden işçileri, Soma’daki üretim zincirinin yalnızca termik santralde çalışanlardan oluşmadığını, santrale kömür sağlayan işletmelerin de yaşanan krizden etkilendiğini dile getirdi.

Maden işçileri, “İşletmemizin 1,4 milyar alacağı var. Hakkımızı almadan buradan dönmeyeceğiz” sözleriyle taleplerini dile getirdi. İşçiler, alacakları için Konya’ya geldiklerini belirterek, maaş ve özlük haklarında yaşanan aksamaların çalışanları mağdur ettiğini söyledi. İşçiler, haklarının bir an önce ödenmesini talep etti.

Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şube Başkan Yardımcısı Turgay Aydoğdu da TES-İş Sendikası’nın başlattığı direnişe destek verdiklerini belirtti. Konya Torku Şeker önündeki eylemin sürdüğünü ifade eden Aydoğdu, işçilerin yaşadığı ekonomik sıkıntıları aileleri üzerinden anlatarak, “Konya Torku Şeker müdürlerinin çocukları okul harçlığı almadan gidebiliyorlar mı? Çocuklara cep harçlığı vermeden çocukları okula gönderebiliyorlar mı? Onlar, bir babanın çocuğunun gözünün içine bakamayacak duruma düşmesini bilebiliyorlar mı” ifadelerini kullandı.

İşçilerin yaşadığı mağduriyete dikkat çeken Aydoğdu, eylem sırasında polisin orantısız güç kullandığını ileri sürdü. Devletin güvenlik güçleri aracılığıyla gösterdiği iradenin işçilerin taleplerinin çözümü için de ortaya konulması gerektiğini savunan Aydoğdu, işçilerin hak arayışını sürdüreceğini belirtti.

TES-İş Sendikası Teşkilatlanma ve Örgütlenmeden Sorumlu Genel Başkan Yardımcısı Fatih Erçelik, Konya’daki açıklamasında Soma ve Kangal termik santrallerinde yaşananları değerlendirdi. Erçelik, şirket yönetimini yeterli yatırım yapmamak, borçlarını ödememek ve işçileri mağdur etmekle eleştirdi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Reisegruppe
title: Reisebericht Paris Herbst 2026
content:
Die Bilder einer „Klasse, die den Kopf wieder hochhebt“


Gespannt saßen wir vor unseren Geräten. „The Revolution will not be televised“, aber scheinbar „live on tiktok“. Ohne große, sichtbare Event-Mobilisierung blockieren die französischen Schüler*innen ihre Oberschulen. Auf dem fruchtbaren Boden einer langjährigen Tradition in Frankreich und einer ersten Blockade in den französischen Koloniegebieten dieses Jahr, beginnt ein Gymnasium einer Pariser Vorstadt aus Wut über die Bedingungen, die sie jeden Tag vorfinden, ihre Schule zu verbarrikadieren. Über die Verbreitung von Videos von der Aktion entsteht schnell eine landesweite Bewegung mit hunderten Nachahmer*innen, die auch die reichen Teile Frankreichs erfasst und nicht lange fackelt, den Protest mit Feuer und Militanz zu untermauern. Die Schüler*innen Frankreichs gehen in Teilen seit 2 Monaten nicht mehr zur Schule und haben sich zu einer Staatsgefährdenden Kraft entwickelt, die selbst mit 5 Milliarden des tief verschuldeten Macron-Regime nicht einzufangen ist. Das ganze steht nicht im Kontext einer Reformbestrebung oder ähnlichem sondern ist die Fortsetzung der Nahel-Revolte von 2023.


Währendessen bekommen wir von Überall aus Europa Nachrichten, wie sich junge Leute dem Aufstand der Schüler*innen anschließen und „wie in Frankreich“ protestieren, blockieren, plündern und angreifen. Wir fragen uns wann es in Deutschland los geht, ob wir als Erwachsene etwas tun können und kommen erstmal nur in Passivität. Uns erreichen die ersten Aufrufe eines Gelbwesten Revivals was mit der aktuellen GenZ-Revolte verknüpft werden soll. Die Lebenserhaltungskosten in Frankreich sind wie in Deutschland enorm gestiegen. Die Polizei hat die Schüler*innen mit allem bekämpft was wir von ihnen kennen, inklusive amputierten Händen, ausgeschossenen Augen und tausenden herabwürdigenden Festnahmen bei Minderjährigen. Dies ruft, verständlicherwise, Empörung bei allen Eltern und empathischen Menschen hervor. Das Land scheint also zu brodeln und meine Güte ist der Vulkan ausgebrochen. Hunderte Verletzte Polizt*innen, Tausende geplünderte Geschäfte und hunderttausende Beteiligte beschreiben nur im Ansatz das was dort am 17.10. an aufständiger Freude, Gemeinschaft und Power stattgefunden hat und was alle die wir getroffen haben nur als „historisch“ beschreiben konnten.


Im Kontext der letzten Geschehnisse war für uns klar, wir müssen dahin um uns selbst ein Bild von der Lage vor Ort zu verschaffen.


Als Deutsche auf einem Protest in Frankreich


An einem regnerischen Herbstag ging es früh los. Ausgerüstet mit Atemmasken, Schutzbrillen und ordentlich Proviant zog es uns in Richtung Innenstadt. Angekommen in der Nähe vom Place de la Republique suchten wir vergebens nach den viel beschriebenen aufständigen Personen. Nach einiger Zeit erfolglosem Suchen breitet sich die erste Enttäuschung in unseren Köpfe aus. Ist der Funke einer neuen Protestbewegung erloschen?


Nicht wirklich. Zum Glück konnten uns vorortig wohnende Genoss*innen Bescheid geben, dass die heutige Demo am Stadtrand noch stattfinden wird. Anscheinend hatten die heftigen Krawalle vom 17.10 dem französischen Innenminesterium so einen Schrecken eingejagt, dass sie aus Angst die Pariser Innenstadt vor jeglicher Demonstrationen schützen wollten.


Also ging es mit der U-Bahn Richtung Osten der franz. Hauptstadt. Schon am Gleis bemerkten wir, dass es um uns herum voller geworden ist. Es schien als ob ganz Paris zur Demonstrationen fahren will. Und BAM! Der Auftaktkundebungsort ist eine riesige Blase an Menschen. Man kann das Ende nur erahnen und wir kriegen Gänsehaut beim Anblick der Jugendlichen auf den Haltestelldächern und den tausenden Leute die ACAB grölen (obwohl das hier eher ACAB singen ist). Die Vorfreude steigt auf das Kommende. Nach kurzer Pinkelpause setzte sich der Protestzug in Bewegung. Es gibt keinen Punkt von dem man aus, das Ende sowie den Anfang der Demo sehen kann. Er ist schlicht zu lang. Sowas haben wir in der Form in Deutschland noch nicht erlebt. Das hier ist kein FFF-Protest, kein inhaltsloses Unteilbar-Bündnis sondern eine über 100.000 Personen-Versammlung, die eine eigene Bewegung darstellt. author: Harriet Williamson
title: King’s College London Made a Pro-Palestine Student Write an Essay As Punishment – Then Reported Her to Prevent for It
content:
A top UK university reported a student to the government’s counterterrorism programme over a “reflective essay” it forced her to write after suspending her for charges related to pro-Palestine activism, Novara Media can reveal.


Niamh Grant, a 22-year-old Social Sciences student at King’s College London (KCL), was informed by a student welfare adviser in emails seen by Novara Media that the university had referred her to Prevent for the essay.


The “reflective essay” was set as a condition for Grant returning to her studies at the prestigious Russell Group university following a suspension in May 2025 over pro-Palestine protests as part of the 2024 student solidarity encampment movement – in which Grant was a leader in negotiations with KCL. 


The university required Grant to reflect on the “health and safety issues” caused when she entered a kitchen area of the university and was part of a group that created an obstruction which “led to the physical injury of staff” at a protest in 2024 – something she denies. It also invited her to reflect on a protest policy which was no longer in effect after it received criticism from civil rights organisations Liberty and Amnesty International.


In the essay, Grant wrote of her horror at the suffering of Palestinians, saying: “From the Palestinian people, one message resounds: to end the genocide. It is not enough to simply acknowledge Palestinian suffering, not enough to sympathise, and not enough to feel guilt. This belief must induce an imperative.”


Turning to KCL, she wrote: “I believe that to be a student is to care about the morality of my institution, and it is because I care about the responsibility given to me as King’s student that I care about my university’s investments in the Israeli arms trade.”


KCL did not consider this essay satisfactory, with the head of student conduct and appeals telling Grant: “I cannot consider this essay provides the necessary assurance that you will not cause any further health and safety concerns, that you appreciate how your actions impacted other members of the King’s community and that you understand the importance of the university’s policies and procedures as related to protest and behaviour.”


Grant then submitted a second reflective essay, where she suggested the university should have “a bit of humility… before it begins to lecture other people and groups about violence, crimes and the obstruction of other people’s lives”. 


Grant drew comparisons with the student struggle against investments in South Africa’s apartheid regime, criticising the university for “disciplin[ing] their own students before citing them as ‘courageous’ years later when it is convenient”.


She also wrote that she drew inspiration from Imam Hussein, a historic figure in Islam who sacrificed his life in standing up against oppression. Grant compared her smaller sacrifice of the interruption of her studies to the greater sacrifice of Hussein, also known as

Husayn ibn Ali

, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad who was killed in the 7th century.


In her essay, Grant wrote that Hussain and his family had left an example of “how we should sacrifice for the cause of fighting injustice and establishing justice on Earth”. 


From correspondence seen by Novara Media, the reference to Hussein appears to be the basis of the university’s Prevent referral. 


Grant told Novara Media that the Prevent referral was “incredibly Islamophobic” and a “method of intimidation”. She believes a Christian student who wrote that they took inspiration from the sacrifice of Jesus Christ would not have been flagged to the government’s counter-terror scheme. 


Grant said she “made an effort to explain what it means to have my degree taken away from me” and said her words were “deliberately decontextualised” to “create a justification for the Prevent referral”. 


“This isn’t something that exists in a vacuum,” she added. “It’s something that universities and schools have in their arsenal to weaponise against visibly Muslim students.” 


Prevent is part of the

 UK government’s counter-terrorism strategy

 and places a legal duty on “specified authorities”, including schools and universities, to have a “due regard to the need to prevent individuals from being drawn into terrorism”.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Shen Pre-Election Rally Canceled, Amidst Accusations of Interference by the Chiang Mayoral Administration
content:
A DISPUTE OVER the use of road rights has led Puma Shen to cancel pre-election rallies, which would have taken place the night before the vote on Saturday.

The Shen campaign’s pre-election rally was canceled last night, stating that the choice to cancel the rally was because of the impact on traffic that it would have, leading to complaints from pedestrians. The Shen campaign stated that it would prefer that voters return home to cast their ballot.

In particular, the Shen campaign stated that it was not allowed to use City Hall Plaza, but only Ren’ai Road. The Shen campaign stated that other possible locations, such as Ketagalan Boulevard, City Hall Plaza, and Beiping East Road in front of the DPP headquarters, were all booked. In response to the traffic considerations, however, with there already being complaints about roads being blocked on a major thoroughfare of the city, the decision was made to cancel. The stage for the construction of the event will be torn down, and the event will be shifted online.

The Chiang campaign was scheduled to hold a pre-election rally on Ketagalan Boulevard on Friday, but stated that it had the rights to City Hall Plaza that day, too, with plans to hold its election day event there on Saturday, and would be willing to allow the Shen campaign to use City Hall on Friday. However, eventually the Chiang campaign also announced that it would be canceling its Saturday election night event and shifting online. The Chiang campaign will still hold its pre-election rally on Ketagalan Boulevard on the 27th.

What has attracted a great deal of notice, however, has been the brief statement by Shen during his cancellation notice that the DPP had difficulty obtaining a venue for its pre-election rally. Consequently, there have been allegations against the Chiang campaign of interfering to try and prevent the Shen campaign from having a rally or attempting to lead the Shen campaign to create traffic difficulties through rallies that might lead to blowback against it. Notably, Shen did not lean into such claims himself when he announced the cancellation of the pre-election rally in a video, but only hinted at it, probably a strategic move to avoid the perception of negative campaigning against Chiang.

DPP politicians have questioned why the Chiang campaign was able to book so many venues so quickly, while it has faced such difficulties. Historical precedents of when past DPP mayoral candidates have had difficulty securing venues for pre-election events have also been raised. On the other hand, the pan-Blue camp has attempted to hit back by suggesting that the Shen campaign required an unusually long period of three to four days to set up a stage for the pre-election rally.

Shen was quicker and more decisive to act in canceling his rally to stem off controversy, but it proves poor optics if Chiang has a pre-election rally, but Shen is unable to. After all, this adds weight to allegations of political interference.

This is not the first time that the Chiang mayoral administration has been accused of attempting to interfere in political activities of the pan-Green camp, such as during the Great Recall Movement. Recall organizers reported being charged fees to rent public facilities that were not imposed when KMT legislators wished to use the same facilities, as well as being required to obtain permits for holding signature collection activities as would normally be required of a protest or march despite the fact that collecting signatures for recalls, after all, is not exactly a march or protest. Touat Books, the flagship civil society cafe/bookstore in Taipei, too, reported harassment during this period through inspections by the city government to find wrongdoing on the part of the business. The cafe/bookstore was accused of “illegal construction” when this was, in reality, the outdoor seating area of the cafe.

author: Ariadna Wdowiak
title: Primeros Auxilios en contexto de manifestación callejera, segunda edición
content:
Movilización de jubiladxs el 24 de septiembre del año 2025. Fotografía: Andrés Manrique (ANRed).


Muchas veces, el primer objetivo de la represión es inducir temor para desairar primero y después desarticular las resistencias populares. Contra ello, ANRed libera la segunda edición de

 “Primeros Auxilios en contexto de manifestación callejera”

, una recopilación de medidas y cuidados básicos a la hora de hacernos de las calles.


Saber de primeros auxilios en contextos donde predomina la violencia puede ser un aporte muy valioso, que tiene en sí mismo un efecto tranquilizador. Además, las personas que no recibieron entrenamiento en primeros auxilios suelen dudar al momento de actuar, o tienen miedo de ayudar por falta de seguridad para recordar las maniobras.


Si bien no frenará la decisión política de mutilar, intentamos generar conciencia sobre la importancia de cuidar nuestros cuerpos, con los que trabajamos y sostenemos nuestras vidas y las de otros, y enfatizamos en aquellas cosas que sí podemos hacer para cuidarnos. En particular, esta guía está orientada a la prevención.


Recordamos que los cuidados son siempre una tarea colectiva, históricamente menospreciada pero fundamental para cualquier resistencia. Este es nuestro aporte.


Estamos hace 32 años en las calles, practicando la comunicación alternativa, comunitaria y popular. Acompañando las luchas siempre, mostrando lo que otros omiten y silencian.

author: Jeunesse Antifa Marseillaise
title: Mit einem Lächeln kämpfen – Interview mit dem Kollektiv „Jeunesse Antifa Marseillaise“
content:
Die französische Bewegung entfaltet eine enorme politische Kraft, dank derer – und das können wir ohne Übertreibung sagen – eine echte Perspektive für eine Neuordnung zwischen Teilen der Klasse entstanden ist, die einander oft misstrauisch gegenüberstehen und durch die rassistischen Mechanismen des Staates auf Distanz gehalten werden. Wenn der Konflikt dieses Ausmaß erreicht, ist eine politische und soziale Polarisierung unvermeidlich, und die liberale Demokratie offenbart ihr autoritäres Wesen. Diese sich abzeichnende Wiederannäherung wird vor allem von den Schülern der Oberschulen in den Vororten vorangetrieben, die die größte Kraft im Zusammenhang mit – im Übrigen – sehr radikalen Forderungen entfalten. Dies lässt sich aus diesem Interview ableiten, das zwar sicherlich parteiisch, aber wirklich wenig ideologisch ist und mit einer Gruppe von Oberstufenschüler aus Marseille geführt wurde, die sich ihrer Stärke so bewusst sind, dass sie keinen Bedarf haben, die Widersprüche und Schwachstellen der Bewegung zu verbergen. Die kleine, aber wichtige Erkenntnis, die man daraus ziehen kann, ist, dass es nicht stimmt, dass Konflikt und Konsens unvereinbare Alternativen sind. Im Gegenteil: Wenn es dem Konflikt gelingt, den materiellen Kern der sozialen Widersprüche radikal anzugehen, schafft er es auch, Konsens zu erzeugen.


Machina (Vorwort)


***


Antonio Alia: Wie kam es zur Mobilisierung in Marseille und was waren die wichtigsten Momente?


Jeunesse Antifa Marseillaise: In Marseille begann die Mobilisierung im vergangenen Jahr mit der Ankündigung von Haushaltskürzungen, der miserablen Verwaltung der Schulplanung und dem Abbau zahlreicher Lehrerstellen an öffentlichen Oberschulen. Die wichtigsten Momente waren die erste große Demonstration am 1. Oktober 2026, bei der es uns gelang, der Polizei die Stirn zu bieten, sowie die Demonstrationen am 17., 24. und 31. Oktober gemeinsam mit den Gelbwesten, auch wenn es bereits zuvor Demonstrationen und Blockaden gegeben hatte.


A.A.: Wie sieht die geografische Verteilung der Mobilisierung aus?


J.A.M.: Die am stärksten mobilisierten Gymnasien in Marseille: Saint-Charles, Montgrand, Thiers, Victor Hugo, Marie Curie (das stark unterdrückt wird), Rempart, Marseilleveyre, Daumier. Andere Gymnasien, die von den Forderungen weniger betroffen sind, wie beispielsweise das Henri IV, mobilisieren sich zur Unterstützung unserer Kämpfe. Alle Campusse der Universität Aix-Marseille (von Marseille und Aix bis nach Arles und Avignon) mobilisieren sich an unserer Seite, und umgekehrt unterstützen die Gymnasiasten die Studierenden. Außerhalb der Region ist die Mobilisierung ebenso bedeutend und hat denselben Umfang.


A.A.: Gibt es einen Unterschied in den Kampfformen zwischen der rassifizierten und der nicht rassifizierten Zusammensetzung der Studierenden?


J.A.M.: Es gibt keinen nennenswerten Unterschied zwischen den Kämpfen rassifizierter und nicht rassifizierter Menschen, aber es gibt einen Unterschied in der medialen Sichtbarkeit rassistischer Natur, der uns zutiefst empört und darauf abzielt, unsere Anliegen zu diskreditieren – was uns dazu antreibt, noch geeinter zu sein. Die Schüler, die Schulen in den Vororten besuchen, haben mit noch baufälligeren Gebäuden zu kämpfen als diejenigen im Stadtzentrum, doch ist ihr Zugang zu den Orten der Mobilisierung möglicherweise erschwert: An den Tagen der Mobilisierung wird der Nahverkehr mit der klaren Absicht eingestellt, die Zahl der Menschen zu verringern, die zu den Demonstrationszügen gelangen können.


A.A.: Wie sah das Leben der Schüler*innen vor der Mobilisierung aus und wie hat es sich danach verändert?


J.A.M.: Vor der Mobilisierung war der Alltag kaum zu ertragen. Überfüllte Klassenräume, abwesende Lehrkräfte, die nicht ersetzt wurden, ausgefallene Unterrichtsstunden wegen fehlender Räume oder Lehrkräfte und ein Klima, in dem man uns sagte, wir sollten den Mund halten und für „Parcoursup“ arbeiten, anstatt auf unsere Forderungen einzugehen. Die Beziehungen zu den Lehrkräften waren meist distanziert, da sie keinen Einfluss auf unsere Bedingungen haben und selbst überlastet sind. Einige unterstützten uns jedoch bereits und diskutierten mit uns über die Studien- und Lehrbedingungen, wenn sich während einer Unterrichtsstunde die Gelegenheit dazu bot – allerdings nie länger als ein paar Minuten. Seit Beginn der Mobilisierung hat sich alles verändert: Wir reden wirklich miteinander, halten gemeinsam Vollversammlungen ab, essen gemeinsam vor …

author: Simon Upitis
title: Protesters Shut Down Bisalloy Steels - Again
content:
Hundreds of protesters shut down Bisalloy Steels on Sunday 15 November, preventing it from operating for 48 hours. This was the eleventh time Wollongong Friends of Palestine (WFOP) had organised a picket of the company.

Bisalloy Steels produces armour plating used by the IDF and by West Bank settlers to oppress Palestinians. Steel plate produced by Bisalloy is used to retrofit civilian vehicles with armour plating, making them bulletproof and allowing them to be fitted with roof-mounted machine guns. Bisalloy is also set to benefit from Australia’s increased military spending via the AUKUS agreement. In July, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy announced a $2 million contract would be awarded to Bisalloy to produce steel for US Virginia-class nuclear submarines. 

The picket had a lively atmosphere. A makeshift stage was set up at one entrance with DJs, live music and poetry readings. Free food and first aid were provided by volunteers. Dozens of activists camped overnight, ensuring that the company couldn't sneak workers through the picket in the early hours of the morning. Attendees came from far and wide, with many travelling down from Sydney. Palestine Action Bega Valley attended as a group. Other groups with an official presence included the NSW Socialists and the Illawarra Greens.

At the other entrance, political discussions were held in gazebos set up on the street, often involving dozens of attendees. One member of WFOP recently returned from the West Bank recounted their experiences defending Palestinian farms from settler violence. Nurses spoke against their regulatory agency’s adoption of a Zionist definition of antisemitism. There was debate about the type of movement required to free Palestine and the tactics and strategies needed to push the struggle forwards. NSW Socialists held a forum with the candidate for Wollongong in the state election, Ryan Chapman. The success of the various workshops and discussions prove the pickets can be a place for left-wing people to gather and discuss live political questions. 

This picket experienced much less police harassment and intimidation than the previous one. In June, the company planned to break through the picket line and bring a busload of workers into the site. We stopped them, but the police maintained a heavy presence on that occasion. One attendee was arrested. Another was violently thrown to the ground, and everyone else was subjected to their petty demands and often thuggish behaviour. Riot squad cops also came down from Sydney. 

This time, we heard on Sunday night that Bisalloy wouldn’t try to bring in workers until we left. Throughout the picket, there was a very minor police presence, normally a single cop car. This was a significant victory. It shows the company wasn’t confident enough to directly confront our community campaign.

Of course, we can’t be complacent. At some point, the company will get fed up with the disruptions and take a more combative and confrontational approach. In the meantime, the campaign remains committed to stopping Bisalloy profiting from genocide.

author: Malik Chiconela Santana
title: Mozambique: A Judicial Solution to a Political Problem
content:
Venâncio Bila Mondlane, the leader of the Mozambican opposition, finds himself awaiting trial (scheduled for November 17) for his alleged role as the progenitor of the seismic protests that followed the 2024 elections and threatened to topple the state. Mondlane is president of the recently formed National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (ANAMOLA) party. He is accused of five crimes by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, namely

public justification of crime, incitement of collective disobedience, public instigation of crime, instigation of terrorism, and incitement of terrorism

. A conviction could mean up to 20 years in prison for the presidential runner-up, the crippling of the opposition, and a transition in the state’s handling of political opponents.


Mondlane’s road to the 2024 ballot was lined with legal and procedural obstacles.

Blocked

 from contesting the leadership of his party at the time, the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO), he left it and allied his campaign with the Democratic Alliance Coalition (CAD), whose electoral eligibility was confirmed on May 9, but was excluded by the National Election Commission (CNE) on July 18. The Constitutional Council (CC) upheld the decision on appeal, arguing that the parties who had formed CAD failed to notify the

Ministry of Justice and Constitutional and Religious Matters

 of their intention to form a coalition. The court framed the decision as a purely technical issue; however, its consequences were undeniably political. Mondlane found himself politically isolated only two months before the elections. Forced to reorganize his campaign, Mondlane forged a last-minute partnership with the Optimistic People for the Development of Mozambique (PODEMOS), running as an independent with the party’s political and parliamentary support.


This chronology illustrates how the political agency of Mondlane and his supporters was repeatedly at odds with applications of the electoral law. It may not establish that each application of electoral law was politically motivated, but, at the very least, it raises a broader question of how ostensibly procedural outcomes can reshape the field of political competition, and suggests that legal procedure is not necessarily neutral.


After the October 9, 2024, vote, the CNE declared Daniel Chapo, candidate of the ruling Mozambique Liberation Front (Frelimo), the winner with about 70%, to Mondlane’s 20%. In December, after more than 300 complaints of electoral crimes and irregularities had been lodged with local and district courts, the Constitutional Council revised those figures to roughly 65% and 24% respectively. The revision was, in effect, an admission that the election commission’s results were dubious at best and fictional at worst. The CC altered the results when, as a body of electoral oversight, it could only order the CNE to recount the votes or annul the elections. Unsurprisingly,

the Mozambican Bar Association

 (OAM), opposition parties, and civil society groups expressed concerns over the CC’s vague legal reasoning and the lack of an evidentiary basis for its alteration of the results.


What ensued in the wake of these opaque elections was a six-month period of unprecedented violence. In Mozambique, several elections have been followed by periods of armed conflict. What made this period unprecedented, however, was that the antagonism was not between the state and an organized army, but rather between the state and a mobilized mass of unarmed civilians. According to a

report

 by the Mozambican NGO Plataforma Decide, 411 civilians were killed, some 3,700 were injured, and around 7,200 were illegally detained between October 2024 and January 2025. These figures were disputed by the then commander-general of the police, Bernardino Rafael, who stated that 96 civilians were killed. Even so, charges have only been brought

against two officers

, and, with no updates, it is unclear whether the prosecution is pursuing these cases at all.


The protests began on October 21, when Mondlane called for a peaceful march in tribute to Elvino Dias, his lawyer, who was assassinated by assailants of no particular origin as he prepared an appeal challenging the preliminary election results. This march, like many that followed, was dispersed violently, including through the use of tear gas and live ammunition. In an environment where constitutionally protected political activities are met with violence, the …

author: Unknown
title: Morti 2 tecnici laziali di Rheinmetall per i detriti di un drone in Kuwait, primo Paese importatore di armi italiane nel 2026
content:
2 tecnici italiani dell’azienda bellica tedesca Rheinmetall sono morti giovedì 26 novembre 2026 in

Kuwait

, colpiti dalle schegge cadute dopo l’intercettazione di droni. Chi li abbia scagliati, al momento, non si sa: il Kuwait accusa l’Iran, che tuttavia con una nota delle stesse forze armate “respinge in modo categorico e assoluto di aver condotto operazioni militari o offensive” nelle ultime ore, scaricando invece le responsabilità su Israele e Usa, accusate di “cercare pretesti per esacerbare l’instabilità nell’area”.


Da Radio Onda d’Urto


Non è nemmeno chiaro, al momento, dove fossero i due, il 65enne Antonio Saccoccio di Formia e il 36enne Emanuele Lo Russo di Roma, colpiti assieme a un cittadino del Kuwait e uno del Pakistan, feriti. Non si fa cenno al luogo dell’impatto nel comunicato diffuso dal Ministero della Difesa del

Kuwait

, dove a ottobre 2026 i 300 militari italiani presenti nel Paese per “Inherent Resolve” avevano lasciato la base di Ali Al Salem, dove ci sono anche militari Usa, più volte presi di mira da attacchi iraniani seguiti ai raid di Washington e Tel Aviv, da fine febbraio 2026.


I 2 tecnici sarebbero stati in Kuwait per manutenzione alle antenne di rilevamento del sistema di difesa antiaerea Skyguard in dotazione alla Marina del Kuwait, fa sapere

Rheinmetall

, azienda bellica tedesca con sede centrale italiana a

Ghedi

, Brescia, nello stesso comparto dove si trova la base militare dell’Aeronautica, con  personale Nato e – nel sottosuolo – svariate bombe nucleari.


La divisione italiana del gruppo tedesco della difesa ha tuttavia il polo produttivo per eccellenza a

Roma, sulla Tiburtina

, nel settore dei sistemi radar e della difesa antiaerea.


Il costo di una singola batteria completa del

sistema Skyguard (e della sua evoluzione Skynex) oscilla generalmente tra i 50 e i 75 milioni di euro,

 secondo quanto si può desumere da alcuni contratti stipulati con vari Governi dalla stessa Rheinmetall, non l’unica azienda privata presente in Kuwait.  Anche Leonardo e altre realtà del comparto aerospaziale e della difesa mantengono personale in Kuwiat, legato all’Italia da uno specifico “Accordo di cooperazione militare” entrato in vigore nell’ottobre 2026 che stabilisce una cornice quinquennale rinnovabile per “l’addestramento congiunto, lo scambio di informazioni classificate, il trasferimento di materiali d’armamento e la cooperazione nella sicurezza marittima”.


Secondo le relazioni governative sull’export militare pubblicate nel 2026,

il Kuwait è  al primo posto tra i destinatari di armamenti italiani

 grazie a una singola autorizzazione individuale da 2,6 miliardi di euro. A maggio 2026, inoltre, Leonardo ha ottenuto un contratto da 320 milioni di euro per equipaggiare i nuovi pattugliatori navali kuwaitiani.


Su Radio Onda d’Urto intervista a Gianni Alioti, ricercatore di

The Weapon Watch

 – Osservatorio sulle armi nei porti europei e mediterranei.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Revocan prisión preventiva de Javier Troncoso Chuñil y se confirma inexistencia de restos de Julia en el predio familiar
content:
Este 27 de noviembre la corte de apelaciones de Valdivia revoco la prisión preventiva a prisión domiciliaria total a Javier Troncoso, uno de los últimos hijos que aún se mantenía en prisión preventiva tras desarrollarse una hipótesis de fiscalía, sin sustento, culpabilizando y criminalizando a la familia. Fueron diez meses de prisión para una medida cautelar que siempre estuvo injustificada y sin pruebas que sustentaran tal hipótesis según la abogada defensora Karina Riquelme.

DECLARACIÓN PÚBLICA Y COMUNICADO OFICIAL DE LA FAMILIA CHUÑIL

Revocación de la Prisión Preventiva por la I. Corte de Apelaciones de Valdivia La Ilustrísima Corte de Apelaciones de Valdivia ha resuelto revocar la prisión preventiva de Javier Troncoso, disponiendo su libertad tras haber permanecido privado de libertad de manera injustificada. Esta decisión judicial confirma lo que nuestra familia ha sostenido categóricamente desde el inicio de la investigación: la carencia de antecedentes graves y mérito para mantener cautelar alguna y la absoluta inconsistencia de la imputación construida por el Ministerio Público.

Resultados Definitivos de ADN del Servicio Médico Legal (SML) De manera paralela, se han recepcionado formalmente los resultados definitivos de los peritajes de ADN elaborados por el Servicio Médico Legal (SML). Dichos análisis científicos ratifican y confirman de forma concluyente que las osamentas recuperadas no corresponden a nuestra madre y abuela, descartando de manera absoluta la presencia de restos de Julia del Carmen Chiuñil Catricura en el predio familiar.

Llamado a Observar los Procesos Judiciales, las Falsas Acusaciones y el Despliegue Mediático Hacemos un llamado urgente a la opinión pública, a las organizaciones de derechos humanos y a los medios de comunicación a examinar con rigor y sentido crítico el desarrollo de este proceso judicial. Durante meses, la Fiscalía Regional desplegó un desmedido aparato mediático y formuló imputaciones públicas apresuradas que criminalizaron a nuestra familia y distorsionaron la realidad de los hechos. La evidencia científica y las resoluciones de los tribunales superiores demuestran hoy la gravedad de las falsas acusaciones y la necesidad imperiosa de garantizar un debido proceso libre de sesgos.

Re afirmación Inquebrantable de la Búsqueda de Julia Chiuñil Catricura La libertad de Javier y la confirmación científica del SML no marcan el fin de nuestra lucha, sino el pilar para reorientar los esfuerzos hacia donde siempre debieron estar: la búsqueda efectiva y seria de Julia del Carmen Chiuñil Catricura. Instamos a las instituciones del Estado a enfocar todos sus recursos técnicos en líneas de investigación reales y rigurosas. Nuestra familia no descansará hasta encontrar a nuestra madre y abuela, y hasta que la verdad prevalezca.

¡SEGUIMOS FUERTES Y UNIDOS BUSCANDO A NUESTRA MADRE Y ABUELA JULIA CHIUÑIL! FAMILIA DE JULIA DEL CARMEN CHIUÑIL CATRICURA

title: Cafer Mahiroğlu soruşturmasında üçüncü dalga: Ece Üner ve Özgürdeniz Bayramoğlu gözaltında
content:
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, Halk TV’nin sahibi Cafer Mahiroğlu’na yönelik yürüttüğü soruşturma kapsamında 12 kişi hakkında yeni gözaltı kararı verdi.


Savcılık, 12 kişi hakkında ‘suçtan kaynaklanan mal varlığı değerlerini aklama’, ‘suç işlemek amacıyla örgüt kurma ve örgüte üye olma’, ‘halkı yanıltıcı bilgiyi alenen yayma’, ‘rüşvet’, ‘ihaleye fesat karıştırma’ ve ‘Vergi Usul Kanunu’na muhalefet’ suçlamalarıyla gözaltı talimatı verdiğini duyurdu.


Aralarında Halk TV sunucuları Ece Üner ve eşi Özgürdeniz Bayramoğlu’nun da bulunduğu dokuz kişi gözaltına alındı. Halk TV Haber Koordinatörü Hakan Kürşad Oğuz ise yurt dışında olduğu için gözaltına alınmadı.


Hakkında gözaltı kararı verilen isimler şunlar:


Ece Üner (Halk TV spikeri)


Deniz Bayramoğlu (Halk TV spikeri)


Haydar Rüzgar (Bustech firma yöneticisi)


Ulaş Eroğlu (İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi Makine İkmal Bakım ve Onarım Daire Başkanı)


Aşkın Tahan (İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi Makine İkmal Bakım ve Onarım Daire Başkanlığı personeli)


Ali Kemal Korgan (Korganlar isimli firma sahibi)


Hamza Okuyucu (HMF Taşımacılık firma sahibi)


Ahmet Keçiyokuşu( Bustech isimli firma yöneticisi)


Halit Akın (Bustech isimli firma satın alma müdürü)


Emre Kaya (Esbakım firma sahibi)


Kürşad Oğuz (Halk TV Haber Koordinatörü)


Recep Ersü (Repar isimli firma sahibi – başka bir soruşturma kapsamında tutuklu)


Başsavcılığın Halk TV’ye yönelik iddiaları


Cafer Mahiroğlu’na yönelik soruşturmada bugüne kadar 19 kişi gözaltına alındı, 8 kişi de tutuklandı.


Savcılık, Mahiroğlu’nun Halk TV’yi satın aldıktan sonra kanalın ekonomik sıkıntı yaşamaması için İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesinden usulsüz ihaleler aldığını iddia ediyor.


2021’de İzmir’de kurulan Bustech Araç Bakım Onarım Hizmetleri AŞ’nin paravan şirket olduğunu, sahibinin Mahiroğlu olduğunu ve bu şirketin belediyenin araç bakım, onarım ve temizlik ihalelerini rüşvet karşılığında aldığını ileri sürüyor.


Bu ihalelerden elde edilen gelirlerin de Halk TV’nin yanı sıra Özdemir Üç Tekstil’e, Mahiroğlu’nun diğer şirketlerine ve yurt içi ve yurt dışındaki kişisel hesaplarına aktarıldığını iddialar arasında.


Paranın farklı hesaplar arasında kısa süre içinde birden fazla kez dolaşıma sokularak aklanmaya çalışıldığı öne süren savcılık, Bustech şirketinin dört yedek parça şirketiyle anlaşarak gerçekte yapılmayan mal ve hizmet alımları karşılığında yüzde 12 ila 14 oranında komisyonla sahte fatura düzenlettiğini de öne sürüyor.


Söz konusu faturalar karşılığında şirketlere verilmesi gereken çeklerin Halk TV’nin kasasında bulunduğunu ileri süren Başsavcılık, bu çeklerden elde edilen parayla Ece Üner ve Özgürdeniz Bayramoğlu’na aylık 1 milyon 650 bin TL kayıt dışı ödeme yapıldığını iddia etti.


Başsavcılık, bu ödemeler karşılığında Üner ve Bayramoğlu’na “talimatlı gerçeğe aykırı haberler yaptırıldığı” iddiasında bulundu.


(HA)

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: ASEAN mass arrests fuel renewed push for New Public Assembly Act
content:
Police arrest protesters, including members of alternative media and student publications, in Sucat, Muntinlupa City, on November 15, 2026. The protesters are part of a delegation who are set to join a protest in Manila against Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump's visit. Photo from Bayan Laguna

The right to assemble and express dissent is constitutionally guaranteed and should not be treated as a privilege granted by authorities.

By Reachelyn Esona Bulatlat.com

It was past 2 p.m on November 15 when hundreds of protesters were arrested in what was described as the largest single-day mass arrest under the administration of Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Before progressive groups from Southern Tagalog could join the anti Pax-Silica and Trump Out protest at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, the Southern Police District blocked and arrested nearly 300 protesters at Sucat People’s Park in Muntinlupa City. Among those who were arrested were 19 student journalists and alternative reporters.

Read: Police violently disperse, arrest hundreds in Muntinlupa protest

The arrested protesters faced inquest proceedings over alleged violations of Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, or the Public Assembly Act of 1985, as well as alarms and scandals, and resistance and disobedience to a person in authority. They were eventually released after prosecutors granted the motion filed by their lawyers.

The arrests, however, renewed a long-standing concern among human rights defenders: instead of protecting the people’s right to peaceful assembly, B.P Blg. 880 has been used to restrict and penalize the exercise of that right.

At a public forum on the human rights legislative agenda organized by Karapatan on November 20, Kabataan Party-list Representative Atty. Renee Co discussed House Bill No. 4574, or the proposed New Public Assembly Act. The bill seeks to repeal the Marcosian decree Batas Pambansa 880 and establish a new legal framework that strengthens the protection of the people’s right to freedom of assembly.

Read: Repressive decrees, issuances, legacies of Marcos dictatorship, remain in force

Co cited a series of arrests and restrictions involving protesters in Muntinlupa, Bulacan, Liwasang Bonifacio, Cebu, and other areas, as well as students who participated in university walkouts. She said authorities have invoked BP 880 to justify restricting assemblies, particularly those held outside designated freedom parks without permits.

Under the existing law, organizers are generally required to secure a permit for public assemblies, except in designated freedom parks and certain other circumstances.

The proposed HB 4574 seeks to change this framework.

According to the bill’s explanatory note, it removes the “no permit, no rally” policy and replaces it with a notice system. Rather than requiring organizers to obtain permission from authorities, the proposed system would require them to notify the appropriate authorities of their planned assembly, with the presumption that assemblies are peaceful.

The bill also provides for the automatic designation of public parks, halls, and plazas as freedom parks in cities and municipalities that fail to designate such spaces. This provision aims to ensure that people have accessible venues where they can exercise their right to peaceful assembly.

These proposed changes are rooted in a broader argument raised by the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL): the right to assemble and express dissent is constitutionally guaranteed and should not be treated as a privilege granted by authorities.

“Our rights do not require permits,” NUPL said.

The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) likewise emphasized that freedom of expression and peaceful assembly must be respected, as guaranteed under Article III, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution.

During the same forum, Karapatan Secretary General Cristina Palabay called for the passage of a new law to replace B.P Blg. 880, arguing that the existing legislation is a remnant of the Marcos dictatorship and no longer responds to the realities faced by protesters today.

Despite these calls, HB 4574 has yet to advance beyond the committee level. Co said the bill was filed last year but has seen little progress, as it is not among the administration’s legislative priorities. She stressed the need to broaden public awareness on the right to peaceful assembly and build public support for the bill to help move it forward in Congress.

author: Jonathan Rosenblum
title: Amazon Workers Step Into Orwell’s 1984 Every Time They Enter Delivery Vans
content:
Drivers are fighting back against a system that monitors their every movement to keep them working at breakneck speeds.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

That Black Friday item you just ordered on Amazon — the holiday gift, household gadget, or perhaps a mundane cable — might be in a warehouse on the other side of the country, but it will land on your doorstep tomorrow. The speed of its delivery is a testament to the remarkable efficiency of Amazon’s intricate supply chain and the labor of the company’s more than 2 million employees and contractors worldwide. In 2025, Amazon workers delivered 13 billion items on the same or next day, including 8 billion items in the U.S. — “a new Prime delivery speed record,” the company boasted.

To move merchandise through this vast and complex network, Amazon relies on an army of workers to move stuff extremely quickly. It keeps the work tempo at breakneck speed through a sophisticated AI-driven system of labor discipline.

Amazon warehouses are notorious places of surveillance in the service of increasing productivity. Managers continually monitor workers’ stow, pick, and pack rates, and then discipline those they consider to be low-performers. They induce speedups by gamifying work and setting up contests where high-performing workers are offered Amazon “swag bucks” — redeemable through Amazon, of course. They monitor each worker’s “time off task” like going to the bathroom or taking brief breaks between moving packages. And they discipline workers who are deemed to need hustling up.

But the Amazon panopticon reaches next-level dystopia when your package arrives at the “last mile” in the supply chain. That’s where one of the quarter-million delivery drivers in the U.S. brings your package from the delivery station warehouse to your door. At the beginning of each shift, drivers are handed an Android phone to log in to Amazon Flex using facial recognition technology. The Flex app provides them a detailed route for the day, showing exactly which packages are to be delivered where, and in what order. After loading up their vans, drivers get into the cabs, where they are under the continual surveillance of the “Netradyne Driver•i,” a sinister-looking windshield-mounted device with camera lenses pointing in all directions, continually recording and monitoring driver compliance with Amazon’s myriad rules. Many of these rules are sensible: Make a full stop at stop signs, don’t run red lights, obey speed limits, and avoid lane drift and sharp accelerating or braking. But Netradyne cameras, installed in Amazon vans beginning in 2021, serve a more expansive purpose beyond monitoring traffic rule compliance — what its manufacturer calls “physical AI deployed at scale.” For drivers, it watches your eye orientation and movement, whether you yawn, and if you look away from the road for too long. It continually looks for cases of “distracted driving,” which are considered major infractions. All of these data points are used to evaluate your behavior every second. And it’s not just AI; human supervisors can also choose to watch you at any moment through the Netradyne cameras.

I’ve worked for the last two years as a part-time Amazon delivery driver. I technically work for a “delivery service partner” company, or DSP. Amazon uses the legal dodge of sham contracting to claim that drivers are not their employees and therefore not their liability, even though we all are required to wear Amazon uniforms, drive Amazon-branded vehicles, and are subject to Amazon work requirements as we deliver Amazon packages. Worse, we are all subject to the Amazon-mandated tracking and oversight system.

When I’m in the Amazon truck, every movement I make is traced by the Amazon Flex app technology and evaluated by AI programs. It records where I am at any moment, which packages I’ve delivered, and whether I’m keeping pace with the algorithm that Amazon has determined I must meet. Readouts at the end of every shift show how each of my deliveries compared to the timing prescribed by Amazon’s algorithmic standard. We are evaluated every week on whether we took accurate photos on delivery, delivered the packages exactly where the customer requested, and got good or bad customer feedback. Through the system, drivers who don’t “make rate” or who don’t meet Amazon’s prescribed standards don’t stay employed …

author: Faiz Naeem
title: Supporting a progressive digital reform agenda for Bangladesh
content:
To: 

Mr. Tarique Rahman

Honourable Prime Minister

Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh


Subject: supporting a progressive digital reform agenda for Bangladesh


Bangladesh’s digital reforms are at a turning point. We, the undersigned organisations, urge your government to protect what has been achieved, restore the safeguards that have been stripped away, and build a legal and institutional framework that centres people’s rights, democratic accountability, and a free, open and secure internet.


Digital reform is an essential part of delivering on your

stated commitment

 to strengthen accountability and prevent authoritarianism. Laws and institutions governing online expression,  privacy, cybersecurity, surveillance and artificial intelligence shape how people participate in public life, access services, organise, communicate and hold power to account.


Prior to the interim government assuming office, the

Digital Security Act, 2018 (DSA) and Cyber Security Act, 2023 (CSA)

 were

repeatedly used to target journalists, activists and others for online expression

, internet

shutdowns were imposed

 during periods of political mobilisation; and

surveillance and interception capabilities expanded

 without sufficient transparency or independent oversight. Some reforms were initiated during the interim administration, which included somewhat

narrowing the criminalisation of some forms of online expression

 through the repeal of the CSA and enactment of the Cyber Security Ordinance, 2025, introducing requirements for explicit consent to process personal data with exemptions to such protection in limited circumstances under the

Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025

, and establishing a

prohibition on internet shutdowns

, now retained in

section


63 of the Bangladesh Telecommunication (Amendment) Act, 2026

, which amends

section 97 of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulation Act, 2001

.


The subsequent legislative process has exposed how easily rights safeguards can be weakened while broader state powers remain intact. The Bangladesh

Telecommunication (Amendment) Act, 2026

 kept the Ordinance’s

wide interception powers

 but removed or diluted several safeguards. The Ordinance had

abolished the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC)

 and replaced it with the Centre for Information Support, prohibited interception for political or ideological purposes, and required every interception to be approved by a court or review council under detailed conditions. But the 2026 Act reversed all three. According to section 64 of the 2026 Act, which amends section 97(A) of the 2001 Act, interception may now be approved

by a court or simply by “an authority constituted by the government”,

 and the government alone decides which agency carries it out. The NTMC,

whose operations were extended for another year by the Ministry of Home Affairs

, continues to function without a clear, public-facing statutory mandate, independent oversight framework or meaningful transparency requirements. The

Personal Data Protection Act, 2026

, likewise,

exempts state authorities on broad and undefined grounds such as national security, public order and public interes

t

, without judicial supervision or any duty of transparency when the exemption on consent requirements for the processing of personal information is invoked.


These concerns are not abstract. The

UN fact-finding investigation

 into the events of July and August 2024 described how surveillance-derived intelligence was used in connection with repression of civil and political rights. A

government committee subsequently reviewed

 the procurement and use of surveillance technologies, but its report has still not been made public.


At the same time, proposals to criminalise “rumours”, “disinformation”, and “defamatory information” through

amendments to the


Cyber Security Act 2026

 would reverse the progress made by repealing earlier speech offences. Our objection is not to how these terms are drafted but to treating them as crimes at all. Under international human rights law, the dissemination of false or unverified information is not in itself a legitimate ground for criminal sanction; the UN Human Rights Committee has made clear that imprisonment is never an appropriate penalty for defamation.  The vaguely defined proposed offences fail this test: for instance, “rumours” could cover any unverified information that creates …

author: Unknown
title: Narges Mohammadi calls for the protection of women against cyber threats
content:
Women in Iran face legal and societal threats. While women's rights organisations continue to call for the strengthening and enforcement of existing laws and institutions that safeguard women's dignity and security, Nobel Peace Prize-winning activist Narges Mohammadi has released a video message.


In her message, shared on a digital platform, Narges Mohammadi called for solidarity with and support for women who are subjected to organised cyber threats and interference because of their activities in social, political, media and human rights fields.


Narges Mohammadi said that, in recent years, she herself has faced harassment, insults, death threats and widespread gender-based cyber violence, adding that these attacks continued even while she was imprisoned.


Addressing the methods of cyber harassment targeting women, Narges Mohammadi explained that these attacks include organised smear campaigns, the exposure of personal information, insults, misogyny, the spread of misinformation and the circulation of fabricated images generated using artificial intelligence (AI). She emphasised that the aim of these attacks is to isolate, intimidate and silence women.


Drawing attention to statistics, Narges Mohammadi said that more than 70 percent of women journalists, activists and those in leadership positions experience cyber harassment. She warned that such attacks must not silence women or force them to withdraw from public life.


At the end of her statement, Narges Mohammadi reiterated the need for solidarity and collective support to protect women facing smear campaigns and cyber threats.

author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 19 November 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Making sense of the Digital Fairness Act, a very unmerry birthday to the Digital Omnibus, and more!

Last week, the European Commission put digital fairness on the menu with a proposal for its long-awaited Digital Fairness Act (DFA) – and we have some food for thought.

This law will strengthen consumer protection against manipulative and exploitative commercial practices, such as fake notifications designed to keep bringing us back to an app, endless scrolling that keeps us online way longer than you intended, and other personalised techniques used by online services that exploit our vulnerabilities. First things first, proposal actually takes some important steps forward by introducing new prohibitions on deceptive design, extending specific protections beyond the biggest online platforms, and recognising the harms associated with addictive digital features. However, we were left wondering – why promise digital fairness yet leave the users to do all the work instead of holding manipulative online services responsible? Read our analysis on Tech Policy Press.

Despite it all, the DFA proposal – something that actually might protect our rights online – is a welcome respite in the current wave of deregulation in the EU. This week, we’re also reckoning with the fact that November 19, 2026 marks one year since the Commission published the proposals for the Digital Omnibus. We, along with many other civil society organisations, had warned that this would be a massive reopening of EU’s core digital protections that would risk dismantling the very foundation of human rights and tech policy in the EU. One year on, it seems like we were granted Apollo’s gift of prophecy. On this unfortunate occasion, we’re standing strong with 100 organisations, experts, academics and more to urge EU lawmakers to not simplify away our rights.

In this edition, you can also explore our extremely thorough guide to the European Parliament’s 1840 amendments to the Digital Omnibus on Data, focusing on what they would mean for privacy, data protection and, ultimately, people’s rights. Yes, 1840, you read that right. Hungry for more? Also read our thoughts on the EU governments’ position on the Digital Omnibus.

1,840 amendments, one basic question: will the Data Omnibus simplify EU digital rules or weaken people’s rights? author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: The death of the word?
content:
Michelangelo,

Cumaean Sibyl

 (c. 1511), Sistine Chapel, Vatican City


This short article was originally published under the title “Morte della parola?” in the Italian newspaper

Paese Sera

 on 8 February 1968. It has been republished in the latest issue of the French magazine

Entétement

, although the original version can be found on the

La Voce di Fiore

 archive website. A Spanish translation of the same can be found at th magazine

Ficción de la razón

.


A book has recently been published in Paris,

Of Grammatology

 (1967), a work destined to cause a stir not only in the field of linguistic studies. Jacques Derrida, one of the most original figures in the new wave of French philosophical criticism, begins with the observation that, today, “through a movement whose necessity we can barely glimpse, everything that, for at least twenty centuries, has tended to be defined under the name of language, is beginning to be summarised under the name of writing”. It does indeed seem that writing—which, according to Rousseau, was nothing more than a complement to speech—is gradually freeing itself from its subordination to the phonetic medium, to the point of reversing its traditional relationship with language: writing would therefore not be a technique in the service of language, but rather, on the contrary, it is language that can be considered a specific case, an aspect, of writing.


To better understand the phenomenon to which Derrida refers when he speaks of writing dissociated from the phonetic element, one need only consider the example of mathematics, whose symbolic notation does not refer to any spoken language. If we consider that today we are witnessing a process of mathematisation across all the sciences, the “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon (readers who have followed recent news regarding the

in vitro

 synthesis of living matter, carried out by certain American scientists, will recall having heard talk of writing and “programmes” even in relation to the most elementary processes of the living cell). The “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon.


On the basis of these premises, Derrida deduces the need for a pure science of writing, which considers writing prior to speech and independently of it: this science is, precisely, “grammatology”; and, to define its aims, it suffices to substitute this term for “semiology”, the term Saussure uses to outline the programme of his famous

Course in General Linguistics

: “We shall call it grammatology… and, as it does not yet exist, we cannot say what it will be; but it has a right to exist, and its place is determined in advance”. The age of speech, which began under the creative power of the verb, is drawing to a close before our very eyes; the character of this new age might be summed up in the following formula: “In the beginning was the written word’’.


Whilst it is true that, from this perspective, linguistics must become a mere branch of grammatology, Derrida seems, however, to overlook the fact that a science already exists which considers language not as speech, but as code and writing; consequently, grammatology itself should necessarily be understood as a sub-branch or a section of that science. This is cybernetics, which, from its beginnings in Wiener’s theories, defined its world as a universe of writing and coding. The very idea of grammatology is already fully contained within the notion of “programme”, one of the key concepts of cybernetics. Etymologically, “programme” —pro-grammer— means “to put the letter (that is,

writing

) first”, whilst “prophecy” means, by contrast, “to put the word first”. Indeed, in the programme assigned to an electronic brain, everything that constitutes the living, phonetic element of language is erased to make way for a system of absolute writing that can be deciphered but not pronounced. author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Harassment won’t stop a son’s search for his missing father
content:
Marklen Lariosa, son of missing Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) labor organizer William Lariosa, speaks during a rally in Davao City on the first anniversary of his father’s disappearance on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kath Cortez/Davao Today

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through.”

Is it a mistake for a son to demand justice and accountability?

Marklen, son of disappeared labor organizer William Lariosa, raised this question following the recent incident of harassment and surveillance he experienced. Members of his family were alarmed after two unidentified individuals were looking for his residence on the night of October 25.

He told Bulatlat that this was the first time such an event had happened since his father, a labor organizer under Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) Southern Mindanao, was abducted in Quezon, Bukidnon, on April 10, 2024.

Marklen could not think of other possible reasons, suspecting that the incident may have something to do with his continuing involvement in campaigns and mobilizations that demand the surfacing of Lariosa. “Is it a mistake for a son to search for his missing father?” he further asked.

Read: After 2 years, son laments continuing disappearance of Mindanao labor organizer

Neighbors of the Lariosa family in their hometown in Davao de Oro province were the ones who encountered the two individuals. They reportedly wore helmets and were on board a black motorcycle, introducing themselves as “collectors” when they were asked.

For Marklen, the response and presence of the two raised suspicions. Aside from the fact that they visited the community around 7 p.m., which is outside the regular working hours, Marklen said that he did not apply for any financial loan.

After the incident, he was concerned for the safety of his family, prompting them to lodge a blotter report with the barangay. However, he stood firm that it won’t stop him from continuing his cause.

Desaparecidos, an organization of families and friends of enforced disappearance victims, denounced the incident, urging the government to put an end to this kind of harassment.

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through,” JL Burgos, Desaparecidos chairperson, said in a statement.

Rights groups Karapatan and the Center for Trade Union and Human Rights (CTUHR) also expressed strong condemnations about what happened.

Marklen, a member of the National Board of Desaparecidos, has raised a possibility that the two individuals who recently visited their neighborhood might be connected to those who visited their house several times prior to the disappearance of his father.

He said they were visited by individuals who allegedly introduced themselves as state agents once in 2022 and three times in 2023, accusing Lariosa of being involved in communist insurgency. There were warnings, he added, that they would get dragged into it if they would not cooperate.

The series of visits was reportedly the primary reason why Lariosa was forced to take refuge in Bukidnon. Marklen affirmed that his father, who remains missing, had been a labor organizer.

On July 8, the Supreme Court required certain commanders and elements of Philippine Army units to comment on the petition for review on certiorari filed by the family.

Read: Military ordered to reply to missing Mindanao labor organizer’s case

Since 2024, KMU Southern Mindanao has documented 57 cases of human rights violations against its members and organizers.

The labor group released a statement on October 24, presenting the faces of some individuals, including former high-ranking New People’s Army (NPA) member Roberto Rosete Jr., who allegedly harassed KMU’s leaders and members.

Read: Groups decry surveillance of KMU office in Southern Mindanao

Marklen called for an end to any form of harassment and intimidation against families of the disappeared, pointing out that achieving justice is their only goal. (RVO)

author: Darius Tahir
title: Health Tech Is Pushing Data-Collecting “Smart” Implants That Raise Cost of Care
content:
Doctors can charge for examining data collected by devices that have little evidence for benefiting patient health.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said.

Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’”

It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer.

Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit, Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t.

Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues.

Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment.

The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court.

Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.”

Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future.

“The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.”

The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “the world’s first and only” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices — from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors — that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance.

However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes.

There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data — is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect.

Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: NO a la guerra: La deserción no es solo una objeción
content:
enviado por FRANCO BERARDI


https://substack.com/@francoberardi1


25.11.2026   

ILDISERTORE


La deserción no es solo una objeción


Un año después de la muerte de Paolo Virno, recurrimos a uno de sus escritos para ayudarnos a comprender la diferencia entre el acto individual de objeción de conciencia y la práctica colectiva de la deserción.


Publicado el 20 de noviembre de 2026


Por 

Giulio de Petra


Cuanto más se refuerza la propaganda que ya existe en la guerra, más se extiende en la opinión pública la convicción de que se trata precisamente de propaganda, y de la peor clase.


Intentaron convencernos de que los correos electrónicos falsos que llegan a todas las escuelas italianas procedentes de ‘Misoginistán’ también son un episodio de ‘guerra híbrida’.


Los menos convencidos de la guerra inminente son los más jóvenes, precisamente aquellos que deberían ir a la guerra, y hacia quienes la pedagogía bélica, viril y practicada en su mayoría por maestros mayores y, por lo tanto, protegidos de cualquier riesgo concreto, tiene mayor fuerza.


Es en este contexto, que lleva a muchos a preguntarse qué se puede hacer eficazmente para contrarrestar la profecía de la guerra antes de que se cumpla, que el tema de la deserción adquiere una nueva relevancia.


Fue Bifo, en 2023, con su libro «Disertate» (véase: 

https://centroriformastato.it/perche-la-diserzione/ 

), quien actualizó una práctica política antigua y controvertida, que había adquirido gran relevancia en la cultura política de la izquierda desde la Primera Guerra Mundial. A partir del libro de Bifo, este enfoque se ha extendido por las movilizaciones antibelicistas de los últimos años, llegando a públicos inesperados.


Recientemente, en una conferencia pública, Virginia Libero, secretaria nacional de los Jóvenes Demócratas (la organización juvenil del Partido Demócrata), declaró con vehemencia en su discurso: «No seremos los soldados en sus guerras. Si estos grupos de derecha nos arrastran a un conflicto real, tomen las armas. Porque organizaremos a los desertores». Esta es una declaración con una fuerte carga política, ya que no solo plantea la posibilidad de la deserción, sino que busca «organizarla». El discurso, como es bien sabido, provocó comentarios indignados y llamados a la defensa del deber constitucional de «defender la patria», lo cual —como ha establecido el Tribunal Constitucional, y vale la pena recordar— puede hacerse no solo mediante el servicio militar, sino también mediante el servicio civil.


Pero no es en eso en lo que queremos centrarnos.


Pier Luigi Bersani también estuvo presente en uno de los muchos programas de entrevistas televisivas donde se comentaron las palabras de Virginia Libero. Tras defenderla de las críticas recibidas, con su característica prudencia emiliana, le sugirió que cambiara la palabra que había utilizado. Hubiera sido mejor, para expresar el mismo concepto de aversión a la guerra, invocar no la «deserción» sino la «objeción de conciencia».


Pero, ¿son realmente intercambiables ambas palabras?


Un año después del fallecimiento de Paolo Virno, queremos recordarlo recurriendo a sus escritos para que nos ayuden a responder a esta pregunta.


En el libro 

En los años de nuestro descontento. Diario de la contrarrevolución 

(Derive e approdi, 2022), Virno publica un texto suyo de enero de 1991, titulado 

La deserción, herencia política de la multitud 

, en el que leemos:


Existe 

una clara distinción entre la objeción de conciencia y la deserción. Aunque a primera vista parezcan similares, estas dos formas de protesta contra la guerra son, en realidad, polos opuestos. La objeción de conciencia no cuestiona la lealtad general al Estado ni desafía sus prerrogativas fundamentales (por ejemplo, el monopolio de la violencia). Más bien, mientras se defiende sin reservas el pacto político-institucional que regula la esfera pública, se afirma una reserva privada, arraigada en las profundidades del individuo. Una irreductibilidad personal, de carácter moral o religioso, se opone a la decisión política del Estado. Esta última nunca corre el riesgo de ser abrogada por la primera, sino que, de hecho, puede incluirla y regularla. La objeción de conciencia es un enclave, un contrapunto, una variante. Que el alma dubitativa tenga su propio refugio institucional no derroca, sino que consolida, los cuerpos militares, ya sean de conscriptos o profesionales.


La deserción es un asunto distinto. Siempre ha sido un acto …

title: Kurdistan Regional Government: We reject the use of military rhetoric and threats
content:
Kurdistan Region’s Prime Minister Masrour Barzani chaired the KRG Council of Ministers’ meeting today. The meeting focused primarily on the KRG’s position regarding measures taken yesterday by the federal government of Iraq.


The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region is committed to fulfilling all its constitutional obligations and demands the full provision of its constitutional rights: “The KRG has consistently expressed its readiness to resolve outstanding issues with the federal government within the framework of the Constitution. Consequently, the KRG expresses its deep concern and strong protest regarding the statement issued on behalf of the spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, which violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region. This statement is a dangerous indication of a lack of belief in the federal system and represents an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime, which contradicts the Iraqi Constitution. The KRG rejects the use of military rhetoric and threats, which appear to stem from a premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.”


The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region has consistently supported measures to combat corruption and illegal activities, and has cooperated and coordinated with the federal government and will continue to do so to eliminate illicit practices. It called for the comprehensive eradication of corruption and oil smuggling across all of Iraq.


The Council of Ministers stressed that the Kurdistan Region is the product of the sacrifices of the heroic Peshmerga and thousands of martyrs; it is not a gift bestowed upon the people of Kurdistan: “The Kurdistan Region has played an active and influential role in establishing the current federal system in Iraq, regards itself as a co-owner of that system, and will never relinquish its constitutional rights, which extend far beyond salaries, budgets, and financial entitlements. They also encompass political rights and the legitimate cause of the people of Kurdistan.”


The KRG Council of Ministers stressed that issues between the Kurdistan Region and the federal government must be resolved through dialogue, negotiations, and mutual understanding within the constitutional framework, calling for the full implementation of the permanent Iraqi Constitution.


“The primary reason these issues remain unresolved is the failure to implement the Constitution, particularly Article 140, which has been neglected for years, with no steps taken to normalize the situation in the disputed Kurdish territories. In accordance with the Constitution, the Federal Council of Iraq should be established, and the Federal Supreme Court reconstituted on a constitutional basis that reflects all components of Iraq.”


The Council of Ministers expressed its gratitude to the Kurdistani people, as well as to all political parties, forces, and components, urging them to maintain their national stance, unity, and solidarity in defense of the constitutional rights of the people of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Region's constitutional framework. It also called upon the Kurdistan Region's representatives in the Iraqi Parliament and the federal government to continue their national role in defending the rights of the Kurdistani people.


The Council of Ministers reaffirmed its support for freedom of opinion and expression. However, it emphasized that anyone who acts against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region, constitutional principles, or Kurdistan’s national interests and incites people to create chaos and oppose the rights of the Kurdistani people should face appropriate legal action.
