title: Guerrillas: We will uphold the PKK's legacy no matter what
content:
The Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) was founded on 27 November 1978 in the village of Fis in the Lice district of Amed (Diyarbakır), in memory of martyr Haki Karer, based on the struggle for Kurdish identity and the vision of a free life. Throughout the PKK movement's history of resistance, major initiatives have continually been undertaken to keep the memory of fallen comrades alive. These initiatives contributed to the growth of the PKK movement over the years and enabled it to accumulate an invaluable legacy and experience. Abdullah Öcalan defines the PKK as the party of martyrs. People’s Defense Forces (HPG) and Free Women’s Units (YJA Star) guerrillas Şîlan Amara and Tîrêj Şêrîn spoke to ANF on the occasion of the 48th anniversary of the PKK's foundation.


 


YJA Star guerrilla Şîlan Amara said that the Kurdish people rose again with the foundation of the PKK: "Comrade Haki laid the foundations of our struggle and the establishment of our party, the PKK. This is a day of rebirth. Millions of people pursue this cause today, and this is the meaning we attach to this day. For us, the PKK represents the existence of a people. Today, the PKK has dissolved itself in accordance with the needs of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan) decided to dissolve the party in accordance with the conditions in the Middle East. Before the PKK was founded, our movement was an Apoist movement. It began as an Apoist group and later developed into the PKK movement. Above all, we are Apoists, and we wage our struggle on the basis of the Apoist legacy, thought and philosophy. Today, our people are in the streets, struggling and demanding their rights.


If we can speak about our rights in parliament today, it is thanks to the PKK. The PKK martyrs created a free life moment by moment and advanced their struggle through self-sacrifice. They wrote epics through their struggle and became the bearers of a free life. They struggled for years for a single purpose. They became the enduring and universal legacy of a genuine thought and philosophy. We have lost 35,000 martyrs, and these martyrs embody the values of this movement. We have reached this day by paying such a heavy price and have waged our struggle on this basis. Today, we need a stronger struggle than ever before. No matter what happens, we will uphold the legacy left behind by the PKK. Today, we continue our struggle as the Apoist movement. We will carry this legacy and keep this flag flying until the end. Our struggle will continue on this basis."


The PKK made the world recognize the existence of the Kurdish people


 


HPG guerrilla Tîrêj Şêrîn said that 27 November is a particularly significant date for the Kurdish people: "I congratulate all our people, the families of martyrs and Leader Apo on the 48th anniversary of the PKK. We are now in November, the month in which the PKK was founded. The PKK, through its foundation and its defense of the Kurdish people and Kurdistan, made the entire world recognize the existence of the Kurds and secured their existence through its struggle. Before the PKK, almost nothing remained in the name of the Kurdish people and Kurdistan, whose existence had been denied. The emergence and foundation of the PKK proclaimed the existence of the Kurdish people to the world. We therefore reiterate that the PKK represents a spirit, a life and a philosophy of life for us.


The Peace and Democratic Society Process is currently underway in Turkey. As part of this process, the PKK has dissolved itself as a party. Its mode of operation as an organization and its political status may have been dissolved. However, the Apoist group existed before the PKK movement. The PKK was founded and developed in this way. It has now dissolved itself as part of this process. However, we remain an Apoist movement and continue to act accordingly. The dissolution of the PKK does not mean that we have abandoned our Apoist struggle. We have our goals and objectives. A legacy was established through the PKK. We have our martyrs, 50,000 martyrs. There is a body of thought. Methods and forms change, but the struggle continues. As the Apoist movement, we will fulfill whatever responsibilities fall upon us during this process for the people of Kurdistan and the existence of Kurdistan. Martyrs are a bridge between human beings and truth, enabling them to attain a passion for life.


We have duties and responsibilities during this important process …

author: Unknown
title: The road to 27 November: The PKK founding Congress and its aftermath
content:
This article is compiled from a piece written by Duran Kalkan and published in a special edition of

 Serxwebûn

marking the 30th anniversary of the founding of the PKK.


For a period, an ideological grouping developed in Ankara among university students around a form of communal life. Through Leader Apo’s [Abdullah Öcalan] understanding of freedom, equality, democracy, sharing, and his way of life and political stance, this grouping acquired a sense of consciousness and organization and was subsequently carried to Kurdistan.


The ideological grouping established among the student youths in Ankara developed, during 1976–77, into a dynamic youth organization in Kurdistan, based primarily on secondary-school students.


Secondary-school young people are generally less experienced and younger, and they require more education. In terms of organizational life, they are also less mature and tend to be closer to their families and family-oriented characteristics. University students, by contrast, represent a more advanced position in these areas.


Indeed, the fact that the first ideological grouping was established among university students served two purposes for the PKK: it helped identify potential cadres capable of educating and training all segments of youth and developing their experience and strength; at the same time, it made it possible to establish the communal way of life, to which university students were more receptive, as the dominant approach within all forms of youth organization.


On the road to the PKK founding Congress


Almost every city and town in Northern Kurdistan, and virtually every place with schools, had such a youth organization and a communal youth life.


In particular, following the martyrdom of Haki Karer on May 18, 1977, the process of developing youth organization and transforming the movement into a party led to a more advanced and mature level of activity and organization.


As the PKK moved toward its Founding Congress, unorganized youth environments, especially among students, had become almost nonexistent.


At the same time, significant progress had been made in discussions about the party and the organization in preparation for the congress.


Leader Apo repeatedly stated that, following the killing of Comrade Haki Karer, he had decided to establish a party as a way of honoring his memory and had prepared a draft party program on this basis.


In short, beginning in the summer of 1977, the process of party formation became an issue on the agenda of the Freedom Movement. Everywhere, the questions of "How should we organize?" and "What should the party look like?" began to be discussed in all their aspects.


The preparation of a draft program and its presentation to the cadres inevitably made these discussions more organized and systematic.


The decision to form a party and the first issue of 

Serxwebûn


On this basis, in November 1977, during the Eid al-Adha period, a meeting of cadres was held in Amed (Diyarbakır) to discuss the question: "How should we organize and form a party?"


The discussions at this meeting were undoubtedly interesting.


In response to Leader Apo’s position, which placed great importance on the organization and, within it, the formation of a party, and which brought these issues onto the agenda for discussion, Şahin Dönmez displayed an unwillingness to form a party and adopted an approach that sought to postpone the process.


Such a debate took place, and the majority of the cadres attending the meeting, particularly Mazlum Doğan, supported Leader Apo’s idea of forming a party.


This meeting did not result in any organizational decision. However, it brought the discussion process, particularly the question of "What kind of organization and party should we have?", more seriously and comprehensively onto the agenda of the youth movement.


Later, in the spring of 1978, a similar meeting was held in Elazığ. The agenda was the same: "What kind of organization and party should we have?"


Similar discussions took place there as well. Unlike the meeting in Amed, however, this gathering marked a step toward a certain organizational differentiation and development, and decisions were taken to make this possible. Thus, following this meeting, youth organization was developed on the one hand to carry out all kinds of practical and organizational activities. title: Those tags make no sense. ‘Modern society’ did not start in the early 2000s. If this graph showed…
content:
wrenchinator-central

:

zolltraak

:


Those tags make no sense. ‘Modern society’ did not start in the early 2000s. If this graph showed the loss of community in modern society (it does not), we would see a continuous development since the 1950s at least and probably long before that.

We would also see 'work’ and 'through family’ being less effected because capitalism has maintained these two social spheres. We do see 'work’ rising as a place to meet a spouse in the 1950s to 1980s, coinciding with a growth in the percentage of women in the workplace. But it would be ridiculous to argue that the dominance of work in our life has declined since then, and yet meeting your spouse at work also took a nosedive in the 2000s.

Instead, the decline we’re seeing can be completely, easily explained by the fact that since the 2000s online dating became an easy way to meet people and allowed people to explore, reject and select far more potential partners than ever before. Which says absolutely nothing about the state of community.

It does open up interesting questions. If over 50% of couples meet outside their existing social circles, does that reduce societal segregation along lines like ethnicity and class? Are people more likely to meet a partner outside their own home town and travel to be with them? Does the lower reliance on meeting friends through existing social circles make it easier for isolated individuals to find partners? The data doesn’t show us this but it would be interesting to explore.

Finally, note that this data was presented in this manner by Marriage Pact, a creepy matchmaking organization committed to pushing US college students to get married. It is worth asking where an organization that sees marriage as one of the highest goals in life stand politically and what it seeks to gain by presenting this data?

title: Bayık: The PKK's struggle secured recognition of the Kurds' existence
content:
Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) Executive Council Co-Chair Cemil Bayık discussed the conditions surrounding the establishment of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), the sociological and political atmosphere of Kurdish society in the 1970s, the values created through half a century of struggle and the movement's strategy for the new period in a special program broadcast on Stêrk TV.


Cemil Bayık said that the PKK was founded at a time when Kurdish identity, language and culture were denied, genocidal policies were pursued, assimilation and economic impoverishment were widespread, and social struggles were subjected to severe repression. He said that half a century of struggle had, above all, instilled national consciousness in Kurdish society and enabled the Kurdish people to rise again. Bayık described the conditions of the period, saying, "They did not regard Kurds as human beings. For a Kurd to gain their acceptance, to be regarded as a human being, they had to abandon their Kurdish identity." He emphasized that economic policies were also an important part of the genocidal process, that Kurdistan's economic resources were plundered and that society was impoverished. Bayık said that the emergence of the PKK had initiated a new period of struggle and organization within Kurdish society, adding, "The movements that emerged before the PKK were divided along regional, sectarian, religious and tribal lines. The Kurdish struggle transcended the boundaries of a single part of Kurdistan and regional boundaries for the first time with the PKK."


Bayık said that the PKK had dissolved after the launch of the Peace and Democratic Society Process by Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February 2025, but that the decision to end the armed struggle did not mean that the struggle itself had ended. He emphasized that this was a change in strategy and method, adding that the PKK would continue its struggle and sustain the values it had created through different means and in a different form. Bayık said that communal organization would form the basis of the new period and emphasized the importance of communes in enabling society to meet its own needs, govern itself and develop a democratic life.


Half a century has passed since the establishment of the PKK. A struggle has been waged at every moment throughout this period. What were the social, economic, political and cultural conditions in Kurdistan before the PKK was founded?


Before answering this question, I would like to congratulate the people of Kurdistan and humanity on the anniversary of the founding of the PKK. The PKK was not founded under favorable conditions or on the basis of already established values. The conditions in which Kurdish society and the Kurdish people lived when the PKK was founded were extremely difficult. The Turkish state was pursuing a policy of genocide against Kurdish society and the Kurdish people. Through this policy, they had concluded that the Kurds and Kurdistan would never be able to rise again. Their policy aimed to turn Kurdistan entirely into a territory where the Turkish state could establish its own nation. They sought to eliminate the Kurdish people altogether. An extremely brutal policy was being pursued. What was written on Mount Ararat after the Ararat rebellion? "Kurdistan is buried here." In other words, there was no longer a Kurdish or Kurdistan question here. That was the conclusion they had reached.


They believed that the policies they had pursued against Kurdish society and the Kurdish people had made it impossible for such a question to emerge again or for the Kurds to survive as such. Their policy was based on eliminating the Kurdish language, identity, values, culture and economy, in other words, everything associated with the Kurds and Kurdistan. As a result, they had fragmented society. They had even created contradictions within Kurdish society. They had alienated Kurdish society from everything that belonged to it. People within Kurdish society had forgotten their enemies and had turned against one another. They had developed such a brutal policy within society. Kurdish society had lost everything as a result of the policies pursued by the Turkish state. It was no longer only the Turkish state that sought to eliminate the Kurds. These policies had alienated the Kurds from their own reality to such an extent that they were destroying themselves.

author: Unknown
title: DEM Party: The constitutional status of the Kurdistan Region must be protected
content:
The Central Executive Board of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) issued a statement concerning the constitutional status of the Başûrê Kurdistan (Southern Kurdistan) administration and recent developments in the region.


The statement described the legitimate, legal and democratic status of the Kurdistan Region, guaranteed under Iraq’s 2005 Federal Constitution, as an expression of the Kurdish people’s historical achievements and the democratic will of the Kurds and all other communities in the region. It emphasised that protecting and strengthening this status is important not only for the Kurdish people, but also for Iraq’s social peace, political stability and democratic future.


The statement noted that tensions have escalated in recent days over the management of border crossings and energy resources, once again highlighting the importance of federalism and constitutional balances. It also drew attention to the need to resolve the administrative, economic and legal disputes between Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government.


The statement said: “Administrative, economic and legal disputes arising between Baghdad and the Regional Government must be resolved within the constitutional framework, through dialogue and negotiations, rather than through unilateral decisions, rhetoric that escalates tensions or militaristic approaches. The Federal Government of Iraq must act through collective consensus, adhering to the spirit of the Constitution and the legitimate rights of the Kurdish people. This is the only path towards a lasting solution.”


The statement also addressed political actors and institutions in Başûrê Kurdistan, emphasising the importance of prioritising democratic consensus during this critical period, resolving disputes through dialogue, and strengthening social unity and institutional functioning.


DEM Party stated that it supports safeguarding the constitutional status and achievements of the Kurdish people and resolving all disputes through peaceful and democratic negotiations. It added that protecting rights and the people's democratic will on the basis of mutual respect would contribute to Iraq's democratisation, as well as regional peace and stability.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: DAR urged to side with the landless Bukidnon farmers
content:
BTLM members stand in front of land they had been tilling within Central Mindanao University in Barangay Dologon, Maramag, Bukidnon. Photo by Franck Dick Rosete/Bulatlat

MARAMAG, Bukidnon — Farmers within a state university here welcomed the recent development in their pursuit of land ownership.

This came after the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) had already conducted its area validation and survey on the land that the concerned farmers had been tilling within Central Mindanao University (CMU) in Barangay Dologon, Maramag, Bukidnon.

The farmers belong to the Bukidnon Free Farmers and Agricultural Laborers Organization (Buffalo), the Triad Agricultural Manpower of Rural Active Workers (Tamaraw), the Landless Tillers Inhabitants of Musuan (Limus), and the Musuan Inhabitants’ Landless Farmers Association (Milfa). They are collectively known as BTLM, with more or less 700 members.

Now, they urged the government agency to conclude the process in favor of the landless peasants.

“This is to have a boundary line between the farmers and Central Mindanao University (CMU) and to avoid conflict,” Herman Santillan, who has been designated as BTLM spokesperson, told Bulatlat in the vernacular.

The three-day land validation and area survey of DAR started on October 6, more than four months from the issuance of Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III’s order declaring all CMU lands “not actually, directly, and exclusively utilized for educational purposes” included in agrarian reform coverage under Executive Order No. 75-2019.

For them, this is the closest to victory for nearly two decades of fighting for land ownership. They are now waiting for the next stage.

CONTEXT: How the issue between BTLM farmers and CMU started

Abdullah Linog, DAR Northern Mindanao assistant director for operations, confirmed that the regional office has already received the transmittal of its Bukidnon office, containing the classification of CMU lands, but it has yet to determine which land can be covered by agrarian reform.

Santillan, however, said that he saw the transmittal from the Bukidnon Provincial Agrarian Reform Office indicating that a total of 1,037 hectares of lands were intended for the agrarian reform beneficiaries.

To respect the status quo, BTLM farmers have not tilled the land. However, they have been maintaining their presence by staying in their makeshift shelter.

Read: Bukidnon farmers guard disputed land due to unsettled demand

They founded the makeshift shelter after their houses were demolished and their ready-to-harvest palay were uprooted in 2024. Because of this, they are planning to file damages against CMU due to the alleged questionable demolition.

“We really file damages because we have all the evidence,” Santillan said. (RVO)

Le travailleureuse vend sa force de travail à un patron, en échange d'un salaire, qu'il ou elle est contraint de faire, parce qu'on ne possède pas les moyens de production, genre les outils, l'usine pour produire des trucs, les terres pour cultiver, un parc immobilier à louer... author: Unknown
title: Groupe de parole MeToo inceste et pédocriminalité Lyon
content:
Dans chaque groupe, deux personnes du collectif s'occupent de la modération et du soutien émotionnel individuel (si besoin, si une personne s'extrait du groupe). Ces personnes sont elles-mêmes concernées et prennent part aux échanges.


Le groupe est consacré aux personnes victimes d'inceste et de pédocriminalité, non aux personnes autrices de ces actes, même si elles ont elles-mêmes été victimes.


Le groupe de parole commence par une explication du déroulé. Ensuite, un tour de parole sert à se présenter (prénom, pronoms), à dire comment on se sent en ce moment et le sujet que l'on veut amener. Après, ça reste libre et d'autres sujets de la thématique peuvent être abordés.


Une vigilance à la répartition de la parole est faite mais il n'est pas obligatoire de s'exprimer.


Groupe sur inscription car limité à 10 personnes. Anonymat garanti, possibilité de se présenter sous pseudo dès l'inscription.


En partageant nos expériences et nos sentiments par la parole et par l'écoute, nous cherchons avant tout à rompre notre isolement, et à trouver une aide et un réconfort moral mutuel. Nous souhaitons également susciter notre capacité à demander de l'aide, c'est pourquoi il est complémentaire et ne se substitue pas à une thérapie souvent nécessaire (bien que coûteuse...).

author: Pudelfreund
title: TSP: „Bedrohung“ für die Beamten: Polizist erschießt Pudel bei Einsatz in Berliner Hotel
content:
Weil ein Mann mit einem waffenähnlichen Gegenstand über den Breitscheidplatz lief, alarmierten Zeugen die Polizei. In einem Hotel machten Beamte den Verdächtigen ausfindig. Es fielen Schüsse.


Ein Polizist hat in der Nacht zu Mittwoch einen Hund in einem Hotel in der Berliner Kantstraße erschossen. Das Tier – es handelte sich nach Polizeiangaben wohl um einen Pudel – sei „eine Art Bedrohung“ für den Beamten gewesen, sagte eine Polizeisprecherin. Zum Schutz des Lebens habe er mit seiner Dienstwaffe auf das Tier geschossen. Es sei wohl noch vor Ort gestorben. Wie viele Schüsse abgegeben worden sind, war den Angaben zufolge zunächst unklar.


Zu dem Polizeieinsatz war es gekommen, weil Zeugen einen Mann mit einem waffenähnlichen Gegenstand auf dem Breitscheidplatz in Charlottenburg gesehen hatten. Wenig später, gegen 4 Uhr, klopften die Beamten der Polizei zufolge an die Tür eines Zimmers im Hotel „The Cloud One“ in der Nähe, in dem sie den Mann vermuteten.


Der Verdächtige habe die Tür geöffnet und die Beamten mit dem waffenähnlichen Gegenstand bedroht. Einen ersten Schuss habe ein Beamter bereits zu diesem Zeitpunkt abgegeben – jedoch ohne jemanden zu verletzen.


Dann sei der Hund aus dem Zimmer gerannt und von einem Beamten erschossen worden. Der 63-jährige Tatverdächtige sei festgenommen und in ein Krankenhaus gebracht worden, weil er psychisch auffällig gewesen sein soll. Bei dem waffenähnlichen Gegenstand handelte es sich nach Angaben einer Polizeisprecherin um ein Tierabwehr-Spray in Form einer Pistole. (dpa, Tsp)

author: Muximba da Silva
title: ‘Essas queimadas destroem os sonhos da gente’: O Amapá sob incêndios e o El Niño
content:
Era 6 de outubro de 2026. O dia estava mais quente que o normal. Maria Tavares havia viajado do município de Tartarugalzinho, estado do Amapá, para votar no 1.º turno das eleições de 2026 na capital, Macapá. Cerca de 228 km percorridos. Quando saiu de casa, deixou o esposo e os filhos cuidando da roça da família. No local, plantações de limão, caju, ameixa, macaxeira e outros frutos da terra que são divididos entre subsistência e fonte de renda para a comunidade de Ponta do Socorro, zona no entorno da Reserva Biológica do Lago Piratuba. Aí vieram as queimadas.


Foi através de uma mensagem no celular que Maria recebeu a notícia. “Um vizinho veio avisar meu esposo que o fogo estava vindo e que ia passar, atravessar a estrada. Aí os meninos foram pra lá [a roça da família], meus filhos, e quando chegaram lá já estava pegando fogo”, relata. O esposo, Paulo Brito, é da família que fundou a comunidade e, junto de Maria e dos filhos, fazem parte da Associação de Agricultores da comunidade.


O que as 57 famílias de Ponta do Socorro estão vivendo faz parte de um aumento expressivo nos incêndios no Amapá.

 Dados do BDQueimadas, do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), revelam que entre 1º de agosto e 16 de novembro de 2026, foram registrados 2.152 focos de calor, quase quatro vezes o que foi medido no mesmo período de 2025, com 569 focos. O levantamento considera as detecções do satélite de referência utilizado pelo programa. Um foco de calor é o registro feito por satélites de um ponto na superfície com temperatura muito alta, que indica um incêndio.


“É uma sensação de impotência saber que tudo que a gente lutou anos para construir, agora ver queimado, destruído, é muito triste.

 “Foi a primeira vez que queimou tudo assim, eu fiquei muito triste, até chorei porque é doloroso a gente ter as coisas da gente, lutar pra ter, e acontecer isso, né?! Essas queimadas destroem os sonhos da gente também”, diz Tavares.


O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo

O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo

O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo

O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo


Os números colocam o Amapá como o estado com o maior aumento percentual de focos de calor entre os nove estados da Amazônia Legal.

 Tartarugalzinho, no período analisado, teve 227 focos, quase o dobro em relação a 2025.


Dados do Núcleo de Hidrometeorologia e Energia Renováveis (NHMET-Iepa) revelam que, em setembro, o Amapá atingiu uma média de temperaturas acima de 34 ºC, sendo a maior dos últimos 58 anos.

“No mês de outubro foram registrados picos de elevações de temperatura ultrapassando os 38 °C, juntamente com a umidade relativa que ficou abaixo dos 30%, que é considerada uma umidade de climas desérticos.

 Isso se deve à intensidade do El Niño, que está intensificando o período de estiagem na nossa região”, comenta o meteorologista Jefferson Vilhena, pesquisador do NHMET-Iepa.


Segundo o quinto boletim do Painel El Niño, publicado pelo Inmet, entre novembro de 2026 e janeiro de 2027, o fenômeno pode levar a temperaturas acima da média em quase todo o país e chuvas abaixo da média em grande parte da Região Norte. O episódio pode ser o mais intenso desde 1950.


Agravados pelo El Niño, incêndios estão ligados à ação humana


Renato Hilário, professor e pesquisador da Universidade Federal do Amapá, explica que esse cenário é propício para o aumento das queimadas no estado.

“O fenômeno pode favorecer condições ambientais que facilitam a propagação do fogo. Isso acontece porque o El Niño intensifica a estação seca em diferentes regiões da Amazônia, reduzindo a umidade da vegetação.

 Com a vegetação mais seca, o fogo consegue se espalhar com maior facilidade, fazendo com que os incêndios atinjam áreas maiores e se tornem mais difíceis de controlar”, explica.


No entanto, Hilário explica que o fogo não deve ser colocado apenas na conta do El Niño. “Embora possam ocorrer incêndios de origem natural na Amazônia, provocados principalmente por raios, esses eventos são relativamente raros. A grande maioria dos incêndios que observamos na região tem origem em atividades humanas. Nesse sentido, o El Niño não é o principal responsável pelo início dos incêndios, já que a origem do fogo está predominantemente relacionada à ação humana”.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Aesthetics, Technology, and Politics in the 2026 Local Elections
content:
THE 2026 LOCAL ELECTIONS have been marked by distinctive and innovative campaigning by the DPP, mostly related to the “Ocean Current” phenomenon. In many ways, the “Ocean Current” phenomenon and the aesthetic and political experimentation it entailed carried out the logical development of aesthetic and political tendencies that date back to the Sunflower Movement. But in the vast amount of aesthetic and cultural references it included, one can also point to how the “Ocean Current” phenomenon reflects contemporary Taiwanese identity trends–as well as its incorporation of data analytics into its political aesthetic.

The most distinctive feature of the “Ocean Current” is perhaps the distinctive ribbon associated with Puma Shen supporters. Many design variations of this ribbon exist, which are released periodically and available openly for supporters to make variations on.

Craze around such ribbons is such that Shen supporters will crowd for hours at DPP city councilor offices, cafes, and other places where limited-edition designs will be released. Especially popular variations are those which involve animal designs, rainbows, or other prominent symbols.

A post shared by Sheena Wu (@nanawuco)

Indeed, the term “Ocean Current” originates with two designers, Ken and Hsu Chia-lun. A poster made by the two designers for Shen gained attention on social media, leading the DPP to seek permission to use the name for the two designers. But, in this sense, many designers have contributed their own poster designs to the “Ocean Current” phenomenon, printing them out and distributing them personally, or distributing them at rallies.

The distinctive “merch” of the “Ocean Current,” then, perhaps takes advantage of the craze of contemporary Taiwanese for merch. Craze for anime collectibles is such that even convenience stores sell and distribute limited-edition anime merchandise. And election collectibles were already a feature of the political landscape, dating back to democratization. The craze about election collectibles is such that Shen will even have areas set up in his political rallies for supporters to trade campaign merch. Nevertheless, from this, one can observe the open, participatory, and tactile nature of the “Ocean Current” phenomenon.

Indeed, Puma Shen emphasized a campaign that, in some form, emphasized expertise, in that Shen often brandished his academic expertise as a researcher in analyzing data to formulate policy. Yet often the focus was on collecting data and opinions from members of the citizenry and communicating them in an open and transparent manner.

Shen used his campaign website in order to collect opinions and what issues the public cared about through the “Mayor, Listen to Me!” platform. This at times led to surprising conclusions, such as discovering that members of the Taipei public were concerned with the decreasing amount of greenery in the urban landscape. Shen collected over 70,000 responses, which were organized according to local area, allowing Shen to come up with specifically tailored policy proposals. The website was gamified and featured interactive cartoon animal characters.

Shen’s campaign website, then, was used to publicize the platforms he came up with. The “Heart Island” website, which resembled Animal Crossing or similar online games and contained detailed policy briefs, was in itself interactive and engaging, as a presentation of policy platforms within a microcosm depicting the city itself. Shen can be found wandering the depiction himself–reportedly along with competitor Chiang Wan-an.

Likewise, one notes the emergence of several websites that compiled lists and maps of stores in Taipei considered pro-Taiwan, pan-Green, or supportive of the “Ocean Current”, such as a store tracker that centered the Shen campaign, and another with a more pro-Taiwan theme.

To this extent, in line with the tactile nature of the “Ocean Current”’s merch, well-designed print publications detailing these policy platforms were distributed by Shen at campaign stops in the form of campaign newspapers. What’s more, however, was that this was not merely a newsletter. Zine versions of the same policy platforms were also rolled out, incorporating the work of writers, artists, designers, and other creatives. An online music contest was also held by the Shen campaign to gather fan-made anthems, similar to past online music contests held by Tsai Ing-wen.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Inquest jury calls for more mental health support for families of police shooting victims
content:
Jury members of the inquest into 21-year-old Trey Angootealuk’s death recommended that Nunavut provide more support for the families whose loved ones have been killed by police.


The jury delivered its verdict following a four-day inquest that heard testimony from the RCMP officers who fatally shot Angootealuk in Rankin Inlet on Nov. 7, 2021, after an extended standoff with four officers in the outskirts of town.


Jurors ruled he died from a gunshot wound to the chest, and that his death was a homicide.


“Nunavut has some of the highest rates of police shootings in the country,” said Nikolai Sittmann, counsel for the Angootealuk family. “In light of this reality, it’s important that families and loved ones affected in these situations get the services and support they need.”


The jury said Nunavut’s Health Department should be responsible for creating the counselling program, with specialized trauma counsellors.


The inquest by Nunavut chief coroner Marianna Cervantes began Monday at the Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet. The jury made its recommendations Thursday afternoon.


Coroner’s inquests are mandatory in Nunavut for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. Juries do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.


The jury was asked to rule on the cause of his death, to provide recommendations for how to prevent deaths of similar circumstance, and to make recommendations for how police can respond in similar incidents.

 


It also recommended that Nunavut RCMP have access to Inuktitut-speaking negotiators at all times and for the territorial government and Inuit organizations to better inform citizens about the safe firearm storage.


Technical recommendations included that infrared devices be incorporated into each RCMP detachment to improve visibility in the night, as well as the introduction of modern drones.


Visibility was a challenge the morning Angootealuk was killed, officers testified, and they couldn’t use their drone to deliver a message during the standoff because it was being used to light up the truck that Angootealuk was in.


The jury also recommended that coroner’s inquests into fatal police shootings be completed within two years of the incident.


The recommendations were largely based on those provided by lawyers for the Angootealuk family, coroner and the RCMP. All three parties were in agreement.


“In these particular circumstances, there may not have been anything exactly more that could have been done, given the danger present and the reality of the situation the ground,” said coroner’s counsel Jessi Casebeer when sharing her recommendations.


“While the recommendations may not go directly to preventing similar deaths, they will go to minimizing the harm of these types of deaths.”

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Father of man killed by police testifies at inquest
content:
The father of the 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man shot and killed by police five years ago testified at the coroner’s inquest into his son’s death on Thursday.


Thomas Angootealuk was emotional as he took to the witness stand for about 10 minutes.


“He was my son,” Thomas Angootealuk said with tears in his eyes, as he held a photo of Trey Angootealuk.


On Nov. 7, 2021, police fatally shot Trey Angootealuk after a standoff

 with

 four RCMP officers in the outskirts of town.


A day earlier, Trey Angootealuk hijacked a truck and shot at police officers before parking and remaining in it for several hours. The standoff ended after police launched a canister through the truck’s rear window and then shot him.


The inquest by Nunavut chief coroner Marianna Cervantes began Monday at the Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet. The jury made its recommendations Thursday afternoon.


Coroner’s inquests are mandatory in Nunavut for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.


The jury has been asked to rule on the cause of his death, to provide recommendations for how to prevent deaths of similar circumstance, and to make recommendations for how police can respond in similar incidents.

 


Thomas Angootealuk told the jury that he always tried to be a good role model for his son. He was training him to operate heavy equipment.


Thomas Angootealuk, a school bus driver, found his son a job as a school bus monitor. They worked together, with Trey Angootealuk making sure kids stayed put in their seats.


“I couldn’t work after losing my son,” Thomas Angootealuk said.


When he did try to return to work, a child asked where his son had gone. Thomas Angootealuk said he broke down.

 


“How am I supposed to answer an eight-year-old boy, who doesn’t know anything about that?”


Two of Angootealuk’s siblings also testified Thursday, sharing fond memories, such as the time he gave caribou meat to elders.

 


“Me and my brother had a bond I’ll never be able to explain to anybody else,” his sister Rosalie Angoshadluk said. “We didn’t need a plan, we just needed to be out together laughing until our stomach hurt and acting like we had all the time we wanted in the world.”

author: By Darren Thompson, Unicorn Riot
title: 10th Annual Walk Against Uranium Brings Hundreds to White Mesa Ute Community
content:
Ute Mountain Ute Reservation — On Saturday, October 17, hundreds joined the White Mesa Ute community in an annual rally and spiritual walk against a uranium mill that is central to the country’s domestic uranium supply chain. Ute Mountain Ute tribal members say that the White Mesa Mill facility located in Blanding, Utah, threatens their environment and pledge to continue their opposition against the operation. 


Event organizer and White Mesa community member Yolanda Badback spoke to a crowd of several hundred, welcoming them to the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation in southeastern Utah. She explained the purpose of the event, what the intention was and what people could expect. “Thank you for coming to White Mesa to help us in our opposition against the uranium mill,” she told the crowd who gathered at the White Mesa Community Center at the beginning of the rally.


“This mill is contaminating our land, our water, and our people and it must be stopped.” 


Yolanda Badback, White Mesa community member, event organizer


The White Mesa Mill is owned and operated by Denver-based Energy Fuels and is the only conventional and fully-licensed uranium mill in the country. The mill sits five miles away from the Ute Mountain Ute reservation in southeastern Utah and has the capacity to produce up to eight million pounds of uranium per year. Last year, the mill produced more than 1,000,000 million pounds of uranium, according to the

company’s website

. 


Aerial view of the White Mesa Mill in Blanding, Utah. Photo contributed by Darren Thompson.


The mill has been licensed since 1980, where it processed natural uranium ore into yellowcake (U₃O₈) for nuclear energy. Today, the mill processes “alternate feeds” including radioactive residues from Superfund and Manhattan Project sites and produces vanadium and light rare earth elements.


The company

announced in July 2026

 that the mill is expanding. Energy Fuels says the expansion will enable large-scale production of heavy rare earth oxides, which are planned to be used to produce rare earth metals, alloys and magnets essential to the automotive, robotics, data center, energy and defense industries.


The planned expansion is two-fold and its first phase is expected to be completed by the end of 2027 and the second phase to be completed by the end of 2028. 


Currently, multiple semi-truck loads are seen arriving at the White Mesa Mill on a daily basis and they’re transporting uranium ore from the

Pinyon Plain Mine

 via two routes in northern Arizona through the Navajo Nation.


The mine is an active uranium mine near Red Butte Mesa, a sacred site to the Havasupai Tribe, and is owned and operated by Energy Fuels.


Since transportation began in 2025, there have been two reported accidents involving the transportation of the mineral on the Navajo Nation.


There are approximately 1,629,000 pounds of U₃O₈ at Pinyon Plain Mine, contained in 82,800 tons at an average grade of 0.98% U₃O₈. It is one of the highest grades of U₃O₈ in the world and the mine’s operations are in the Baaj Nwaavjo I’tah Kukveni – Ancestral Footprints of the Grand Canyon National Monument.


Related – May 2026:

Indigenous Grand Canyon National Monument Designation Wins in Appeals Court


The National Monument was established by President Joe Biden on August 8, 2023 and led by a coalition of tribes including the Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Navajo Nation, Paiute bands, and Pueblo of Zuni. The Havasupai and other tribes have opposed the uranium mine since the mine’s beginning in 1980 and its leaders continue to voice their opposition to the mine’s operations. 


“We came up here and saw all these mining trucks and it really broke our hearts, but that’s not going to stop us” said Havasupai tribal citizen Carletta Tilousi during the rally. “We are the water people and we came here to support the White Mesa community and all of you, because this issue doesn’t just affect this community.” 


The Havasupai have been monitoring the operations of the Pinyon Plain Mine and they have voiced several concerns regarding the permit’s request to raise the minimum arsenic levels in three groundwater wells at the mining operation.


Related – June 2026:

Anti-Uranium Summit Sheds Light on Toxic Industry


Recently, the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality denied the tribe’s appeal that amended the mining permit to raise the minimum arsenic level 10%, from 0.05 to 0.055 milligrams.

content:
The Imrali delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) met with Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) Chair Devlet Bahçeli in Ankara on Thursday.


The meeting, held in Bahçeli’s office in the MHP parliamentary group section of the Turkish Parliament, was attended by DEM Party deputies Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, as well as lawyer Faik Özgür Erol. The meeting, which lasted approximately one hour, focused on the current state of the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the legal and political requirements of the present phase. The Imrali delegation had last met with Bahçeli on October 9.


The Imrali delegation had also held talks with Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek on Wednesday. According to the DEM Party’s press office, the meeting focused on the legal aspects of the ongoing process to resolve the Kurdish question, as well as conditions in prisons. Particular attention was given to the situation of sick prisoners and problems related to the execution of sentences.

title: Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court strengthens Baghdad’s control over the Kurdistan Region
content:
The dispute between the Iraqi central government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) over control of border crossings, energy resources and public revenues is intensifying. On Wednesday, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court issued a ruling on the constitutional division of powers between Baghdad and Hewlêr (Erbil), largely upholding the central government’s recent decisions. Meanwhile, Iraqi border guard forces have begun implementing the first measures.


On November 24, the government in Baghdad announced a series of decisions aimed at strengthening federal control over border crossings and the energy sector. These include closing officially unrecognized border crossings, transferring control of oil fields in territories disputed between Baghdad and Erbil to the federal Oil Ministry, and tightening oversight of oil transportation and exports.


The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) subsequently warned in a joint statement against interference with the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, describing any violation of those rights as a red line.


Baghdad rejects allegations of foreign interference


Amid the dispute, the media office of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi rejected allegations that the decisions had been made at the behest of other countries. It stated that all measures taken within Iraq’s internationally recognized borders were based on the country’s sovereign decision-making authority, constitutional powers and legal obligations.


“Our decisions are Iraq’s own, our will is national, and our points of reference are the Constitution and the law. Iraq’s overriding interests are the guiding principle for our positions and actions,” the Prime Minister’s office stated.


Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council also intervened in the dispute. It called on the central government, the regional government and all political forces to abide by the 2005 Constitution. At the same time, the council reiterated that the authority to interpret the Constitution rests exclusively with the Federal Supreme Court.


Regional government rejects the language of weapons and threats


The Kurdistan Regional Government discussed Baghdad’s decisions at a meeting. In a statement issued afterward, it emphasized its willingness to cooperate in combating corruption, oil smuggling and other illegal activities, but rejected the central government’s approach.


“We have always acted jointly and in coordination with the federal government to prevent and put an end to all illegal activities. However, we reject the language of weapons and threats,” the regional government stated.


the Kurdistan Regional Government stated that efforts to combat corruption and oil smuggling must extend across the entire territory of Iraq. At the same time, it announced legal action against individuals who undermine the constitutional status and interests of the Kurdistan Region and incite the population to conflict.


Federal Supreme Court reaffirms Baghdad’s extensive powers


In its ruling announced during a public session on November 25, the Federal Supreme Court clarified the constitutional powers of the central and regional governments in several key areas. The ruling is final and binding on all state institutions.


Citing Articles 109 and 110 of the Iraqi Constitution, the court ruled that the protection of international borders falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the central government. Accordingly, Baghdad has the authority to deploy federal security forces along the external borders of the Kurdistan Region and take appropriate security measures.


Furthermore, under Law No. 30 of 2016, federal authorities have extensive supervisory and regulatory powers over all border crossings in Iraq. However, customs inspections at border crossings in the Kurdistan Region must be carried out in coordination with the regional government. According to the court, the introduction of a unified nationwide electronic monitoring system for border crossings and customs offices also falls within Baghdad’s jurisdiction.


In customs and fiscal policy, the court also reaffirmed the central government’s authority to introduce uniform regulations nationwide, monitor compliance with them, and ensure that public revenues generated from taxes, fees and other non-oil sources are transferred to the state treasury.

author: Jessica Corbett
title: Armed Conflict Hinders Efforts to Contain Deadly Ebola Outbreak in the Congo
content:
The outbreak has killed more than 5,900 people, while fighting prevents health workers from reaching affected communities.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Three months after the United Nations senior Ebola coordinator warned that the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo was “growing exponentially,” government data showed Thursday that confirmed cases have topped 12,000 and left over 5,900 people dead.

The epidemic’s figures still rank behind the 2014-16 West African outbreak — which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 — but it is “the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll” from a decade ago, according to The Associated Press, which published a series of graphs demonstrating how fast-growing this crisis is.

Since the outbreak — caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus — was declared in May, it has spread to eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces. Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data recently revealed that just 15% of new cases come from contacts known to health authorities, and a Reuters analysis of satellite ⁠imagery found the death toll may be underestimated in two hard-hit areas.

Dozens of residents in eastern Congo say they have been unable to locate the bodies of relatives who died in the ongoing Ebola outbreak, while others say loved ones have been buried without their knowledge https://t.co/o5tKFPtRTS pic.twitter.com/PdCpb9Wa6R

The World Health Organization (WHO) said last Friday that “no new cases have been reported from Kenya or Nigeria; and no new country has reported confirmed cases,” but “the high-level transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for continued need for readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection, and coordinated preparedness and response measures.”

The response in the DRC has been hindered by lack of community trust in authorities, poor infrastructure, and armed conflict, particularly between the army and the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) — one of dozens of militant groups in the resource-rich eastern part of the country, and led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted⁠ of conscripting child soldiers by the International Criminal Court in 2012.

Summarizing remarks from Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO’s incident manager in the DRC, the AP reported Wednesday that “the fighting between the army and rebel groups has prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus, and left some treatment centers with fewer staff.”

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.

WHO temporarily moved its Mongbwalu team and partner staff to Bunia after fighting disrupted road access, Smallwood said. Mongbwalu, a mining town northwest of Bunia, is where the outbreak was first detected in May.

The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) said Wednesday that “the security situation has deteriorated significantly in several localities” due to clashes between DRC forces and the CRP, and Bangladeshi peacekeepers helped with that evacuation of health workers.

UN peacekeepers faced “significant logistical challenges,” including “difficult terrain, poor road conditions, and the fragile state of a wooden bridge,” before they reached the healthcare workers, who were evacuated by air to Bunia, MONUSCO noted.

“These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement,” the mission said. “This intervention is part of MONUSCO’s support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence.”

author: Mark Blackburn
title: Resolutions at upcoming UCP convention calls land acknowledgements ‘humiliating’ and ‘politically compelled’
content:
As members of the ruling United Conservative Party (UCP) in Alberta get set to meet in Calgary, two resolutions dealing with land acknowledgements and land claims is getting pushback from the Blackfoot Confederacy.

According to the UCP resolution page, one resolution put forward by the riding associations in Highwood, Edmonton-Gold Bar, Innisfail-Sylvan Lake, Sherwood Park, CalgarySouth East, calls for the province to end land acknowledgements.

“Publicly funded institutions should promote approaches to shared history and civic unity that are inclusive of all Albertans and grounded in accuracy, respect, and common purpose,” resolution WG-2026-P-27 says.

“Many Albertans view these statements as performative, politically compelled, and unnecessarily humiliating, particularly when citizens are repeatedly reminded that they are “guests” or “settlers” in their own country regardless of how many generations their families have lived, worked, and contributed to Alberta.

The resolution adds that land acknowledgements also foster “resentment and social division.”

The second is listed as a “policy resolution” put forward by the Edmonton-Gold Bar riding association that “supports Alberta using all available legal avenues to challenge federal land claims, including Indigenous claims that may infringe on private property owners and their rights.

It calls for the province to resolve “disputes through the courts and constitutional processes to protect Alberta’s interests while ensuring clarity, stability, and accountability in land governance.

“Albertans must take a stand against the federal government’s plan to ‘protect’ thirty percent of land and water in the country. This is a direct threat to private land ownership,” it says.

On Thursday, the Blackfoot Confederacy issued a statement “expressing strong opposition” to the resolutions.

“Both resolutions raise significant concerns regarding Treaty recognition, the protection of First Nations rights and the government-to-government relationship between Blackfoot Nations and the Province of Alberta,” the statement said.

“Blackfoot Confederacy Chiefs reject efforts to characterize First Nations land claims as a threat to private property ownership. Many of these claims arise from the Crown’s failure to honour Treaty promises and fulfill its fiduciary obligations to First Nations. These claims seek to remedy historical injustices and address outstanding legal obligations of the Crown.”

Relations between First Nations in the province and the provincial government led by Premier Danielle Smith have been stone-cold since the province allowed a vote on sovereignty in Canada. The province is also asking the courts to quash a constitutional challenge launched by several First Nations over the sovereignty act.

The Siksikaitsitapi Blackfoot Confederacy is made up of Kainai, Siksika, Blackfoot, Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni Nations.

The UCP convention starts Nov. 27 and runs through the weekend.

Before moving to become the APTN News social media producer, Mark was the executive producer for the news in eastern Canada. Before starting with APTN in 2009, Mark worked at CBC Radio and Television in Newfoundland and Labrador and Ottawa.

author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
title: Genocide, Displacement and Malnutrition Threaten Pregnancies in Gaza
content:
Doctors in Gaza report rising congenital abnormalities as pregnant women face exposure to bombs and toxic substances.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Faiqa al-Arini, 33, gave birth to her first child on October 19 at Al-Awda Maternity Hospital in central Gaza. She was forced to deliver early, at the beginning of her ninth month of pregnancy, after developing high blood pressure.

Al-Arini gave birth to a baby girl through a cesarean section. They named her Nour. After the delivery, the new mother remained in the intensive care unit while the newborn was transferred to the neonatal ward. Al-Arini did not see her daughter at all that first day.

Whenever she asked, “Where is my baby?” the nurses and her family members reassured her that the infant was in the neonatal ward.

The following day, Al-Arini began to feel that something was wrong. She recalled not hearing her daughter cry when she was born. She started questioning her family and was determined to get up and look for the baby herself if the nurses did not bring her. Eventually, her husband, Muhammad Abdel Jawad, 37, confronted her with the news.

“You know it is better to hear this from us than from someone else,” he told her. “Our baby has a congenital deformity. She was born without hands.”

Abdel Jawad had seen his daughter immediately after her birth. When he had asked the doctors about the main factors that could cause such abnormalities in newborn babies, the doctors pointed to the dust from missiles, toxic chemicals, and the unhealthy environment where displaced people are forced to live across the Gaza Strip.

According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the number of recorded congenital abnormalities among newborns has been increasing year after year. The ministry confirmed that 260 cases of congenital abnormalities had been recorded among newborns by the end of September 2026, compared with 184 cases in 2022. The number of recorded cases reached 322 in 2025, representing a 75% increase over a three year time period. However, the Ministry of Health says these figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital abnormalities among newborns or determine their causes.

Ashraf Qeshta, an obstetrics and gynecology specialist at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, says that the number of cases of miscarriage and congenital abnormalities among pregnant women has exceeded normal levels. He attributes this to several factors produced by the genocide, most notably the inhalation of toxic gases, exposure to missile remnants, living in an unhealthy environment, malnutrition, and other hardships imposed by war.

“We are seeing a significant number of congenital abnormalities. For example, babies are being born without skulls, others without limbs, and some with serious health problems, such as non-functioning or damaged kidneys, or heart defects,” Qeshta told Mondoweiss.

Even in cases where doctors believe that the congenital abnormality is caused by exposure to bombs and toxic substances, proving this requires advanced medical testing, sophisticated equipment, and qualified specialists. According to Qeshta, these are precisely the resources the Ministry of Health lacks, making it difficult to investigate and establish the different causes with scientific certainty.

Al-Arini said her pregnancy was extremely difficult. She was repeatedly displaced from one place to another and faced severe economic hardship, including famine, as her pregnancy began during the final months of the famine in 2025.

“Like all women in the Gaza Strip, we live under the same conditions,” al-Arini said. “We are displaced, we go hungry, we live in fear, and we narrowly escape death almost every day. Bombs and missiles explode beside us, and shrapnel flies over us. This is the reality for all women in Gaza.”

“But the effects of all these things are now beginning to show on us. I am happy that I gave birth to a girl, and I love her very much. I had indeed wished she would be born with limbs, but their absence does not make her any less my daughter, nor does it change anything about my feelings toward her. However, it makes me think deeply about the condition of our homeland, and about how even giving birth here has become fraught with danger. A baby can be born with congenital abnormalities because of the conditions we are living in,” she said.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Proteger el agua y celebrar la vida: "Somos el territorio, somos el cerro Famatina"
content:
Por Graciela Castañeda

*


Este libro es parte de la historia viva de un movimiento que traspasa los límites provinciales, recorre el país y se expande por el mundo, por cada lugar de nuestra Madre Tierra habitado por personas que trabajan, estudian y miran su entorno como algo más que una posesión material; personas amigadas con la naturaleza, que parten de la empatía, la solidaridad, la compasión y el amor. Comunidades conscientes que el territorio nos fue dado para vivir en armonía, honrando a la Pachamama.


Desde hace años que pensamos en publicar un libro que recogiera nuestra historia, un material colectivo, pleno de sensibilidad, dignidad y alegría. Un libro donde se pudieran leer las historias de quienes participaron de esta lucha, donde cada texto mantuviera la esencia, el sentir y el parecer de quien lo escribiera.


En el 2025, a punto de cumplir los 20 años en defensa de nuestro Cerro Famatina, decidimos poner manos a la obra y concretar este libro. Se invitó a los defensores y las defensoras del territorio a una construcción colectiva, popular, libre y abierta que rescatara la historia viva de esta pueblada, la invitación dirigida a las y los protagonistas era clara: plasmar sus vivencias, expresar su sentir y su hacer en estos años de lucha incansable y sostenida.


Fue una propuesta nacida del amor, la gratitud y la esperanza, guida por el deseo de unión comunitaria, que permitiera superar el individualismo y nos uniera detrás de objetivos comunes y propios: el agua para los pueblos desde la defensa del territorio que nos legaron nuestros antepasados

.

 Aquellas y aquellos que tan sabiamente comprendían que no eran dueños de la Tierra, que nuestro pasar es efímero pero la Pacha queda y tiene que seguir siendo el hogar de las nuevas generaciones.


Fue así que, convocadas las voces a la escritura, primero fue el silencio y luego, tímidamente, aparecieron los primeros escritos, hasta que los textos nos inundaron. Allí estaba la escritura hilada en relatos, en poesías y en cantares que hoy son parte de este libro: "Wamatinag madre del agua". Un escrito que nos trae las historias de todas y todos los que aceptaron el desafío de poner en palabras una parte significativa de sus vidas.


Aquí están las voces de quienes recuerdan sus infancias cuando partían con sus madres y sus padres a los cortes de rutas, a las asambleas; o cuando jugaban, cantaban y reían en los refugios creciendo juntos y hoy se reconocen en hermandad.


Están quienes con joven ímpetu sentían que algo tenían que aportar a esta causa, tal vez pensándolo solo como una aventura o con la típica rebeldía de la adolescencia, pero luego se dieron cuenta que estaban plantando los cimientos de algo más grande, que lejos estaba de pasar a ser una anécdota de juventud.


Los adultos, que traían consigo un amplio bagaje desde sus profesiones y haceres —agricultores, docentes, artesanos, profesionales, trabajadores— fueron abriendo camino, promoviendo las reuniones, leyendo e investigando mucho para informar a la comunidad también cuentan sus experiencias.


También están las historias de los mayores que, en forma individual o en escritura colectiva, rescatan sus vivencias. Sintieron el llamado de sus ancestros, de su cerro, del agua que da vida y es indispensable para proveer los frutos de la Madre Tierra. Al hacer oír sus voces sintieron que su lucha no fue en vano y renovaron su esperanza. Y, más aún, están también las historias de quienes ya partieron, pero dejaron sus huellas en acciones y en palabras.


Con esa infancia, esa juventud, acompañada por esos y esas adultas conscientes, nacieron las asambleas que también tienen su espacio en el libro. Contamos, además, con el aporte de investigadoras e investigadores que nos acercaron sus trabajos para que fueran parte del libro, nutriéndolo con el saber académico, ese que está a favor de la vida.


Al leer y releer cada página nos inunda la emoción, se renueva la esperanza pues somos conscientes de que, aunque en nuestro entorno parezca avanzar el caos, "el Famatina no se toca" es grito sagrado que nos congrega y nos hace fuertes.


A no dudarlo, el eco de "Wamatinag madre del agua" llegará lejos, se convertirá en sinónimo de nuestra frase insignia porque es canto de lucha esperanzada, amorosa voz que retumba en nuestros corazones al sentirnos comunidad y afianza nuestro sentir de que somos parte del territorio que habitamos.


*Integrante de las asambleas riojanas.

author: Software Architektur im Stream
title: Fishbowl 'Friction is a Feature: Navigating the Inevitable Tensions of Software Architecture'
content:
Software architecture doesn’t live in diagrams – it’s forged in the gaps between teams, technologies, timelines, and trade-offs. Today, that landscape is shifting fast. LLMs and agentic workflows promise to erase friction – but often amplify it through toolchain sprawl, quality drift, and shifting accountability.


Yet friction is a signal. The most resilient teams channel it through shared understanding, recognizing that we’re shaping socio-technical systems – aligned through collaborative modelling woven into everyday decisions across architects, developers, QA, analysts, etc.


This fishbowl session confronts the reality behind the hype: how AI-generated code collides with architectural rigor, QA concerns, and production constraints. We’ll examine classic tensions (Conway’s Law, legacy vs. innovation, business urgency vs. technical debt) alongside new ones (toolchain sprawl, quality drift, over-reliance on generative AI).


As a conference attendee, you’re invited to step into the circle and challenge assumptions. Whether you’re an architect, engineer, QA lead, or system analyst, you’ll walk away with a refreshed perspective of timeless insights – and the courage to question them when it matters most.


This is a live stream from iSAQB Software Architecture Gathering.

author: Esperanza
title: PANGUIPULLI REÚNE A PUEBLOS INDÍGENAS DE AMÉRICA LATINA EN EL 2° CONGRESO INTERNACIONAL DE TERRITORIOS INDÍGENAS DE CONSERVACIÓN
content:
Por Comunicaciones Füta Mawiza


El encuentro, que se extenderá hasta el viernes 27 de noviembre, convoca a representantes de pueblos originarios, organizaciones territoriales y redes internacionales de conservación para compartir estrategias de gobernanza, defensa y conservación biocultural de los Territorios de Vida.


Comenzó en Panguipulli el

2° Congreso Internacional de Territorios Indígenas de Conservación

, que se extenderá hasta el viernes 27 de noviembre bajo el lema

“Estrategias y desafíos para el resguardo de los Territorios de Vida”

. Organizado por la Iniciativa Füta Mawiza, el encuentro reúne a representantes de pueblos indígenas, organizaciones territoriales, redes internacionales y experiencias comunitarias de conservación de distintos países de América Latina. Entre las articulaciones convocadas se encuentran la Red Territorios de Vida TICCA Latinoamérica, la Red de Mujeres Originarias por la Defensa del Mar (RDM), la Identidad Territorial Lafkenche (ITL) y la Federación por la Autodeterminación de los Pueblos Indígenas (FAPI), de Paraguay, junto a diversas organizaciones y experiencias locales impulsadas por pueblos originarios en lo que hoy conocemos como Chile y otros territorios de Abya Yala (América Latina).


Esta segunda versión da continuidad al proceso de articulación iniciado en septiembre de 2024 en Kurarewe, reafirmando el compromiso de fortalecer las estrategias de los pueblos indígenas y sus alianzas para el resguardo, la gobernanza y la conservación biocultural de los Territorios de Vida. 


El propósito es avanzar desde el ejercicio de los derechos colectivos, el reconocimiento de los conocimientos, las instituciones y las formas propias de relacionarse con la naturaleza. 


En este contexto, el congreso constituye un espacio de intercambio político y territorial frente a los desafíos que enfrentan los territorios, particularmente ante las presiones extractivas, la crisis climática y las distintas amenazas que afectan la continuidad de los sistemas de vida.


 Durante tres jornadas, el programa contempla paneles internacionales sobre derechos e incidencia política, gobernanza territorial, reconocimiento y registro de los Territorios de Vida, soberanía de datos, cartografía participativa y monitoreo biocultural. También se abordarán experiencias de mujeres indígenas defensoras de la vida, investigación propia, metodologías interculturales y transmisión intergeneracional de conocimientos. Entre las actividades destacan las salidas a terreno que se desarrollarán el jueves 26 para conocer experiencias de conservación y resguardo en el territorio mapuche de Panguipulli, además de muestras de cine indígena, espacios de conversación y actividades culturales.


La participación de representantes de Argentina, Paraguay, Guatemala, Panamá, México, El Salvador, Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Perú y Chile permitirá poner en diálogo distintas experiencias y fortalecer redes de colaboración entre pueblos y organizaciones de la región.


2° Congreso Internacional de Territorios Indígenas de Conservación

. Panguipulli 2026.


Pero ¿qué entendemos por Territorios de Vida? Esta noción reconoce la estrecha relación que existe entre un pueblo indígena y un territorio, área o conjunto de bienes comunes, cuando a ese vínculo se suma una gobernanza local efectiva y la conservación de la naturaleza. No se trata únicamente de espacios naturales que requieren protección, sino de territorios habitados, construidos y cuidados a través de generaciones, donde se preservan memorias, conocimientos, normas propias y formas de organización. Desde esta perspectiva, los pueblos indígenas no son solamente actores vinculados a la conservación, sino protagonistas de su definición, gobernanza y continuidad. El congreso busca contribuir a visibilizar estas experiencias y proyectar acuerdos y estrategias conjuntas que fortalezcan el reconocimiento de los derechos colectivos y el protagonismo de los pueblos en el resguardo de la biodiversidad y la vida.


De lo que hoy es Chile están presentes personas y organizaciones de:

Kawésqar Waes, Isla de las Guaitecas, Chonchi y Ancud en Chiloé, Walaywé, Cochamó, Purranque, Puyehue de Osorno a la cordillera, San Juan de la Costa, Lago Ranco, Valdivia, Kurarewe, Mehuín, Temuco, Trewako, Lago Budi, Lonquimay, Galvarino, Cañete, Quintero, Freirina, Caleta Chañaral de Aceituno, San Pedro de Atacama, Toconao y Arica.

author: Julia Conley
title: The FCC Approves SpaceX’s Plan for 1 Million Space Satellites
content:
Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Federal Communications Commission’s approval on Wednesday of SpaceX’s plan to deploy one million orbital data center satellites into space by 2040 was not “just irresponsible,” said one environmental advocate.

“It’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.”

Whitehouse was among the critics who noted that the approval had been granted without an environmental review, which is required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the deployment of one million “orbital space modules,” which SpaceX has said would form a new data center constellation called “Starmind,” would open “a bold new frontier” and allow the U.S. to lead “the world into the era of super intelligence.”

The satellites would process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth, according to SpaceX, the space exploration company led by Republican megadonor Elon Musk.

The environmental legal group Earthjustice said they also risk “changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky,” and denounced the commission for releasing the decision as families across the U.S. were preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving.

“Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”

The number of satellites in space has already grown rapidly in the last several years, with 15,000 satellites in orbit in 2026 — up from 1,400 just over a decade ago.

Satellites cause emissions as they are placed in space through rocket launches, and other environmental impacts include debris from potential collisions — especially as the number of satellites grows — degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution.

Astronomers spoke out against SpaceX’s plan earlier this year, saying it would prevent scientists from studying the night sky with modern telescopes, as well as disrupting ecosystems and humans’ biological clocks due to extreme light pollution.

On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s licensing of Musk’s plan.

“The proposed constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” said the group. “The intended and unintended radio emissions from a constellation of such unprecedented size would imperil radio astronomy research, and the waste heat generated by the data centers would produce a thermal signature that would increase the infrared background of the sky and threaten the efficacy of sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research. In addition, atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy.”

“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” the AAS added.

Earthjustice emphasized that the approval came as Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the permitting reform bill that would prevent future administrations from revoking licenses for projects including data centers and would block courts from enforcing environmental review laws …
